items.title: Quantum-resistant signing on AWS, Part 2: Enforce your ML-DSA algorithm policy with SCPs and IAM
items.summary: You want to set a cryptographic algorithm policy and stop non-compliant choices from being made in your Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment. This post shows you how. As you adopt post-quantum cryptography, one of the first decisions you face is which algorithms and parameter sets fit your business needs, balancing security against signature size, key size, and performance. Your cloud environment’s job is to let you express that decision and enforce it consistently, so an approved choice stays fully usable while an excluded one cannot be introduced. This post works through one concrete example on AWS: taking an organization’s cryptographic algorithm policy and turning it into preventive and detective controls. The same patterns apply to whatever your approved set is today and whatever it becomes as standards evolve. This post is Part 2 of a two-part series on quantum-resistant signing on AWS. Part 1, Build a software supply chain with ML-DSA , is for builders and constructs an end-to-end ML-DSA signing pipeline for binaries, container images, and software bills of materials. This part is for the security, governance, and compliance teams who decide which algorithms that pipeline, and everything else in the organization, is permitted to use, and who need that decision enforced. AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) supports the ML-DSA digital signature scheme (FIPS 204) through three parameter sets, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87, targeting NIST security categories 2, 3, and 5. All three are strong, standardized choices. Each one trades signature size, key size, and speed against security margin, the amount of cryptographic strength a parameter set holds in reserve above its target security category. ML-DSA-44 is the most compact and fastest. ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 carry a larger security margin, which is what you want for signatures that must stay trustworthy over a long lifetime. Throughout this post, the examples use the same example policy: an organization that has standardized on ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 and wants ML-DSA-44 kept out of its approved set. That is a standardization decision, not a judgment that ML-DSA-44 is insecure (see the following note). Wherever you see ML-DSA-44 in the controls that follow, read it as the variant your policy doesn’t include; the mechanics are identical for any allow/deny split you choose. The approved set here is also the one the Part 1 architecture deploys: ML-DSA-87 for the root certificate authority (CA) and ML-DSA-65 for the subordinate CA and the code-signing key. Part 1 makes the choice; this post makes it stick. Note : ML-DSA-44 is a valid choice. ML-DSA-44 is a fully NIST-standardized parameter set (FIPS 204) at NIST security category 2, which targets roughly 128-bit-class classical security (category 2 is benchmarked against the collision resistance of SHA-256). It produces the smallest signatures and public keys of the three variants (a 1312-byte public key and 2420-byte signature) and is the fastest to sign and verify, which makes it a strong fit for constrained devices, high-volume signing, and bandwidth- or storage-sensitive workloads. You would choose ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87 instead to gain extra security margin for long-lived signatures or to align with an internal standard, not because ML-DSA-44 is weak. What success looks like The approved variants (ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 in the example) remain fully usable throughout. What you want to rule out is the introduction of a variant outside the policy (here, ML-DSA-44). Concretely, within the AWS service surfaces in scope, principals shouldn’t be able to: Create ML-DSA-44 key material Use existing ML-DSA-44 keys for signing or verification Stand up private certificate authorities (CAs) that would introduce ML-DSA-44. And any drift from those settings should be detected. Scope and limitations These controls operate on AWS service APIs, principally AWS KMS, AWS Private Certificate Authorit y (AWS Private CA), and AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) . They don’t and can’t govern cryptography that runs on compute you control. For example, OpenSSL or an application might perform ML-DSA-44 signing on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, container, or AWS Lambda function. Protocol-level use, such as OpenSSH’s hybrid ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 public key authentication, is also outside the reach of Service control policies (SCPs) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and isn’t addressed in this post. Certificate material brought in through acm:ImportCertificate or iam:UploadServerCertificate is also not algorithm-aware (see the Private CA section). Other TLS-terminating or signing services (for example Amazon CloudFront and Amazon API Gateway ) and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere aren’t covered in this post and should be assessed separately. ( Part 1 of this series uses IAM Roles Anywhere with ML-DSA certificates; controls for that service are out of scope here.) These controls are intended to be applied as defense in depth . You can apply all of them or only a subset, depending on how prescriptive you want to be: A blanket SCP at the organization root prevents member accounts from creating or using ML-DSA-44 keys. (SCPs don’t apply to the management account, so workloads there aren’t restricted.) An SCP at a production organizational unit (OU) restricts keys only in production accounts. If you need flexibility inside an account, use IAM permission boundaries instead of account-wide settings enforced through an SCP. Choose the combination that matches your operating model. The policy examples here are written to apply across all AWS Regions. If you need to scope a control to specific Regions, add an aws:RequestedRegion condition. The policies in this post are illustrative starting points. Authoring, validating, and maintaining the specific SCPs, IAM policies, and permission boundaries for your environment is your responsibility. Test all policies in a non-production environment before deployment and adjust example values (such as policy names and key Amazon Resource Names (ARNs)) to match your organization’s approved standards. A note on cryptographic agility Your algorithm policy isn’t fixed forever, and these controls shouldn’t be either. The point of expressing the policy as AWS controls is that you can revise it as your needs and the relevant standards change, tightening, loosening, or swapping the approved set without re-architecting. Treat the examples here as a template you adjust to whatever your current policy is. A deny-based control that names specific algorithms is, in effect, an allow-list of everything it does not name. The risk is default-allow: any parameter set you have not explicitly denied is permitted, so a newly introduced variant, including one you have not yet evaluated, becomes usable until you notice it and add it to the deny list. Deprecation of an already-approved variant is easy to handle in this model, because you simply add the deprecated variant to the deny list. What the model does not catch on its own is the arrival of something new. Review these controls periodically and pair the deny-list with detection so a variant outside your policy surfaces quickly rather than waiting to be discovered. The alternative is to write the condition against the approved set rather than the excluded one. A Deny that uses StringNotEquals with a list of approved key specs fires when the request’s key spec matches none of them, so a new or not-yet-evaluated variant is blocked by default until you add it. That closes the default-allow gap, at the cost of a policy update before anyone can use a newly approved variant. The family-level SCP in Part 1 of this series takes this shape: it denies creation of any signing key whose key spec isn’t ML_DSA_* . The examples in this post take the other shape and name the excluded variant, so that approved variants stay usable without a policy change. Both are valid. Choose based on whether you would rather block something new first and approve it later, or notice it first and decide then. { "Sid": "OnlyApprovedMlDsaVariants", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_*" }, "StringNotEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": ["ML_DSA_65", "ML_DSA_87"] } } } The StringLike clause scopes the statement to ML-DSA key specs so it doesn’t affect other key types; the StringNotEquals clause denies any ML-DSA variant outside the approved list. Just as algorithms and key sizes will be introduced over time, or move from approved to unapproved, so will AWS service operations. The set of operations through which an ML-DSA-44 key can be used today (AWS KMS Sign , Verify , and GetPublicKey ) reflects current service capabilities and might expand as AWS releases new features. If your policy is to block use in addition to creation, you should periodically review the list of operations you restrict, because services evolve over time. Background: Key spec compared to signing algorithm AWS KMS support for ML-DSA introduces three key specs— ML_DSA_44 , ML_DSA_65 , and ML_DSA_87 —that all use a single post-quantum signing algorithm: ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 . This distinction drives which controls are effective. kms:KeySpec : Reflects the KeySpec property of the key. It’s evaluated both on CreateKey (the requested key spec) and on AWS KMS key resource operations that act on a specific key, including Sign , Verify , and GetPublicKey . This makes kms:KeySpec a reliable lever for both preventing creation of ML-DSA-44 keys and restricting use of existing ones, because it can single out ML_DSA_44 from ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87 . kms:SigningAlgorithm : Reflects the signing algorithm supplied on Sign and Verify , which is ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 for all three variants. It therefore can’t distinguish ML-DSA-44 from the approved variants and shouldn’t be used for this purpose. The practical consequence: for keys held in AWS KMS, preventing ML-DSA-44 key material from being created is the most robust single control. If no ML-DSA-44 KMS keys exist, none can be used for signing through AWS KMS and none can become the subject key of a certificate. CA keys and TLS server keys are separate material: AWS Private CA generates and holds a CA’s key pair in its own HSMs, and ACM-issued, imported, or uploaded TLS certificates carry their own keys, so those surfaces are governed by the AWS Private CA and certificate controls later in this post. Where ML-DSA-44 KMS keys already exist, their use can additionally be restricted with kms:KeySpec . Organization and account-level blocking using SCPs SCPs can be applied at the organization root or to a specific OU to restrict ML-DSA-44. Placement determines the effective scope: it applies organization-wide when attached at the root; attached to an OU, it applies to the accounts within that OU. An SCP is the broadest-scope preventive control available. Note that SCPs apply to member accounts and OUs but not to the organization’s management account, so avoid running ML-DSA-44-capable workloads in the management account, where an SCP will not restrict them. The following example SCP denies both the creation of ML-DSA-44 keys ( kms:CreateKey ) and their use ( kms:Sign , kms:Verify , kms:GetPublicKey ), matching on the ML_DSA_44 key spec in each case. The creation deny stops new keys from being created; the usage deny covers keys that already exist, whether created before the SCP was attached or living in an account that later joins the OU, because kms:KeySpec is also evaluated at request time on those usage operations.SCPs are guardrails: a Deny in an SCP can’t be overridden by any IAM policy within member accounts. Attach the following SCP at the organization root (or relevant OU): { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } }, { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyUsage", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": [ "kms:Sign", "kms:Verify", "kms:GetPublicKey" ], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] } Scope the usage deny to the three key-spec-aware actions. Limit the use of Deny to kms:Sign , kms:Verify , and kms:GetPublicKey (testing confirmed kms:KeySpec is evaluated on all three). Avoid a blanket kms:* : a wildcard that would also catch management operations such as DescribeKey , DisableKey , and ScheduleKeyDeletion , which you need to inspect or clean up those same keys, effectively locking you out of managing the keys you’re trying to remove. If you use multi-Region keys, also add kms:ReplicateKey to the creation deny: replicating an ML-DSA-44 primary key creates a new ML-DSA-44 key in another Region, and kms:KeySpec is evaluated on ReplicateKey as well. Combining with a family-level guardrail. This SCP governs which ML-DSA parameter set is allowed; it says nothing about RSA or ECDSA. Part 1 of this series includes a complementary SCP that denies creation of any signing key whose key spec isn’t ML-DSA. Attached together, they require every new signing key to be ML-DSA and to be an approved variant. Operational considerations. A blanket Deny at the organization root is the strongest control but has trade-offs: it removes any ability to create ML-DSA-44 keys anywhere in scope, with no exception path, which can block legitimate testing and might cause infrastructure as code (IaC) or pipeline runs that attempt ML-DSA-44 creation to fail. To preserve flexibility, consider scoping the Deny to a production OU and using IAM permission boundaries (see the following section) in build and non-production accounts. What the caller sees. When an SCP denies a request, the caller receives an AccessDenied error indicating an explicit deny in a service control policy. For same-account and same-organization requests, the error includes the type of the denying policy and, as the enhanced error messages roll out across services, its ARN. The error doesn’t expose the SCP policy contents, and the user being blocked often can’t see the SCPs applied to their environment. Document the SCP ARN and its purpose internally so support teams can map an AccessDenied quickly. Prevent ML-DSA-44 key creation in AWS KMS (principal-level) The following IAM policy blocks ML-DSA-44 at the principal level. It is the identity-based counterpart to the SCP shown earlier, useful when you want per-account or per-role control rather than an organization-wide guardrail. Attach it to the IAM role or user you want to constrain. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] } Key

Protocol-level use, such as OpenSSH’s hybrid ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 public key authentication, is also outside the reach of Service control policies (SCPs) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and isn’t addressed in this post.

Certificate material brought in through acm:ImportCertificate or iam:UploadServerCertificate is also not algorithm-aware (see the Private CA section). Other TLS-terminating or signing services (for example Amazon CloudFront and Amazon API Gateway) and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere aren’t covered in this post and should be assessed separately. (Part 1 of this series uses IAM Roles Anywhere with ML-DSA certificates; controls for that service are out of scope here.)

These controls are intended to be applied as defense in depth. You can apply all of them or only a subset, depending on how prescriptive you want to be:

  • A blanket SCP at the organization root prevents member accounts from creating or using ML-DSA-44 keys. (SCPs don’t apply to the management account, so workloads there aren’t restricted.)
  • An SCP at a production organizational unit (OU) restricts keys only in production accounts.
  • If you need flexibility inside an account, use IAM permission boundaries instead of account-wide settings enforced through an SCP.

Choose the combination that matches your operating model. The policy examples here are written to apply across all AWS Regions. If you need to scope a control to specific Regions, add an aws:RequestedRegion condition.

The policies in this post are illustrative starting points. Authoring, validating, and maintaining the specific SCPs, IAM policies, and permission boundaries for your environment is your responsibility. Test all policies in a non-production environment before deployment and adjust example values (such as policy names and key Amazon Resource Names (ARNs)) to match your organization’s approved standards.

A note on cryptographic agility

Your algorithm policy isn’t fixed forever, and these controls shouldn’t be either. The point of expressing the policy as AWS controls is that you can revise it as your needs and the relevant standards change, tightening, loosening, or swapping the approved set without re-architecting. Treat the examples here as a template you adjust to whatever your current policy is.

A deny-based control that names specific algorithms is, in effect, an allow-list of everything it does not name. The risk is default-allow: any parameter set you have not explicitly denied is permitted, so a newly introduced variant, including one you have not yet evaluated, becomes usable until you notice it and add it to the deny list. Deprecation of an already-approved variant is easy to handle in this model, because you simply add the deprecated variant to the deny list. What the model does not catch on its own is the arrival of something new. Review these controls periodically and pair the deny-list with detection so a variant outside your policy surfaces quickly rather than waiting to be discovered.

The alternative is to write the condition against the approved set rather than the excluded one. A Deny that uses StringNotEquals with a list of approved key specs fires when the request’s key spec matches none of them, so a new or not-yet-evaluated variant is blocked by default until you add it. That closes the default-allow gap, at the cost of a policy update before anyone can use a newly approved variant. The family-level SCP in Part 1 of this series takes this shape: it denies creation of any signing key whose key spec isn’t ML_DSA_*. The examples in this post take the other shape and name the excluded variant, so that approved variants stay usable without a policy change. Both are valid. Choose based on whether you would rather block something new first and approve it later, or notice it first and decide then.

{
  "Sid": "OnlyApprovedMlDsaVariants",
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Action": "kms:CreateKey",
  "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": {
    "StringLike": {
      "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_*"
    },
    "StringNotEquals": {
      "kms:KeySpec": ["ML_DSA_65", "ML_DSA_87"]
    }
  }
}

The StringLike clause scopes the statement to ML-DSA key specs so it doesn’t affect other key types; the StringNotEquals clause denies any ML-DSA variant outside the approved list.

Just as algorithms and key sizes will be introduced over time, or move from approved to unapproved, so will AWS service operations. The set of operations through which an ML-DSA-44 key can be used today (AWS KMS Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey) reflects current service capabilities and might expand as AWS releases new features. If your policy is to block use in addition to creation, you should periodically review the list of operations you restrict, because services evolve over time.

Background: Key spec compared to signing algorithm

AWS KMS support for ML-DSA introduces three key specs—ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87—that all use a single post-quantum signing algorithm: ML_DSA_SHAKE_256. This distinction drives which controls are effective.

  1. kms:KeySpec: Reflects the KeySpec property of the key. It’s evaluated both on CreateKey (the requested key spec) and on AWS KMS key resource operations that act on a specific key, including Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey. This makes kms:KeySpec a reliable lever for both preventing creation of ML-DSA-44 keys and restricting use of existing ones, because it can single out ML_DSA_44 from ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87.
  2. kms:SigningAlgorithm: Reflects the signing algorithm supplied on Sign and Verify, which is ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 for all three variants. It therefore can’t distinguish ML-DSA-44 from the approved variants and shouldn’t be used for this purpose.

The practical consequence: for keys held in AWS KMS, preventing ML-DSA-44 key material from being created is the most robust single control. If no ML-DSA-44 KMS keys exist, none can be used for signing through AWS KMS and none can become the subject key of a certificate. CA keys and TLS server keys are separate material: AWS Private CA generates and holds a CA’s key pair in its own HSMs, and ACM-issued, imported, or uploaded TLS certificates carry their own keys, so those surfaces are governed by the AWS Private CA and certificate controls later in this post. Where ML-DSA-44 KMS keys already exist, their use can additionally be restricted with kms:KeySpec.

Organization and account-level blocking using SCPs

SCPs can be applied at the organization root or to a specific OU to restrict ML-DSA-44. Placement determines the effective scope: it applies organization-wide when attached at the root; attached to an OU, it applies to the accounts within that OU. An SCP is the broadest-scope preventive control available.

Note that SCPs apply to member accounts and OUs but not to the organization’s management account, so avoid running ML-DSA-44-capable workloads in the management account, where an SCP will not restrict them.

The following example SCP denies both the creation of ML-DSA-44 keys (kms:CreateKey) and their use (kms:Sign, kms:Verify, kms:GetPublicKey), matching on the ML_DSA_44 key spec in each case. The creation deny stops new keys from being created; the usage deny covers keys that already exist, whether created before the SCP was attached or living in an account that later joins the OU, because kms:KeySpec is also evaluated at request time on those usage operations.SCPs are guardrails: a Deny in an SCP can’t be overridden by any IAM policy within member accounts.

Attach the following SCP at the organization root (or relevant OU):

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "kms:CreateKey",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyUsage",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "kms:Sign",
        "kms:Verify",
        "kms:GetPublicKey"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Scope the usage deny to the three key-spec-aware actions. Limit the use of Deny to kms:Sign, kms:Verify, and kms:GetPublicKey (testing confirmed kms:KeySpec is evaluated on all three). Avoid a blanket kms:*: a wildcard that would also catch management operations such as DescribeKey, DisableKey, and ScheduleKeyDeletion, which you need to inspect or clean up those same keys, effectively locking you out of managing the keys you’re trying to remove. If you use multi-Region keys, also add kms:ReplicateKey to the creation deny: replicating an ML-DSA-44 primary key creates a new ML-DSA-44 key in another Region, and kms:KeySpec is evaluated on ReplicateKey as well.

Combining with a family-level guardrail. This SCP governs which ML-DSA parameter set is allowed; it says nothing about RSA or ECDSA. Part 1 of this series includes a complementary SCP that denies creation of any signing key whose key spec isn’t ML-DSA. Attached together, they require every new signing key to be ML-DSA and to be an approved variant.

Operational considerations. A blanket Deny at the organization root is the strongest control but has trade-offs: it removes any ability to create ML-DSA-44 keys anywhere in scope, with no exception path, which can block legitimate testing and might cause infrastructure as code (IaC) or pipeline runs that attempt ML-DSA-44 creation to fail. To preserve flexibility, consider scoping the Deny to a production OU and using IAM permission boundaries (see the following section) in build and non-production accounts.

What the caller sees. When an SCP denies a request, the caller receives an AccessDenied error indicating an explicit deny in a service control policy. For same-account and same-organization requests, the error includes the type of the denying policy and, as the enhanced error messages roll out across services, its ARN. The error doesn’t expose the SCP policy contents, and the user being blocked often can’t see the SCPs applied to their environment. Document the SCP ARN and its purpose internally so support teams can map an AccessDenied quickly.

Prevent ML-DSA-44 key creation in AWS KMS (principal-level)

The following IAM policy blocks ML-DSA-44 at the principal level. It is the identity-based counterpart to the SCP shown earlier, useful when you want per-account or per-role control rather than an organization-wide guardrail. Attach it to the IAM role or user you want to constrain.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "kms:CreateKey",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Key points:
  1. The condition value is ML_DSA_44 (underscores, not hyphens).
  2. This policy blocks CreateKey only. To also block use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys at the principal level, add the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey deny shown in the Restricting use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys section.
  3. For comprehensive, non-overridable coverage, deploy as an SCP rather than relying solely on principal-level policies.
IAM permission boundaries

IAM permission boundaries set the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant to an IAM role or user and can be used as an alternative or complement to using SCPs. The effective permissions are the intersection of the identity-based policy and the boundary, and a Deny in a boundary can’t be overridden by an attached policy. Boundaries are useful where you want per-account or per-role flexibility (for example, in build or non-production accounts) rather than a blanket, multi-account deny.

Operational consideration. A permission boundary only takes effect on principals that have it attached. To rely on boundaries as a control, you need a mechanism to enforce the boundary on all IAM principals programmatically. One example enforcement mechanism would be an SCP that denies iam:CreateRole, iam:CreateUser, iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary, and iam:PutUserPermissionsBoundary unless the approved boundary is set (using the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key), and denies iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary and iam:DeleteUserPermissionsBoundary outright so the boundary can’t be removed after the fact. You would also want to probe for non-conforming principals periodically and respond, perhaps by automatically attaching the PermissionsBoundary. IAM users shouldn’t be used, but the enforcement should account for the possibility that they exist.

Because a boundary only sets a ceiling and does not itself grant anything, it opens with Allow on all actions, then denies ML-DSA-44 key creation specifically. The following permission boundary denies creation of ML-DSA-44 keys:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AllowAll",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "kms:CreateKey",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

To also block use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys for the principals carrying this boundary, add the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey deny statement shown in the following section (which also uses kms:KeySpec).

Restricting use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys

As described in the Background section, kms:KeySpec is also evaluated on Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey, reflecting the KeySpec of the key being used. You can therefore deny those operations when kms:KeySpec equals ML_DSA_44 while continuing to permit ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87. The IAM policy below, attached to an IAM principal, does exactly that.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyUsage",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "kms:Sign",
        "kms:Verify",
        "kms:GetPublicKey"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

This deny can also live in an AWS KMS key policy. The same kms:KeySpec deny can be placed directly in the key policy of an AWS KMS key. A key policy is a resource policy, so the statement must include a Principal element. Identity policies and SCPs do not name principals to which they apply. A deny in the key policy is a resource-side backstop that protects a specific key, while an SCP gives non-overridable organization-wide coverage. To turn the previous example into an AWS KMS key policy, add a Principal element to the statement (for example "Principal": {"AWS": "*"}, or a more specific principal), and keep the rest of it the same.

Additional approaches

Depending on your goals you might also want to remove the key material itself rather than only deny its use. Remember that it is difficult to know what data has been signed by a specific key, unless you track that somehow. Deleting a key that was used will make signature verification impossible. Take great care to make sure keys are not used before deleting them.

  1. Disable or schedule deletion of the keys. Disabling stops key use immediately and is reversible. Key deletion is definitive but irreversible after the waiting period, so confirm before scheduling.
  2. Deny Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey by specific key ARN. You can target named keys rather than the whole key spec. To do this, you would list the exact key ARNs in the Resource element of the IAM policy (no condition key required). This is effective for targeting a single key specifically, but it is difficult to maintain lists of key ARNs. Use this strategy sparingly. If you’re considering using an IAM policy naming a key ARN, remember that a Deny in the key policy of the target key accomplishes the same goal and is attached to the key itself.
  3. Finding existing keys (only needed if you disable or delete). A Deny in an IAM policy or SCP, based on kms:KeySpec, doesn’t require you to know which keys exist – it applies by key spec at request time. If you want to disable or delete existing ML-DSA-44 keys, you need to locate them. AWS KMS has no server-side filter for key spec, so you must enumerate keys with ListKeys and call DescribeKey and inspect each KeySpec. This client-side filtering pattern is common across AWS APIs and is well supported by pagination in the AWS SDKs. You can also use AWS Config to record and query KMS key resources.

Reference: Choosing a KMS key spec – kms:KeySpec condition key

Approved ML-DSA variants and control of AWS Private CA

AWS Private CA sets a certificate authority’s (CA’s) signing algorithm at creation time, in the CertificateAuthorityConfiguration parameter of CreateCertificateAuthority (valid values include ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87). There is currently no condition key for the algorithm, so an SCP cannot enforce signing algorithm. The approach in this section controls who can create CAs and pins the algorithm in that trusted path, backed by AWS CloudTrail-based detection.

Recommended approach
  1. Restrict who can create CAs. Deny acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority broadly via SCP, and allow it only for a small set of trusted roles or an approved provisioning pipeline. This removes the ability for arbitrary principals to stand up a CA with an unapproved algorithm.
  2. Pin the algorithm in the trusted path. Have that approved pipeline or infrastructure-as-code template hard-code SigningAlgorithm to ML_DSA_65 or ML_DSA_87 in CertificateAuthorityConfiguration. Because AWS Private CA exposes no algorithm condition key, this provisioning path is the enforcement point. Note that the CA’s algorithm pins the signature on the certificates it issues; the subject key in each certificate comes from the CSR, which AWS Private CA copies without validating its algorithm, so pin the CSR key algorithm in the same issuance pipeline.
  3. Control the trust chain. On the PKI side, only add approved CAs to your trust stores and issuance hierarchies, and do not trust or subordinate CAs that could issue ML-DSA-44. This prevents an unapproved CA from being introduced into a trusted path.
  4. Detect drift. Use CloudTrail to capture CreateCertificateAuthority calls and AWS Config to flag any CA whose configuration uses ML_DSA_44, so an unapproved CA is caught quickly.

Part 1 of this series shows what this looks like in practice: it creates an ML-DSA-87 root CA and an ML-DSA-65 subordinate CA with CreateCertificateAuthority, activates them, and distributes the resulting chain to verifiers. In the model described here, those are the calls that only your approved provisioning pipeline is allowed to make.

Setting the ML-DSA value in CertificateAuthorityConfiguration. The same variant goes in both the KeyAlgorithm and SigningAlgorithm fields (for example, KeyAlgorithm=ML_DSA_65 with SigningAlgorithm=ML_DSA_65). Note a difference in signing algorithms between AWS KMS and AWS Private CA. With AWS Private CA, the SigningAlgorithm takes the variant value directly (ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87), and doesn’t accept ML_DSA_SHAKE_256. In contrast, AWS KMS uses ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 as its signing algorithm. Be aware that some older AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) builds omitted descriptions of the ML-DSA variants from the built-in CLI help, so don’t rely on the help in the AWS CLI to determine valid values. For more information, see CertificateAuthorityConfiguration API Reference.

Known limitation. Some surfaces have no algorithm condition key, so you enforce them through provisioning and detection rather than policy. acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority has no condition key for the algorithm, and acm:ImportCertificate and iam:UploadServerCertificate are not algorithm-aware, so a disallowed signature setting on a created, imported, or uploaded certificate cannot be blocked by an IAM policy or SCP condition. Govern these through your provisioning process, restrict who can call them, and deny the import and upload actions entirely where they are not required. The controls above remain the available mitigation.

In particular, iam:UploadServerCertificate doesn’t support any method to prevent use of particular algorithms, and AWS doesn’t recommend using this API to generate and upload certificates. This API predates ACM and exists mainly to cover AWS Regions or partitions where ACM is not yet available. While a new Region or partition is being built out, workloads can still need a TLS server certificate before ACM support has shipped there, and uploading a certificate to IAM gives you a place to store and reference it in the meantime. Once ACM is available in that Region, you should use ACM instead. Outside that narrow case, deny iam:UploadServerCertificate unless it is genuinely required.

ACM-issued leaf certificates. A CA’s own key and signing algorithm are separate from the leaf certificates that ACM issues from it. If you use ACM to request leaf certificates, you can constrain the leaf’s key algorithm with the acm:KeyAlgorithm condition key on acm:RequestCertificate. This lets you allow-list approved algorithms for leaf certificates using SCPs or IAM policies, similar to the AWS KMS examples earlier in this post. Be aware that, at the time of writing, ACM doesn’t offer ML-DSA leaf certificates. So a policy like this is a forward-looking defense-in-depth control rather than an immediate ML-DSA-44 risk. The IAM example below is illustrative (using example approved algorithms). Since this is an evolving part of the service, be sure to validate this in your environment before relying on it.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "RestrictACMLeafKeyAlgorithm",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "acm:RequestCertificate",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {
          "acm:KeyAlgorithm": [
            "EC_secp384r1",
            "RSA_2048"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

This example uses StringNotEqualsIfExists so it denies only requests that specify a disallowed algorithm. With plain StringNotEquals, a request that omits acm:KeyAlgorithm would also be denied, because the missing key makes the condition evaluate true. Choose the operator that matches whether you want to block requests that leave the algorithm unspecified.

Prevent ML-DSA-44 usage in TLS for NLB and ALB

Elastic Load Balancing, for both network load balancers (NLB) and application load balancers (ALB), terminates TLS on behalf of your applications. The certificates used by these listeners are requested through or imported into ACM, or uploaded to IAM. A listener’s configured security policy and its certificate determine what’s offered during negotiation. At the time of writing, ACM requests and imports accept RSA and ECDSA keys only, and NLB and ALB listeners accept RSA and ECDSA certificates only, so no ML-DSA certificate can be bound to a listener today. As with the ACM leaf-certificate policy earlier, the controls in this section are forward-looking defense in depth rather than a mitigation of an immediate ML-DSA-44 risk.

Certificate controls (the effective mechanism for ML-DSA-44)

Because the listener API calls reference a certificate only by ARN, you can’t write an SCP on CreateListener, ModifyListener, or AddListenerCertificates that inspects the certificate’s algorithm. IAM conditions can’t reference attributes of a separately-referenced resource. Keeping ML-DSA-44 out of TLS therefore relies on there being no ML-DSA-44 certificate material to associate:

  1. Configure your private CA to issue only ML_DSA_65 or ML_DSA_87 certificates, and control who can create CAs.
  2. Prevent ML-DSA-44 key creation in AWS KMS, so that no KMS-held ML-DSA-44 key can become the subject key of a certificate. TLS server keys for ACM-issued, imported, or uploaded certificates are not KMS keys; those are governed by items 1 and 3.
  3. Control imported and uploaded certificates through your provisioning process or deny the import and upload actions where not required, as described in the AWS Private CA section.
Detective controls

CloudTrail records the certificate and listener API calls in this section: certificate creation and import (acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority, acm:ImportCertificate, iam:UploadServerCertificate) and listener configuration (CreateListener, ModifyListener, AddListenerCertificates). Whether the algorithm shows up in the event depends on what the call itself carries. Creation calls that take the algorithm as an input record it: kms:CreateKey logs the KeySpec, and acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority logs the signing algorithm. That makes CloudTrail effective for catching the creation of ML-DSA-44 key material or a CA. A listener binding references its certificate only by ARN, so the certificate’s algorithm does not appear in that event. To evaluate the algorithm of a bound or imported certificate, use AWS Config resource evaluation as the detective backstop.

Summary for TLS

The primary preventive control is the certificate material itself: with no ML-DSA-44 CA, no ML-DSA-44 KMS key, and certificate import and upload controlled, no ML-DSA-44 certificate can be issued or bound. Where you also operate an allow-list of permitted TLS security policies, the elasticloadbalancing:SecurityPolicy condition key (on CreateListener and ModifyListener) can additionally constrain which TLS policies listeners can use.

Summary of controls

The following table maps the example policy (allow ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87, exclude ML-DSA-44) to the available controls. Modify the controls to limit use to the approved set of algorithms your policies require.

Area Control Status Block ML-DSA-44 key creation (Organization-wide or for all accounts in an organization OU) SCP on kms:CreateKey using kms:KeySpec Fully supported via condition key Block ML-DSA-44 key creation (per account or per role) IAM policy or permission boundary using kms:KeySpec Supported; requires programmatic enforcement of boundaries Block use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys Deny Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey using kms:KeySpec (key policy, IAM, or SCP); optionally disable and delete keys Supported using kms:KeySpec (not kms:SigningAlgorithm) Only allow approved variants in Private CA Restrict who can create CAs; pin ML_DSA_65 or ML_DSA_87 in provisioning path No algorithm condition key; enforce using process and detection Limit variants in imported or uploaded TLS certificates Process controls, or deny import or upload APIs (prefer ACM over iam:UploadServerCertificate) APIs aren’t algorithm-aware Block use of ML-DSA-44 in TLS with network load balancers (NLB) and application load balancers (ALB) Restrict TLS policy using elasticloadbalancing:SecurityPolicy; control cert material TLS-policy restriction supported; no per-cert algorithm condition Detect use of unapproved variants CloudTrail (API-level) and AWS Config custom rules Supported using custom AWS Config rules; not managed rules
Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to use ML-DSA as an example of turning a cryptographic algorithm policy into enforceable AWS controls. The key lever is the kms:KeySpec condition key: it keeps your approved parameter sets (ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87) fully usable while preventing the creation and use of a parameter set you’ve excluded (ML-DSA-44) on the CreateKey, in addition to the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey operations, where kms:SigningAlgorithm can’t tell the variants apart. Applied as defense in depth across SCPs, IAM policies, permission boundaries, and KMS key policies, and extended to the surfaces that have no algorithm condition key (AWS Private CA, certificate import, and Elastic Load Balancing TLS) through provisioning controls plus AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config drift detection, these controls give you a consistent way to keep an unapproved variant out of your accounts.

The pattern isn’t specific to ML-DSA-44. Because your algorithm policy will change as standards and your own requirements evolve, treat these controls as a reusable template and re-point the same condition keys and guardrails at whatever your approved set becomes. This adaptability is the practical meaning of cryptographic agility: changing what you allow without re-engineering how you enforce it.

To get started, review ML-DSA keys in AWS KMS and Choosing a KMS key spec, and test the example policies in a non-production environment before you deploy them.

To see the workloads these controls govern, read Part 1 of this series, which builds a complete ML-DSA signing pipeline, from key creation and PKI through artifact signing and verification, using the approved set enforced here.

items.title: Quantum-resistant signing on AWS, Part 1: Build a software supply chain with ML-DSA
items.summary: Software supply chain attacks have grown in both frequency and sophistication. Recent high-profile compromises of build systems and open source dependencies demonstrate that attackers increasingly target the trust mechanisms that verify software integrity. Those trust mechanisms rely on digital signature algorithms, and today many use traditional algorithms such as Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) and the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) . If a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could forge these signatures, an attacker could potentially inject unauthorized code into signed artifacts, fabricate build attestations, or impersonate legitimate publishers. Using quantum-resistant signatures today defends against threats that might emerge in the future. Since 2025, the Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0 (CNSA 2.0) , published by the US National Security Agency (NSA), has required US National Security Systems (NSS) to “support and prefer” quantum-resistant signatures for software and firmware, with exclusive use mandated by 2030. The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) takes full effect in December 2027. It requires manufacturers to maintain verifiable software integrity throughout a product’s lifecycle. Organizations that ship software to US federal agencies or sell products in the European market face converging deadlines that demand action now. Amazon Web Services (AWS) provides the building blocks to construct a quantum-resistant software supply chain today using production-ready, generally available services. In this post, I show you how to combine Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) keys in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , ML-DSA certificate hierarchies in AWS Private Certificate Authority , and ML-DSA trust anchors in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Roles Anywhere into an end-to-end signing architecture for binaries, container images, and software bills of materials (SBOMs). This post is Part 1 of a two-part series on adopting ML-DSA signatures, standardized in NIST FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) signatures, on AWS. As of Oct 2026, this series is the first end-to-end guide from any cloud provider for post-quantum signing across the software supply chain, from establishing an ML-DSA root of trust to enforcing algorithm policy across an organization. This part is for builders and walks through constructing and operating the signing pipeline. Part 2, Enforce your ML-DSA algorithm policy with SCPs and IAM , is for security and governance teams and shows how to turn the algorithm choices made here into preventive and detective controls across an organization. Understanding the harvest now, forge later threat After a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) exists, the mathematical problems protecting today’s public-key cryptography can be solved efficiently. Attacks that are impractical today because of the computational complexity suddenly become practical using a CRQC. Most discussions of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) focus on the harvest now, decrypt later threat to data confidentiality. The asymmetric keys protecting data in transit can be efficiently derived using a CRQC, exposing the data that was meant to be protected. Digital signatures rely on the same asymmetric mathematical problems that a CRQC would break. This means that software supply chains face a parallel threat that targets integrity rather than confidentiality. An attacker who records signed artifacts today can forge those signatures in the future on a totally different artifact, using a CRQC. Consider firmware signed with ECDSA P-256 and deployed to a fleet of embedded devices in 2026. These devices verify the firmware signature on every boot for their 15-year operational lifetime and can’t be recalled to re-sign after deployment. If a CRQC becomes operational in 2035, an attacker could produce a valid-looking signature over tampered firmware, and every device in the fleet would accept it as authentic on next restart. For organizations that rely on classical digital signatures as the primary mechanism for verifying software integrity, this weakens a critical link in the verification chain. This is why CNSA 2.0 specifies aggressive timelines for digital signatures: the artifacts you sign today must remain trustworthy for their full operational lifetime. ML-DSA is designed to resist attacks from both classical and quantum computers. AWS KMS, AWS Private CA, and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere all support ML-DSA, making it possible to address the forge-later threat across your supply chain today without additional tooling. Architecture overview: Five pillars of a quantum-resistant supply chain The architecture comprises five trust pillars that together protect your software delivery pipeline: ML-DSA key management in AWS KMS – All signing keys are generated and protected in FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3 hardware security modules (HSMs). Private keys never leave the HSM boundary. ML-DSA public key infrastructure (PKI) through AWS Private CA – A certificate hierarchy (root CA, subordinate CA, end-entity certificates) binds ML-DSA public keys to identities, establishing who signed what. CA private keys are generated and stored in hardware-protected HSMs managed by the service and never leave the HSM boundary. Quantum-resistant workload identity (for external build agents) – For continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) agents running outside AWS that authenticate through X.509 certificates, IAM Roles Anywhere with ML-DSA certificates ties the signer’s identity back to the same quantum-resistant root of trust. ML-DSA artifact signing – Build outputs (binaries, container image manifests, packages) are signed using AWS KMS ML-DSA keys. Signatures are stored alongside artifacts in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . ML-DSA SBOM integrity attestation – The SBOM for each release is wrapped in an in-toto Statement that names the artifact it describes by digest, and the Statement is signed with the same ML-DSA code-signing key. This provides quantum-resistant proof that the dependency manifest hasn’t been tampered with and that it belongs to the artifact it accompanies. These pillars create a chain of trust: AWS Private CA protects the root CA key in its own HSMs, issues certificates that bind identities to AWS KMS code-signing keys, IAM Roles Anywhere uses those certificates to authenticate build agents, and authenticated agents sign every artifact and SBOM they produce. Figure 1: End-to-end quantum-resistant software supply chain on AWS Figure 1 illustrates this architecture in four layers, numbered in the order you build them: Root of trust (Pillars 1 and 2) – Establish your AWS Private CA hierarchy and create your code-signing key in AWS KMS. Workload identity (Pillar 3) – Register the CA as an IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchor and issue ML-DSA certificates to build agents, ensuring the signer’s identity chains back to the same quantum-resistant root of trust. Artifact signing (Pillars 4 and 5) – Sign binaries, container images, and SBOMs using the authenticated build agent. Verification and enforcement – Validate signatures at deployment and enforce ML-DSA-only policies. A container image pushed to Amazon ECR (for the container signing example). Building the ML-DSA PKI foundation Start by creating the certificate hierarchy that will anchor your supply chain trust. AWS Private CA generates and stores its own CA signing keys internally in hardware-protected HSMs when you create a certificate authority. Use ML-DSA-87 (NIST security category 5, defined as at least as hard to break as exhaustive key search on AES-256) for the root CA because it protects the longest-lived trust anchor. Use ML-DSA-65 (NIST security category 3) for the subordinate CA to balance security with smaller signature sizes for frequently issued certificates. The parameter sets used here, ML-DSA-87 and ML-DSA-65, are also the approved set in the example algorithm policy that Part 2 of this series turns into enforceable controls. If your organization has standardized on a different set, substitute it in the commands that follow; the build steps don’t change. Step 1: Create the root CA in AWS Private CA When you specify KeyAlgorithm: ML_DSA_87 , Private CA generates an ML-DSA-87 key pair internally. You don’t need to create a separate AWS KMS key for the CA. aws acm-pca create-certificate-authority \ --certificate-authority-configuration '{ "KeyAlgorithm": "ML_DSA_87", "SigningAlgorithm": "ML_DSA_87", "Subject": { "CommonName": "PQC Supply Chain Root CA", "Organization": "Example Corp", "Country": "US" } }' \ --certificate-authority-type ROOT After creation, the root CA is in PENDING_CERTIFICATE state. Activate it by self-signing its certificate. This is where you set the root CA’s validity period (10 years is typical for a root): # Retrieve the root CA's CSR aws acm-pca get-certificate-authority-csr \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --output text > root-ca.csr # Self-sign the root CA certificate (valid for 10 years) ROOT_CERT_ARN=$(aws acm-pca issue-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --csr fileb://root-ca.csr \ --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_87 \ --validity Value=3650,Type=DAYS \ --template-arn arn:aws:acm-pca:::template/RootCACertificate/V1 \ --query CertificateArn --output text) # Retrieve and install the self-signed root certificate aws acm-pca get-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --certificate-arn $ROOT_CERT_ARN \ --query Certificate --output text > root-ca-cert.pem aws acm-pca import-certificate-authority-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --certificate fileb://root-ca-cert.pem Step 2: Create a subordinate CA for code signing aws acm-pca create-certificate-authority \ --certificate-authority-configuration '{ "KeyAlgorithm": "ML_DSA_65", "SigningAlgorithm": "ML_DSA_65", "Subject": { "CommonName": "PQC Code Signing CA", "Organization": "Example Corp", "Country": "US" } }' \ --certificate-authority-type SUBORDINATE After creation, the subordinate CA enters PENDING_CERTIFICATE state with no link to the root. Activate it by signing its certificate signing request (CSR) with the root CA: # Retrieve the subordinate CA's certificate signing request aws acm-pca get-certificate-authority-csr \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --output text > sub-ca.csr # Sign the CSR using the root CA (this establishes the trust hierarchy) SUB_CERT_ARN=$(aws acm-pca issue-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --csr fileb://sub-ca.csr \ --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_87 \ --validity Value=1825,Type=DAYS \ --template-arn arn:aws:acm-pca:::template/SubordinateCACertificate_PathLen0/V1 \ --query CertificateArn --output text) # Retrieve the signed certificate and import it to activate the subordinate CA aws acm-pca get-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --certificate-arn $SUB_CERT_ARN \ --query Certificate --output text > sub-ca-cert.pem aws acm-pca import-certificate-authority-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --certificate fileb://sub-ca-cert.pem \ --certificate-chain fileb://root-ca-cert.pem Step 3: Create the code-signing key in AWS KMS Your build agents use this key to sign artifacts, so their IAM roles need the kms:Sign permission on it. The end-entity certificate issued by your subordinate CA binds an identity to this key’s public key. aws kms create-key \ --key-spec ML_DSA_65 \ --key-usage SIGN_VERIFY \ --description "PQC code-signing key for supply chain" \ --tags TagKey=Purpose,TagValue=CodeSigning Create an alias for convenient reference in your CI/CD scripts: aws kms create-alias \ --alias-name alias/pqc-code-signing \ --target-key-id Step 4: Issue the end-entity code signing certificate To issue a certificate, you need a CSR. Because the ML-DSA private key never leaves the AWS KMS HSM, you can’t generate the CSR locally with OpenSSL. Instead, you construct the CSR’s TBS (to-be-signed) structure containing your subject name and public key, sign it remotely by calling aws kms sign , and assemble the final CSR from those components. For a working implementation that assembles an ML-DSA CSR around a KMS-managed private key and signs it with AWS KMS, see Post-quantum (ML-DSA) code signing with AWS Private CA and AWS KMS and its diy-code-signing-kms-private-ca sample on GitHub (Java, built with Maven). There is no AWS CLI-only path for this step: the CSR must be constructed and signed in code, and the sample is the reference implementation. After you have the code-signing.csr file, issue the certificate from your subordinate CA: # Issue a code-signing certificate valid for one year, signed by the subordinate CA using ML-DSA-65. # Replace with the ARN that create-certificate-authority returned for the subordinate CA in Step 2. CODE_SIGNING_CERT_ARN=$(aws acm-pca issue-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --csr fileb://code-signing.csr \ --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_65 \ --validity Value=365,Type=DAYS \ --template-arn arn:aws:acm-pca:::template/CodeSigningCertificate/V1 \ --query CertificateArn --output text) # Retrieve the issued certificate aws acm-pca get-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --certificate-arn $CODE_SIGNING_CERT_ARN \ --query Certificate --output text > code-signing-cert.pem This certificate binds the signer identity to the AWS KMS code-signing key material. Note that the certificate validity period (365 days in this example) determines how long verifiers can validate signatures by checking the certificate alone. AWS Private CA lets you choose the validity period of an issued certificate, as long as it ends no later than the issuing CA’s own certificate; in this example the subordinate CA certificate from Step 2 is valid for 1,825 days, so the three-year option below fits inside it. For artifacts that must remain verifiable beyond the certificate’s expiry, consider these approaches: Longer certificate validity – For private PKI, code-signing certificates are commonly issued with multi-year validity (for example, Value=1095,Type=DAYS for 3 years) because you control the issuance policy. Trusted timestamping (RFC 3161) – Countersign each signature with an RFC 3161 timestamp from a Time Stamping Authority (TSA) at signing time. The timestamp proves the signature was created while the certificate was valid, allowing verification indefinitely. AWS doesn’t provide a managed TSA; use a third-party TSA or operate your own. Re-signing – Before a certificate expires, re-sign active artifacts with a newly issued certificate. Distribute the certificate chain (root CA certificate, subordinate CA certificate, and end-entity certificate) to systems that need to verify your signatures. Signing artifacts with ML-DSA in your CI/CD pipeline With the PKI hierarchy in place, integrate ML-DSA signing into your build process. The approach depends on artifact type. ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes (compared to 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256), and the latency of the AWS KMS Sign operation for ML-DSA is comparable to existing asymmetric operations. The larger signature size has negligible impact when stored alongside multi-megabyte container images or packages, but is worth accounting for in size-constrained environments like embedded device images transmitted over low-bandwidth links. Binary and package signing Most build outputs, including compiled binaries and packages, are far larger than the 4,096-byte limit that AWS KMS places on the message passed to aws kms sign . Make the EXTERNAL_MU method your pipeline’s default: compute the 64-byte message representative (mu) externally with OpenSSL 3.5, then pass only mu to AWS KMS. This handles an artifact of any size and never needs to change as your artifacts grow. AWS KMS also accepts content directly with --message-type RAW , up to 4,096 bytes. Use RAW only for inputs whose size is fixed by construction, such as the 71-character manifest digest in the container image example that follows. An artifact that fits today is likely to outgrow the limit later, and a pipeline that depends on RAW fails when it does. Both methods produce cryptographically identical signatures. The verifier doesn’t need to know which method was used; standard ML-DSA verification applies in either case. # Retrieve the public key aws kms get-public-key --key-id alias/pqc-code-signing \ --query PublicKey --output text | base64 --decode > pk.der # Extract raw public key bytes from the DER-encoded SubjectPublicKeyInfo. # The BIT STRING starts at offset 17 for all ML-DSA key sizes. # Expected output: 1,312 bytes (ML-DSA-44), 1,952 bytes (ML-DSA-65), or 2,592 bytes (ML-DSA-87). openssl asn1parse -inform DER -in pk.der -strparse 17 -noout -out pk_raw.bin # Compute mu per FIPS 204 Section 6.2 printf '\x00\x00' | cat - artifact.bin > m_prime.bin openssl dgst -shake256 -xoflen 64 -binary pk_raw.bin > pk_hash.bin cat pk_hash.bin m_prime.bin | openssl dgst -shake256 -xoflen 64 -binary > mu.bin # Sign the mu value aws kms sign \ --key-id alias/pqc-code-signing \ --message fileb://mu.bin \ --message-type EXTERNAL_MU \ --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 \ --query Signature --output text | base64 --decode > artifact.bin.sig Store the .sig file alongside the artifact in Amazon S3 or your package repository. Protect the integrity of both the artifact and its signature by enabling S3 Object Lock (WORM protection) or at minimum S3 Versioning with restricted write access. If an attacker can modify or delete either file, verification can’t be trusted. For comprehensive guidance, see Security best practices for Amazon S3 . Container image signing For container image signing, use the OCI referrer pattern, defined in the OCI Image and Distribution Specifications v1.1 . A referrer is an artifact, such as a signature or an SBOM, whose manifest names another image in its subject field. Registries that support the pattern, including Amazon ECR, return these artifacts when a client asks for an image’s referrers. This approach uses AWS KMS ML-DSA keys to generate the signature and stores it as a referrer of the image: # Repository URI used by ORAS here and in the SBOM steps; replace the account ID and Region ECR_URI=111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/myapp # Authenticate ORAS to Amazon ECR aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | \ oras login --username AWS --password-stdin 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com # Get the image manifest digest IMAGE_DIGEST=$(aws ecr batch-get-image \ --repository-name myapp \ --image-ids imageTag=v1.2.0 \ --query 'images[0].imageId.imageDigest' --output text) # Sign the digest. It is a fixed 71 characters, so RAW is safe here (see Binary and package signing). # AWS CLI v2 expects blob parameters to be base64, so write the digest to a file and pass it with fileb:// echo -n "$IMAGE_DIGEST" > digest.txt aws kms sign \ --key-id alias/pqc-code-signing \ --message fileb://digest.txt \ --message-type RAW \ --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 \ --query Signature --output text | base64 --decode > image.mldsa.sig # Attach signature as OCI referrer using ORAS oras attach $ECR_URI@$IMAGE_DIGEST \ --artifact-type "application/vnd.example.mldsa-signature.v1" \ image.mldsa.sig:application/octet-stream At deployment time, your admission controller retrieves the referrer artifact and verifies the ML-DSA signature before allowing the image to run. See Verifying a container image signature before deployment later in this post for the full verification workflow and admission control implementation. SBOM signing A software bill of materials (SBOM) is a structured inventory of every component, library, and dependency included in a software release. It lists package names, versions, suppliers, and dependency relationships. Organizations use SBOMs to track vulnerabilities, verify license compliance, and respond quickly when a compromised component is disclosed. Signing the SBOM file on its own proves that the inventory hasn’t been tampered with since it was signed, but not which artifact it describes. If the image signature and the SBOM signature are independent of each other, an attacker who holds a legitimately signed SBOM for a clean image can present it alongside a different signed image and claim that the two correspond. Attaching the SBOM to the image as an OCI referrer doesn’t close this gap by itself, because the subject field of a referrer manifest is set by whoever pushes the referrer; it’s a discovery mechanism, not a cryptographic binding. The binding must be inside the bytes that the signature covers. To create that binding, wrap the SBOM in an in-toto Statement before signing it. A Statement names the artifacts it describes in its subject field, by digest, and carries the SBOM as its predicate . Because the image manifest digest is part of the signed content, a verifier can confirm that the SBOM in hand was issued for exactly the image it is about to deploy, and a swapped SBOM or a swapped digest fails verification. Embedding the SBOM in the image filesystem is another way to bind the two, because the image digest then covers the SBOM bytes. This post uses the Statement approach because it also works for SBOMs generated by scanning a finished image, for artifacts that have no filesystem such as binaries and firmware, and for images that are already in your registry, and because the SBOM stays readable from the registry without pulling the image. Generate the SBOM with your preferred tool (such as Amazon Inspector SBOM Generator (Sbomgen) for container images), wrap it in a Statement, and sign the Statement with the same EXTERNAL_MU step you use for binaries: # Scan the pushed image by digest so the inventory describes exactly the manifest you signed. # Sbomgen reuses the registry login from the oras login step in the previous section. inspector-sbomgen container --image $ECR_URI@$IMAGE_DIGEST -o sbom.json # Wrap the SBOM in an in-toto Statement whose subject is the image manifest digest. # This puts the digest inside the signed bytes, which binds this SBOM to this image. jq -n \ --arg name "$ECR_URI" \ --arg digest "${IMAGE_DIGEST#sha256:}" \ --slurpfile sbom sbom.json \ '{ "_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v1", "subject": [{"name": $name, "digest": {"sha256": $digest}}], "predicateType": "https://cyclonedx.org/bom", "predicate": $sbom[0] }' > sbom.statement.json # Sign using EXTERNAL_MU (same mu computation as binary signing above, # with sbom.statement.json as the input) # ... compute mu from sbom.statement.json ... aws kms sign \ --key-id alias/pqc-code-signing \ --message fileb://mu.bin \ --message-type EXTERNAL_MU \ --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 \ --query Signature --output text | base64 --decode > sbom.statement.json.sig # Attach the Statement and its signature to the image as an OCI referrer so # verifiers discover them alongside the image signature oras attach $ECR_URI@$IMAGE_DIGEST \ --artifact-type "application/vnd.example.mldsa-sbom-attestation.v1" \ sbom.statement.json:application/vnd.in-toto+json \ sbom.statement.json.sig:application/octet-stream Ship the Statement and its .sig file together; the SBOM itself is the Statement’s predicate field, and verifiers extract it after verification. The same pattern binds an SBOM to a binary or package: set the subject digest to the SHA-256 of the file instead of an image manifest digest. The Verifying a binary or SBOM signature section later in this post walks through the full verification workflow, including the subject check that completes the binding. Quantum-resistant workload identity for build agents Signing artifacts with ML-DSA keys addresses the integrity of the artifacts themselves. Separately, build agents running outside AWS (on-premises Jenkins, self-hosted GitHub Actions runners, or third-party CI/CD systems) authenticate using X.509 certificates or OIDC tokens typically signed with RSA or ECDSA. These authentication credentials represent a classical cryptographic dependency in the pipeline. IAM Roles Anywhere with ML-DSA certificates replaces that dependency: the credential that the external build agent presents, and the CA that vouches for it, no longer rely on algorithms that are vulnerable to quantum attack. (The TLS connection that carries the request still authenticates the AWS endpoint with a traditional certificate, as public TLS does today; that is a transport concern separate from the signing identity this post is about.) Build agents running on AWS with an attached IAM role don’t have this dependency: their API requests are authenticated with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) , which uses a symmetric hash-based message authentication code (HMAC-SHA256). Symmetric schemes like this are already considered quantum-resistant, so no additional action is needed. Step 1: Register a workload identity CA as a trust anchor For this walkthrough, reuse the subordinate CA that you created earlier; that avoids the monthly charge for a second CA, and the commands that follow assume it. In production, use a dedicated subordinate CA for workload identity certificates, separate from your code-signing CA. This limits the blast radius if either CA is compromised and has to be revoked, and it lets you apply different issuance policies to the two certificate types. # Use the ARN that create-certificate-authority returned when you created the # subordinate CA earlier. If you no longer have it, list your CAs and copy the # ARN of the SUBORDINATE one. aws acm-pca list-certificate-authorities \ --query "CertificateAuthorities[?Type=='SUBORDINATE'].[Arn,Status,CertificateAuthorityConfiguration.Subject.CommonName]" \ --output table SUB_CA_ARN=arn:aws:acm-pca:us-east-1:111122223333:certificate-authority/abc-123 # replace with yours # Register the subordinate CA as an IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchor aws rolesanywhere create-trust-anchor \ --name "PQC-CI-CD-Trust-Anchor" \ --source "sourceType=AWS_ACM_PCA,sourceData={acmPcaArn=$SUB_CA_ARN}" \ --enabled Step 2: Create the build agent role and a profile that references it An IAM Roles Anywhere profile specifies which IAM roles a workload can assume after it authenticates with a certificate from your trust anchor. Create the role first. Its trust policy lets IAM Roles Anywhere assume it only through your trust anchor and only for a certificate whose subject common name identifies the build agent; without those conditions, any certificate that the trust anchor CA issues could assume the role. Its permissions policy grants only what signing requires, on only the code-signing key. Save the trust policy as build-agent-trust.json , replacing the trust anchor ARN with the one that create-trust-anchor returned in Step 1: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com"}, "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity"], "Condition": { "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:us-east-1:111122223333:trust-anchor/ta-id" }, "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "pqc-build-agent-01" } } } ] } Save the permissions policy as build-agent-permissions.json , replacing the resource with your key’s ARN ( aws kms describe-key --key-id alias/pqc-code-signing --query KeyMetadata.Arn --output text ): { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["kms:Sign", "kms:GetPublicKey", "kms:DescribeKey"], "Resource": " " } ] } Create the role, attach the policy, and then create a profile that references the role: aws iam create-role \ --role-name PQCBuildAgentRole \ --assume-role-policy-document file://build-agent-trust.json aws iam put-role-policy \ --role-name PQCBuildAgentRole \ --policy-name pqc-code-signing \ --policy-document file://build-agent-permissions.json aws rolesanywhere create-profile \ --name "PQC-Build-Agent-Profile" \ --role-arns "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/PQCBuildAgentRole" \ --enabled Step 3: Issue the build agent certificate and configure the credential helper Generate the build agent’s ML-DSA-65 key pair and CSR locally with OpenSSL, have the subordinate CA issue a client authentication certificate for it, and then configure the IAM Roles Anywhere credential helper to present that certificate: # Generate the build agent's key pair and CSR. The CN must match the # aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN condition in the role's trust policy. openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-65 -out build-agent-mldsa-key.pem chmod 400 build-agent-mldsa-key.pem openssl req -new -key build-agent-mldsa-key.pem \ -subj "/C=US/O=Example Corp/CN=pqc-build-agent-01" \ -out build-agent.csr # Issue a 30-day client authentication certificate from the subordinate CA # registered as the trust anchor in Step 1. BUILD_AGENT_CERT_ARN=$(aws acm-pca issue-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn $SUB_CA_ARN \ --csr fileb://build-agent.csr \ --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_65 \ --validity Value=30,Type=DAYS \ --template-arn arn:aws:acm-pca:::template/EndEntityClientAuthCertificate/V1 \ --query CertificateArn --output text) aws acm-pca get-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn $SUB_CA_ARN \ --certificate-arn $BUILD_AGENT_CERT_ARN \ --query Certificate --output text > build-agent-mldsa.pem # In production, store the private key in a TPM or HSM rather than as a plaintext file. aws_signing_helper credential-process \ --certificate build-agent-mldsa.pem \ --private-key build-agent-mldsa-key.pem \ --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:us-east-1:111122223333:trust-anchor/ta-id \ --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:us-east-1:111122223333:profile/profile-id \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/PQCBuildAgentRole The helper produces short-lived AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) credentials scoped to the build role, replacing long-lived AWS access keys. In production, protect the ML-DSA private key with hardware-backed storage such as a Trusted Platform Module (TPM), an HSM, or an encrypted credential store with restricted file permissions. The plaintext file path shown here is for demonstration purposes. The private key authorizes access to your code-signing infrastructure and should be treated with the same protection level as any signing key. On Linux build agents, at minimum restrict the file to chmod 400 owned by the service account and consider using a PKCS#11 provider to avoid storing the raw key on disk entirely. Verification and policy enforcement A signing architecture is only as strong as its verification. Producing signatures is half the story. The other half is giving the systems and people that deploy your artifacts, such as deployment pipelines, Kubernetes admission controllers, and engineers installing a package, a concrete way to verify those signatures and make trust decisions before an artifact is deployed or run. Distributing your trust chain Before any verifier can check a signature, it needs to trust the CA that issued the code-signing certificate. This trust is established through a trust store: a local collection of root CA certificates that a system treats as authoritative. Trust stores exist in operating systems (such as /etc/pki/ca-trust/ on Linux, Keychain on macOS), language run-times (Java cacerts ), container base images, and custom application configurations. For private PKI hierarchies like the one in this post, your root CA certificate isn’t in any default public trust store. You must explicitly add it to the trust stores of every system that will verify your signatures. Common approaches include: Baking the root CA certificate into your container base images during the build process Distributing it through configuration management ( AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store , AWS Secrets Manager , or your existing configuration tooling) Publishing it to an internal S3 bucket with versioning and access logging Storing it as an OCI artifact in Amazon ECR alongside the images it protects Treat trust store management with the same rigor as credential management. If an attacker can inject a rogue root certificate into your trust stores, they can make forged signatures appear valid. Restrict write access to trust stores and audit changes through AWS CloudTrail or your system-level audit logs. Exporting your certificate chain requires exporting the root CA, and then any subordinate CAs that issue certificates that will be involved in verifying signatures: # Export the root CA certificate aws acm-pca get-certificate-authority-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --query Certificate --output text > root-ca.pem # Export the subordinate CA certificate. Select only the Certificate field: for a # subordinate CA this call also returns CertificateChain, and --output text would # print both on one tab-separated line, producing a file that OpenSSL can't parse. aws acm-pca get-certificate-authority-certificate \ --certificate-authority-arn \ --query Certificate --output text > sub-ca.pem # Bundle the full chain for verifiers cat root-ca.pem sub-ca.pem > trust-chain.pem Verifiers use this chain to confirm that the code-signing public key was issued by a CA they trust. The CAs in this post are created without a revocation configuration, and the verification commands that follow don’t check revocation status, which keeps the walkthrough short. In production, configure a certificate revocation list (CRL) or an Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) responder on the subordinate CA (see Plan your AWS Private CA certificate revocation method in the AWS Private CA User Guide; both work with ML-DSA CAs). If you use a CRL, distribute it alongside the trust chain and add -crl_check -CRLfile to the openssl verify command below, where is the CRL that AWS Private CA publishes to your S3 bucket, so that a revoked code-signing certificate fails verification. Verifying a binary or SBOM signature Verify the code-signing certificate against the trust chain, confirm that it is a code-signing certificate issued to the signer you expect, extract its public key, and then verify the signature with OpenSSL 3.5. The second check matters: a chain check alone accepts every certificate that the CA hierarchy has issued, including the build agent client certificates from the previous section, so pin the expected subject in your verifier configuration: # Step 1: Verify that the code-signing certificate chains to the trusted root CA and carries the # Code Signing extended key usage. -purpose codesign (OpenSSL 3.2 and later) rejects a certificate # that chains correctly but was issued for another purpose, such as a build agent's client # authentication certificate from the same subordinate CA. # trust-chain.pem contains the root CA and subordinate CA certificates distributed in the previous section. openssl verify -CAfile trust-chain.pem -purpose codesign code-signing-cert.pem # Confirm that the certificate was issued to the signer you expect. Replace with the # common name in your code-signing certificate's subject. openssl x509 -in code-signing-cert.pem -noout -subject -nameopt RFC2253 | grep -q "CN= " || { echo "Unexpected signer"; exit 1; } # Step 2: Extract the public key from the verified certificate. openssl x509 -in code-signing-cert.pem -pubkey -noout > signing-key.pem # Step 3: Verify the artifact signature using the trusted public key. openssl pkeyutl -verify \ -pubin -inkey signing-key.pem \ -in artifact.bin \ -sigfile artifact.bin.sig \ -rawin A successful verification prints Signature Verified Successfully and returns an exit status of 0 . A failed verification prints Signature Verification Failure and returns a nonzero exit status. In shell scripts, check the exit status of each command, or run the block with set -e , so that a failed certificate chain check stops the script before signature verification and a failed signature check blocks downstream actions.
