items.title: Filter, reshape, and redact logs before export with Transformers
items.summary: Logpush delivers logs in batches as quickly as possible, enabling Cloudflare to provide information almost in real time. During our recent Birthday Week , we made Logpush available on all self-serve plans and Transformers generally available. Those changes were among eight major updates to Cloudflare Observability and reflect our commitment to make every Cloudflare feature available to everyone . This post takes a deeper look at how Transformers work inside Logpush's export pipeline. Observability teams use Logpush to export Cloudflare logs to security information and event management systems (SIEMs), analytics platforms, and object storage. Before those logs reach their destination, teams may need to remove health checks, omit sensitive fields, or reshape records for dashboards and investigations. Today, this often requires a separate processing service that teams must deploy, scale, monitor, and maintain. For example, a team that collects logs from multiple CDNs can add a static provider field to normalize records before they reach its analytics platform. Teams also pay to export, ingest, and store records they discard as soon as they arrive, so filtering them before delivery can reduce downstream data volume and cost. With Transformers, that processing moves into the Logpush export workflow.Teams define a SQL query to filter records, redact sensitive data, and reshape the output by adding, renaming, removing, or nesting fields. Logpush applies the query before export, so each destination receives data in the form it needs. We made this workflow simple for customers by embedding a SQL transformation engine in Logpush's high-throughput export pipeline while keeping performance and resource use predictable. How Logpush Transformers work A Transformer is a SQL query written for a specific Logpush dataset. The query references fields from that dataset and defines which records and fields Logpush should export. Logpush applies the query to each batch before export. Records that do not match the WHERE clause are removed. For the remaining records, the output of the SELECT statement becomes the exported record. Transformers can change the structure and contents of each record, and the transformed results are exported in NDJSON format. Customers can create, preview, and manage Transformers in the Cloudflare dashboard through Transformer Studio or programmatically through the API . After saving a Transformer, they can attach it to a compatible NDJSON Logpush job that uses the same dataset. Each update creates a new version, so customers can review how a Transformer has changed over time. The following example reshapes a Cloudflare HTTP request log to match a team-defined schema used across CDN providers. It does not convert between serialization formats: both the input and output use NDJSON. The Transformer renames and nests fields, redacts part of the client IP address, adds provider and error information, removes unused fields, and filters out internal and health-check traffic: The resulting NDJSON record uses the normalized schema: How Transformers executes SQL with Apache DataFusion and Arrow Cloudflare's data pipeline ingests more than one billion events per second. Its Logpush delivery service, which we call Bufstream, delivers more than 110 million Logpush records per second to customer destinations. It runs across hundreds of Kubernetes pods, each claiming a time slice of data from Buftee , Cloudflare's distributed log-based in-house message broker. This model distributes work horizontally across Logpush jobs. Job volume follows a Pareto-like distribution: most jobs operate at lower volumes, while a small number of high-volume jobs process millions of logs each second. Transformers needed to meet the same operational requirements as the rest of Logpush: reliable delivery, high throughput, and predictable resource use without introducing additional failure scenarios into the export hot path. Our initial prototype ran customer-defined WebAssembly Transformers in Cloudflare Workers, which provides globally distributed, isolated compute. However, invoking a Worker would insert a network call into the Logpush export path. That remote dependency could introduce transient timeouts and retries, reducing delivery throughput and increasing delivery latency. We decided to keep Transformer execution in-process within our delivery service to prioritize reliability and delivery throughput. We evaluated several SQL execution engines and selected Apache DataFusion , which already powers Cloudflare Basin . Apache DataFusion is a Rust query engine built on Apache Arrow, with a SQL planner and vectorized, columnar execution engine. In a benchmark, executing a prepared Transformer against a synthetic 5,000-row http_requests batch from a single Go goroutine took about 3 ms, equivalent to roughly 1.6 million rows per second. Attaching a Transformer to a job adds CPU work to its processing path. Bufstream uses per-job transform parallelism so high-volume jobs can execute transform batches concurrently. Embedding DataFusion in Bufstream lets those batches use the service's existing delivery infrastructure, including its scheduling, batching, and destination controls, without introducing a separate transformation tier or network hop. Choosing DataFusion meant connecting Bufstream, which is written in Go, to an engine written in Rust. The next challenge was moving typed batches efficiently across that boundary. The final design of the in-process Transformer pipeline is shown in the diagram below. From records to columns Bufstream receives compressed Logpush batches containing Cap'n Proto records from Buftee. For a job with a Transformer attached, Bufstream decompresses the batch, parses the eligible logs, and builds a typed Apache Arrow RecordBatch before executing the transform. Apache Arrow is a language-independent, columnar in-memory format designed for efficient analytics on modern CPUs and GPUs. It represents flat and nested data as typed, contiguous columns. Arrow IPC gives Bufstream and DataFusion a standard way to exchange batches across the foreign function interface (FFI) boundary between Go and Rust, exposed through a C application binary interface (ABI) and called from Go using cgo , Go's mechanism for calling C code. The Go and Rust runtimes do not share ownership of transform data. Go passes a pointer to its input Arrow IPC buffer to Rust only for the duration of the cgo call, and Rust does not retain that pointer after returning. Rust owns the transformed output buffer; Go copies it into Go-managed memory and then explicitly releases the Rust allocation. This makes ownership and lifetimes explicit across the language boundary, avoiding cross-runtime memory-management bugs. Using Arrow IPC means the Rust DataFusion wrapper can use an Arrow StreamReader to read typed RecordBatch values, rather than parse individual rows from an intermediate format such as JSON and rebuild typed Arrow columns for execution. Field types, nullability, and nested values are represented consistently on both sides of the boundary, so DataFusion receives data in its native columnar model. Crossing the Go/Rust boundary is not free: batches still need to be serialized, decoded, and managed in memory. Arrow IPC keeps that work batch-oriented and avoids per-record parsing and conversion. This makes the boundary a better fit for Logpush's high-throughput delivery pipeline while retaining schema validation against the Logpush dataset definition. Every Arrow batch needs a schema describing its fields and types. Rather than infer that schema from the logs in a particular batch, Bufstream supplies a generated schema from each Logpush dataset's specification. This gives DataFusion a stable view of the available fields and types, enabling query validation. The table named in a Transformer's FROM clause selects which dataset schema the query uses. For example, this Transformer queries the http_requests dataset: Executing the transform When a customer saves a Transformer through the API or Transformer Studio, Cloudflare stores its SQL query in R2. Bufstream retrieves the query through a multi-layer cache and translates it into a reusable DataFusion logical plan that defines the scan, filters, projections, and expressions. Bufstream prepares this plan once per time slice of a job's data and reuses it for every Arrow batch in that slice. For every new Arrow batch, the Rust wrapper binds the batch as the plan’s table input, executes the query, and returns Arrow batches containing the selected records and fields. Transformers are designed to fail closed. If a transform cannot be executed, Bufstream neither advances the job's delivery offset nor sends the untransformed batch. Delivering raw data in place of transformed data could violate the schema, filtering, or redaction assumptions of downstream pipelines, so Bufstream opts to re-attempt failed transforms instead. To prevent a persistently failing job from consuming capacity needed by healthy jobs, Bufstream progressively delays retries and reports errors on the job. Jobs that remain in a failing state for an extended period are automatically disabled. Customers can monitor successful and failed transformations, data volume before and after transformation, and transformation duration in the Transformer Health view of the Health tab in Logpush. Returning to the export pipeline After execution, Bufstream converts the Arrow output into NDJSON logs. It batches, gzip-compresses, and uploads those logs to the configured destination. Destinations accept data at different rates and can temporarily slow down. Bufstream adjusts the number of upload goroutines while respecting destination concurrency limits. By embedding SQL execution in Bufstream, Transformers use Logpush’s existing distributed infrastructure, batching, and destination controls. Cloudflare’s data pipeline handles that complexity, while customers create and apply a Transformer with only a few steps. Get started Open Transformer Studio from the Logpush page in the Cloudflare dashboard and follow these steps: Choose the Logpush dataset you want to transform. Write your SQL query and preview it against a sample record. Save the Transformer. Attach it to a matching Logpush job. Transformers is available on Free, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans. See the Transformers documentation for setup details and the Logpush pricing documentation for current pricing information.

Attaching a Transformer to a job adds CPU work to its processing path. Bufstream uses per-job transform parallelism so high-volume jobs can execute transform batches concurrently. Embedding DataFusion in Bufstream lets those batches use the service's existing delivery infrastructure, including its scheduling, batching, and destination controls, without introducing a separate transformation tier or network hop.

Choosing DataFusion meant connecting Bufstream, which is written in Go, to an engine written in Rust. The next challenge was moving typed batches efficiently across that boundary.

The final design of the in-process Transformer pipeline is shown in the diagram below.

From records to columns

Bufstream receives compressed Logpush batches containing Cap'n Proto records from Buftee. For a job with a Transformer attached, Bufstream decompresses the batch, parses the eligible logs, and builds a typed Apache Arrow RecordBatch before executing the transform.

Apache Arrow is a language-independent, columnar in-memory format designed for efficient analytics on modern CPUs and GPUs. It represents flat and nested data as typed, contiguous columns. Arrow IPC gives Bufstream and DataFusion a standard way to exchange batches across the foreign function interface (FFI) boundary between Go and Rust, exposed through a C application binary interface (ABI) and called from Go using cgo, Go's mechanism for calling C code.

The Go and Rust runtimes do not share ownership of transform data. Go passes a pointer to its input Arrow IPC buffer to Rust only for the duration of the cgo call, and Rust does not retain that pointer after returning. Rust owns the transformed output buffer; Go copies it into Go-managed memory and then explicitly releases the Rust allocation. This makes ownership and lifetimes explicit across the language boundary, avoiding cross-runtime memory-management bugs.

Using Arrow IPC means the Rust DataFusion wrapper can use an Arrow StreamReader to read typed RecordBatch values, rather than parse individual rows from an intermediate format such as JSON and rebuild typed Arrow columns for execution. Field types, nullability, and nested values are represented consistently on both sides of the boundary, so DataFusion receives data in its native columnar model.

Crossing the Go/Rust boundary is not free: batches still need to be serialized, decoded, and managed in memory. Arrow IPC keeps that work batch-oriented and avoids per-record parsing and conversion. This makes the boundary a better fit for Logpush's high-throughput delivery pipeline while retaining schema validation against the Logpush dataset definition.

Every Arrow batch needs a schema describing its fields and types. Rather than infer that schema from the logs in a particular batch, Bufstream supplies a generated schema from each Logpush dataset's specification. This gives DataFusion a stable view of the available fields and types, enabling query validation. The table named in a Transformer's FROM clause selects which dataset schema the query uses. For example, this Transformer queries the http_requests dataset:

Executing the transform

When a customer saves a Transformer through the API or Transformer Studio, Cloudflare stores its SQL query in R2. Bufstream retrieves the query through a multi-layer cache and translates it into a reusable DataFusion logical plan that defines the scan, filters, projections, and expressions. Bufstream prepares this plan once per time slice of a job's data and reuses it for every Arrow batch in that slice. For every new Arrow batch, the Rust wrapper binds the batch as the plan’s table input, executes the query, and returns Arrow batches containing the selected records and fields.

Transformers are designed to fail closed. If a transform cannot be executed, Bufstream neither advances the job's delivery offset nor sends the untransformed batch. Delivering raw data in place of transformed data could violate the schema, filtering, or redaction assumptions of downstream pipelines, so Bufstream opts to re-attempt failed transforms instead.

To prevent a persistently failing job from consuming capacity needed by healthy jobs, Bufstream progressively delays retries and reports errors on the job. Jobs that remain in a failing state for an extended period are automatically disabled. Customers can monitor successful and failed transformations, data volume before and after transformation, and transformation duration in the Transformer Health view of the Health tab in Logpush.

Returning to the export pipeline

After execution, Bufstream converts the Arrow output into NDJSON logs. It batches, gzip-compresses, and uploads those logs to the configured destination. Destinations accept data at different rates and can temporarily slow down. Bufstream adjusts the number of upload goroutines while respecting destination concurrency limits.

By embedding SQL execution in Bufstream, Transformers use Logpush’s existing distributed infrastructure, batching, and destination controls. Cloudflare’s data pipeline handles that complexity, while customers create and apply a Transformer with only a few steps.

Get started

Open Transformer Studio from the Logpush page in the Cloudflare dashboard and follow these steps:

  1. Choose the Logpush dataset you want to transform.
  2. Write your SQL query and preview it against a sample record.
  3. Save the Transformer.
  4. Attach it to a matching Logpush job.

Transformers is available on Free, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans. See the Transformers documentation for setup details and the Logpush pricing documentation for current pricing information.

items.title: Patched Is Not Evicted: Inside CCB's Threat Actor Profile of The Gentlemen
items.summary: In about a year, The Gentlemen went from a Qilin affiliate crew in a $48,000 payment dispute to one of the two most active ransomware operations in the world. Its edge isn't novel malware. It's packaging: a centrally maintained pool of an estimated 14,700 pre-compromised FortiGate devices handed to affiliates as a service, an EDR-killer suite that the operators maintain themselves, worm-like propagation that tries up to 21 remote execution paths per host, and a 90/10 revenue split designed to recruit affiliates. Kevin Holvoet, Threat Research Center Lead at the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB), joins Sean O'Connor to walk through CCB's new TLP:CLEAR threat actor profile. We'll cover what the May 2026 leak of the group's own backend revealed, and how chain victimization turns one breach into leverage against the next. We'll also look at how a national CSIRT weighs a public government claim of Russian state interest against the technical evidence. Then the Monday question. Patching CVE-2024-55591 doesn't evict access the group has already catalogued. Recovery plans that assume backups are safe from a domain compromise won't hold. And blocklisting drivers loses to an actor that weaponizes new BYOVD bugs within days.

items.title: Google DevSite Flaw Let Attackers Execute Remote Code Through Forged Flask Sessions
items.summary: A critical vulnerability in Google’s shared DevSite platform could have allowed an unauthenticated attacker to forge Flask session cookies and trigger remote code execution across several Google-owned developer websites, according to researcher Simon Koeck. The issue affected the OAuth flow used by Google developer documentation sites, including developers.google.com, firebase.google.com, developer.android.com, source.android.com, and docs.partner.android.com. Google reportedly fixed the flaw on October 7, 2026, after receiving the report in August and awarding the researcher $90,000 through its Vulnerability Reward Program. The bug chain started with a Flask session cookie issued by the DevSite OAuth endpoint . Flask’s standard session mechanism signs cookies to protect them from changes, but it does not encrypt their contents. That means users can read the stored data, even though they can’t alter it without the server’s secret signing key. Flask documentation states that the SECRET_KEY is used to sign session cookies and other security-sensitive data securely. In this case, the cookie reportedly held more than a CSRF token and return URL. After decoding the compressed payload, the researcher found a serialized OAuth flow object that included a Google OAuth client ID and client secret. Critical Google DevSite Flaw The discovery became more serious when Simon Koeck confirmed that the exposed OAuth client secret also served as the Flask session signing key, exposing the key within session data. Anyone who obtained a cookie could recover the secret, generate a new valid signature, and create a forged session that the server would trust. This removed the main security control protecting the application from client-side session tampering. The forged-session issue alone could have enabled attackers to alter values held in the Flask session. The code-execution risk came from how the DevSite OAuth callback handled an object stored in that session. The application reportedly Base64-decoded the OAuth flow data and passed it to Python’s pickle.loads() function. Python’s documentation warns that the pickle module is not secure and that developers must unpickle only data they fully trust, because a malicious pickle payload can execute code while it is being restored. An attacker with the signing key could therefore create a valid session containing a crafted pickle object. When the OAuth callback processed the forged cookie, it would verify the signature, retrieve the attacker-controlled flow object, and unpickle it. That could cause the server to run code chosen by the attacker. Simon Koeck did not run system commands on Google infrastructure. Instead, the proof of concept used a harmless time-delay payload. Requests containing the forged payload were reportedly delayed by the exact number of seconds specified in the serialized object, showing the server processed the data and ran the selected Python function. This was an especially dangerous chain because no Google account was required to reach the OAuth authorization endpoint and receive the session cookie. The issue also affected a shared platform rather than one isolated site, expanding its possible impact across Google’s developer web properties. Google’s prior fixes for critical cloud code-execution issues show why this category receives high priority in vulnerability-reward programs. In a separate 2026 case, Google addressed a CVSS 10.0 Application Integration flaw that enabled remote code execution in production environments. The case combined several dangerous design choices. First, a client-side cookie contained sensitive OAuth material. Second, the exposed OAuth secret was reused as the Flask signing secret. Third, the application deserialized session-controlled data with pickle, which is unsafe once an attacker can bypass integrity checks. Simon Koeck said Google remediated the problem by rotating the exposed OAuth client secrets , invalidating sessions signed with them, separating Flask SECRET_KEY values from OAuth credentials, and moving OAuth flow objects to server-side storage. The safer design is for a browser cookie to carry only an opaque session reference. At the same time, sensitive state remains on the server. Developers should also remove pickle from data paths that a browser, user, partner integration, or external system can influence. JSON or another data-only format, combined with strict schema validation, prevents deserialization from becoming code execution. For related coverage, readers can review Cyber Security News reporting on Google Cloud production RCE vulnerabilities and Google Gemini CLI command-execution flaws . Google’s DevSite incident is another reminder that a signed session is only trustworthy when the signing key stays secret, and the application never turns attacker-controlled session data into executable objects. items.title: The Hidden AI Security Risks Threatening Businesses
Critical GitLab Vulnerability Enables Arbitrary Code Execution Attacks on Servers
items.summary: GitLab has released urgent security updates to fix a critical vulnerability that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected servers without logging in. Tracked as CVE-2026-97229, the flaw carries the maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and affects both GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. The company released patches on October 12, 2026. The vulnerability involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s CI/CD regular expression compiler. GitLab says insufficient regular expression validation could allow an unauthenticated attacker to trigger code execution through a specially crafted expression inside a CI/CD configuration. Regular expressions are text patterns used to match or filter data. Here, processing a malicious pattern could compromise the GitLab server itself. According to GitLab’s security advisory , exploitation is possible under certain conditions. The published description does not provide a complete attack sequence or identify the exact conditions required. However, the CVSS vector indicates network access, low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction. It also assigns high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. This is server-side code execution, rather than malicious JavaScript running in a visitor’s browser. That difference makes the issue particularly serious for organizations hosting development projects on affected GitLab installations. Successful exploitation could threaten the server’s data and operation. The release notice does not state that attackers have exploited this vulnerability in real-world attacks. GitLab credited security researcher joaxcar with reporting the issue through its HackerOne bug bounty program. The company previously patched critical GitLab CI/CD regex vulnerabilities in September. Those earlier flaws required authentication, while the newly disclosed issue could allow exploitation without an account. The advisory does not establish whether these vulnerabilities share the same underlying cause. Affected Versions and Required Updates The affected releases are GitLab CE and EE versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8, from 19.3 before 19.3.4, and from 19.4 before 19.4.2. Administrators should upgrade affected self-managed installations immediately to the corresponding patched release. GitLab.com already runs the patched version, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. The release also addresses other security weaknesses, including cross-site scripting, authorization failures, and a prompt-related issue in GitLab Duo Agent Platform. Earlier GitLab security updates covering CI/CD authorization flaws show why administrators should review the full patch notice rather than focus only on the headline vulnerability. GitLab warns that version 19.3.4 has a known bug affecting merge request pages when the Ona integration is enabled. A fix is planned for 19.3.5. Administrators should account for this issue during upgrades without overlooking the urgent security fix. GitLab’s linked instance security guidance provides broader protection advice. items.title: WhatsApp Attachment Deploys Malware That Gains SYSTEM Access on Windows
items.summary: A malicious WhatsApp attachment is being used to deploy a Windows remote access trojan that can reach SYSTEM-level access, giving its operators deep control over infected machines. The campaign begins with a ZIP archive carrying a financial-document lure and an executable named Statement.exe . Once the recipient opens the file, the malware starts a long, hidden chain that moves from a user-level process into a Windows service running with LocalSystem rights. The final payload, named VulcanRAT207.A, gives remote operators the ability to collect system data, run commands, manage files, capture screens, record keystrokes, create or change local accounts, and deploy more payloads. The campaign also uses a signed driver to terminate selected security processes and creates a scheduled task that can restart the RAT with SYSTEM privileges after a reboot. This makes the WhatsApp-delivered file a serious risk for organizations where staff receive invoices, statements, tax files, or payment-related documents through messaging apps. Analysts at Morphisec identified the malware chain and described how it moves from a WhatsApp attachment to a full WebSocket-based RAT connection. Their research shows that the actors split the activity into separate stages for unpacking, privilege elevation, code injection, payload download, security-tool disruption, persistence, and remote control. WhatsApp Attachment Deploys Malware This design reduces the amount of suspicious behavior visible from any single file and makes investigation harder. The first executable is heavily packed with NRV2E compression, which hides the real loader from basic static checks. After it runs, the loader checks whether the machine looks like a real user system rather than an automated analysis environment. It reviews disk space, display details, memory, CPU resources, event logs, Registry keys, virtual-machine markers, and security products. It also uses timing checks meant to stop execution in slow sandboxes or emulated systems. VulcanRAT207.A full attack chain (Source – Morphisec) Similar use of the PoolParty Variant 7 injection method was reported in Cyber Security News coverage of ValleyRAT LINE installer activity , showing why defenders should watch unusual Windows thread-pool and I/O completion behavior. If the malware does not already have administrator permissions, it attempts elevation through COM objects and can fall back to the Windows runas function. It then enables SeDebugPrivilege , restores a clean copy of ntdll.dll to remove user-mode security hooks, and injects downloader shellcode into the process hosting the Windows Task Scheduler service. Instead of using the more common CreateRemoteThread method, it uses PoolParty Variant 7 and the Windows I/O completion system to run code inside the trusted service process. Since the Task Scheduler runs as LocalSystem, later components inherit SYSTEM access rather than needing to elevate again. The injected shellcode contacts 61[.]18[.]208[.]27 over port 8888 and downloads a deployment bundle into memory. The bundle includes a legitimate Intel-signed VulkanInfo utility, a malicious vulkan-1.dll , a vulkan-1.bin RAT container, and a deployment DLL. The threat uses a technique known as DLL sideloading, where a legitimate application loads an attacker-controlled DLL placed beside it. The same method has appeared in other WhatsApp-focused campaigns, including this report on WhatsApp Web session hijacking , where trusted Windows programs were also abused to load malware. Before setting up persistence, the deployment DLL attempts to install GoFly64.sys , a legitimately signed Chinese network-filter driver. It creates a temporary driver file and service, then sends process IDs to the driver through the 0x12227A control code. Malware act at kernel level Morphisec found that this path targets bdservicehost.exe and bduserhost.exe , which are connected to Baidu security software. The use of a signed driver is important because it allows the malware to act at kernel level and end selected protection processes. Security teams should treat unexpected driver-service creation, especially from temporary paths under the Windows drivers directory, as a high-priority event. For persistence, the malware writes vulkaninfo-64.exe , vulkan-1.dll , and vulkan-1.bin into C:\Program Files\Common Files\ . It then creates a SYSTEM scheduled task named USOPrivate Kit or USOPrivate , using names that may look related to normal Microsoft update activity. HTTP Shellcode (Source – Morphisec) When the task starts the signed VulkanInfo utility, the application searches its local folder for vulkan-1.dll and loads the malicious file. The DLL reads the nearby .bin file, rebuilds the final RAT in memory, and keeps the trusted host process running. Earlier Cyber Security News reporting on TA4922 malware delivery chains also documented the use of Vulkan-related files such as vulkan-1.dll and vulkan-1.bin in the wider malware ecosystem. VulcanRAT207.A communicates with the same server through WebSocket version 13 after first using HTTP for stage retrieval. The RAT can gather host details, user accounts, network connections, installed applications, running processes, services, event logs, and files selected by the operator. It can also open remote command shells, capture the desktop, log keystrokes, control the mouse and keyboard, alter clipboard data, block network traffic through Windows Filtering Platform rules, and inject payloads into other processes. Its command set can create a local administrator account, change passwords, download files, run executables, and even register additional drivers. Organizations should block executable content received through WhatsApp and other messaging platforms, particularly ZIP files that claim to contain financial statements or tax documents. Endpoint teams should hunt for Task Scheduler processes showing unusual memory activity, creation of the USOPrivate Kit task, unexpected files in C:\Program Files\Common Files\ , and execution of vulkaninfo-64.exe from that directory. Monitoring signed-driver installation and process termination attempts against endpoint-security products can also help stop this chain before the RAT becomes active. Morphisec found that this path targets bdservicehost.exe and bduserhost.exe, which are connected to Baidu security software. The use of a signed driver is important because it allows the malware to act at kernel level and end selected protection processes.

Security teams should treat unexpected driver-service creation, especially from temporary paths under the Windows drivers directory, as a high-priority event.

For persistence, the malware writes vulkaninfo-64.exe, vulkan-1.dll, and vulkan-1.bin into C:\Program Files\Common Files\.

It then creates a SYSTEM scheduled task named USOPrivate Kit or USOPrivate, using names that may look related to normal Microsoft update activity.

HTTP Shellcode (Source – Morphisec)

When the task starts the signed VulkanInfo utility, the application searches its local folder for vulkan-1.dll and loads the malicious file. The DLL reads the nearby .bin file, rebuilds the final RAT in memory, and keeps the trusted host process running.

Earlier Cyber Security News reporting on TA4922 malware delivery chains also documented the use of Vulkan-related files such as vulkan-1.dll and vulkan-1.bin in the wider malware ecosystem.

VulcanRAT207.A communicates with the same server through WebSocket version 13 after first using HTTP for stage retrieval.

The RAT can gather host details, user accounts, network connections, installed applications, running processes, services, event logs, and files selected by the operator.

It can also open remote command shells, capture the desktop, log keystrokes, control the mouse and keyboard, alter clipboard data, block network traffic through Windows Filtering Platform rules, and inject payloads into other processes.

Its command set can create a local administrator account, change passwords, download files, run executables, and even register additional drivers.

Organizations should block executable content received through WhatsApp and other messaging platforms, particularly ZIP files that claim to contain financial statements or tax documents.

Endpoint teams should hunt for Task Scheduler processes showing unusual memory activity, creation of the USOPrivate Kit task, unexpected files in C:\Program Files\Common Files\, and execution of vulkaninfo-64.exe from that directory.

Monitoring signed-driver installation and process termination attempts against endpoint-security products can also help stop this chain before the RAT becomes active.

items.title: Leading digital change when nobody prepared you for it
items.summary: By Louise John, Head of IT Service Delivery at Virgin Active For IT managers, unexpected projects and changing business priorities are normal part of the job. You might have spent months planning your team’s workload, but only to be told with little warning that a new software solution needs to be implemented within six weeks. Whatever the circumstances, the responsibility for delivering these projects often falls on IT teams, even when they have had little involvement in the decisions behind them. As a manager, this can be particularly challenging because you are expected to deliver results within tight deadlines, while also managing your team’s existing workload, keeping up staff morale while also protecting them from burnout. So, how can you support your team when unexpected projects land on their desks? Prioritise and manage expectations The first thing I would recommend is establishing what actually needs to be delivered and by when. If a new software implementation has been given a six-week deadline, what are the absolute essentials that need to be completed within that timeframe? Rather than attempting to deliver everything at once, identify what is achievable and communicate this to senior leadership. Managing expectations upwards is just as important as managing the team responsible for delivery. It’s also important to involve your team in these conversations. Be honest about what is expected, explain the priorities and ask what they realistically believe can be achieved. Protect your team’s wellbeing Unexpected projects inevitably create pressure, particularly when teams are already managing demanding workloads. As a manager, you need to recognise this and consider what additional support might be required. Could working hours be more flexible? Can existing projects be paused or reassigned? Do you need additional resources? If employees are required to work extra hours, can they take time back once the project is completed? It’s also important to establish boundaries and make sure your team isn’t expected to deliver everything simultaneously. When workloads become overwhelming, it helps to focus on one task at a time rather than worrying about the hundred things still to do. Finally, don’t underestimate the importance of keeping morale high. Even during the busiest periods, celebrating small wins, recognising people’s efforts and maintaining a sense of humour can make a big difference. Ultimately, IT managers cannot always control the projects or deadlines handed to them, but they can control how they support their teams through them. Louise is speaking at DTX + UCX London 2026 , taking place at ExCeL London on 14 and 15 October. Join Louise on Wednesday 14 October, from 12:10pm to 12:50pm , on the Design & Delivery Stage , for a panel discussion titled Caught in the middle: Leading digital change when nobody prepared you for it . She will be joined by Rebecca d’Orazi Flavoni, Digital Growth and Training Consultant at RDF Training & Consulting; Greg Ferrari, Executive Director of Performance and Transformation at AAT; and Roger Kirby, Senior Enterprise Architect at AstraZeneca. Together, they will explore how managers can balance pressure from senior leadership, protect their teams from burnout and successfully deliver digital change, even when they haven’t been given the tools or context to do so.

items.title: Google AitM Phishing Kit Uses WebSockets to Bypass MFA in Real Time
items.summary: A Google account phishing kit uses live WebSocket connections to guide victims through fake sign-in screens, relay authentication requests, and steal authenticated sessions. The campaign shows how attackers can get past MFA by forwarding login steps in real time rather than breaking the security checks themselves. The operation targets people linked to research organizations in Taiwan. Its emails pose as invitations to academic and policy events, using real event details, false sender identities, and hidden registration links to make a credential theft attempt look like routine professional correspondence. Researchers from Cisco Talos identified the campaign, tracked as UAT-11985, during mid-2026 and detailed its phishing kit in an October threat research report published on October 8. Their analysis describes an operator-driven system that combines HTTP requests with WebSocket updates to mirror Google’s authentication process. Google AitM Phishing Kit The emails impersonated the Taiwan European Union Centre, NCCU Institute of International Relations, and Taiwan Research Institute. When a recipient checked the supposed senders with those institutions, none could confirm the individuals were employees or representatives. Accurate event information helped the attackers build trust around fabricated identities. Each message followed a similar pattern: a policy-themed opening, praise tailored to the recipient, and registration instructions. Impersonated Taiwan European Union Centre event (Source – Cisco Talos) The approach draws victims toward the same session theft risk seen in Tycoon 2FA phishing attacks , where a convincing login page sits between users and a real authentication service. Talos noted signs of AI-assisted writing, including repeated sentence patterns, broad compliments, and quick changes for different topics and recipients. However, the researchers could not prove that a large language model wrote the complete emails. The finding supports likely AI assistance, not confirmed fully automated content generation. The attackers also copied legitimate event posters and replaced their QR codes with malicious ones. Talos suggested that printed posters could expose additional people who never received the original email. A familiar design therefore offered no assurance that its registration code led to a safe destination. How the WebSocket MFA Relay Works Victims first encounter a fake Google Form that redirects them to a copied Google sign-in page. Unlike a basic password collection form, the kit lets an operator control each authentication stage. Similar JWR WebSocket phishing techniques show how persistent connections can support live interaction, although that framework targets banking and payment information. The kit separates data uploads from screen updates. HTTP POST requests send browser details, account identifiers, passwords, and challenge submissions to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Legitimate poster (left) and modified poster (right) (Source – Cisco Talos) A persistent WebSocket connection carries instructions back to the page, telling it which authentication screen to display next. This split keeps uploads separate while allowing rapid changes during login. The first request, google_login_start , collects language settings, user-agent information, screen size, and mobile-device status. After creating a session, the script opens its WebSocket connection. The google_input_identifier event then sends the victim’s email address or phone number for checking against Google’s real authentication service. When a password is entered, google_login_check forwards it with the account identifier and browser information. If Google requests another verification step, the attacker updates the fake interface through WebSocket messages. Form forcibly redirects to a spoofed Google login page (Source – Cisco Talos) Talos reports that this coordinated relay enables the theft of authenticated session tokens, allowing account takeover after the victim completes the requested checks. The page also hides its JavaScript through Base64 strings and repeated array rotation. Its interface supports Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and English. Talos assessed with moderate confidence that Simplified Chinese was the developer’s main working language; that finding alone does not establish nationality or state sponsorship. The important distinction is that a completed MFA prompt does not guarantee a safe session. As documented in Mirage2FA session cookie theft , attackers can reuse authentication material captured during a relayed login. Organizations should favor phishing-resistant authentication, verify unexpected invitations independently, and investigate suspected session theft rather than relying only on password changes. items.title: Ledger Confirms Unauthorized Hardware Implant in Crypto Wallet Sold by CryptoBilis
items.summary: Ledger has confirmed that a cryptocurrency hardware wallet linked to reported fund losses contained an unauthorized hardware implant, bringing physical tampering into its investigation of devices sold through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis. The finding raises supply chain security concerns, but Ledger has not confirmed how the implant worked or whether it caused every reported theft. In an October 10 statement , Ledger Support said, “Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant.” CryptoBilis has stopped selling all hardware wallets while the investigation continues, and Ledger is contacting affected customers. The company’s October 11 update said all confirmed cases connected to the October 9 draining incident involved devices sold through CryptoBilis. Ledger described the number of affected devices as limited and said its own systems and direct sales channels remained unaffected. It is also working with relevant authorities. 72 hour update on reseller CryptoBilis incident As the investigation continues, we are working with relevant authorities. The volume of impacted devices is limited. We know this is concerning, especially for those directly affected, and we are reaching out to impacted users.… — Ledger (@Ledger) October 11, 2026 The investigation began after customers reported missing cryptocurrency from wallets associated with devices purchased through CryptoBilis, which serves Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines. Blockchain investigator Specter estimated possible losses above $86 million across Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tron. That figure has not been independently confirmed, and Ledger has not established a final loss total. Hardware Implant Raises Supply Chain Concerns Hardware wallets normally keep private keys offline, reducing exposure to malware on connected computers. A physical implant creates a different risk because an added component could target information displayed during setup rather than attack the wallet’s core security system. Security researcher Mark Karpelès described suspected implants that monitor the wallet screen and send the recovery phrase through a cellular connection. Reported components include a small circuit board, a microcontroller, an antenna, an LTE chip, and an eSIM. These findings remain researcher observations, not a complete technical explanation confirmed by Ledger. A recovery phrase allows someone to restore a wallet and control its funds. If an attacker captures that phrase during setup, they may not need continued access to the original device. Earlier reporting on fake Ledger apps targeting macOS users shows how criminals also seek these secrets through software tricks. PoisonSeed phishing campaigns have similarly used false wallet upgrade pages to collect recovery phrases. A separate post by Johannes claimed a modified device had been bought from an official reseller in Europe. The account said that wallet had not lost funds. This claim has not been confirmed by Ledger and should not be treated as proof that the confirmed CryptoBilis incident extends beyond its stated scope. Ledger advises CryptoBilis buyers not to initialize unused devices. Customers who already completed setup should move assets to a new device purchased from Ledger and use a newly generated recovery phrase. Reusing the old phrase would not address the risk of that phrase already being exposed. Affected users should contact official Ledger Support and report suspected theft to local law enforcement. Ledger also warned that scammers may exploit the incident and said it will never call, send direct messages, or request a customer’s 24-word recovery phrase. The company is reviewing reseller controls and hardware protections. It has reminded distributors to buy only through authorized channels and never restock returned products. The investigation still needs to establish where tampering occurred, how many devices were modified, and which losses are directly connected to the confirmed implant. Ledger has not publicly identified who installed the unauthorized hardware component. Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min. items.title: Microsoft to expand Azure Maia system to multi-gigawatt deployments
items.summary: Azure Maia 200 now in production; Azure Maia 300 coming in 2027 As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. YouTube Video Click here to load media Maia 200: Driving the workloads that Microsoft runs at scale The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. Maia 300: Scaling more useful AI within every megawatt AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Azure Maia 300 system Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. Azure Maia 200 now in production; Azure Maia 300 coming in 2027

As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services.

The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot, and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models, Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios.

Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.

YouTube Video

Click here to load media

Maia 200: Driving the workloads that Microsoft runs at scale

The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system.

That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure.

Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden.

Maia 300: Scaling more useful AI within every megawatt

AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve.

Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. items.title: A simple script to benchmark/exercise vim syntax highlighting

'.vim' if empty ( get ( b :, 'current_syntax' , '' )) echoerr 'Cannot load syntax for: ' . syntax_name qall ! endif syntime on for lnum in range ( 1 , line ( '$' )) call synID ( lnum , 1 , 1 ) endfor let report_file = getcwd () .. '/output-' .. strftime ( '%Y%m %d -%H%M%S' ) .. '.txt' let saved_columns = & columns let & columns = max ([ saved_columns , 2000 ]) let raw_report = execute ( 'syntime report' ) let & columns = saved_columns let entries = [] let total = [] let name_width = strlen ( 'NAME' ) for report_line in split ( raw_report , " \n " ) if report_line =~ # '^\s*TOTAL\s\+COUNT\>' continue endif let fields = matchlist ( report_line , \ '^\s*\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(.*\)$' ) if ! empty ( fields ) call add ( entries , fields [ 1 : 7 ]) let name_width = max ([ name_width , strlen ( fields [ 6 ])]) else let fields = matchlist ( report_line , '^\s*\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\d\+\)\s*$' ) if ! empty ( fields ) let total = fields [ 1 : 2 ] endif endif endfor let aligned_report = [ printf ( 'Syntax: %s Lines: %d ' , syntax_name , line ( '$' )), '' ] call add ( aligned_report , printf ( ' %-13s %8s %7s %12s %12s %-*s %s ' , \ 'TOTAL' , 'COUNT' , 'MATCH' , 'SLOWEST' , 'AVERAGE' , name_width , \ 'NAME' , 'PATTERN' )) for fields in entries call add ( aligned_report , printf ( ' %-13s %8s %7s %12s %12s %-*s %s ' , \ fields [ 0 ], fields [ 1 ], fields [ 2 ], fields [ 3 ], fields [ 4 ], \ name_width , fields [ 5 ], fields [ 6 ])) endfor if ! items.summary_html:
Because I dislike tree-sitter, I've been looking at optimizing vim syntax-based code highlighting, sending ~30 pull requests as a result. It's surprisingly non-trivial to profile syntax highlighting, as vim has some pty/terminal relate checks, as well as a bunch of screen/display optimizations, so I've been using the following script quite extensively:

" Profile a runtime syntax file with a sequential full-buffer parse.
" Pass this as Vim's vimrc, e.g.:
"   src/vim -Nu profile_syntax.vim file.py
" Inputs are extended to 100,000 lines. The report is written to
" output-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.txt in the current directory.
set nocompatible
execute 'set runtimepath^=' . fnameescape(getcwd() . '/runtime')
filetype on

function! ProfileSyntax()
  let input_lines = getline(1, '$')
  let target_lines = 100000
  " Repeat the original input, using a partial final copy if needed.
  while line('$') < target_lines
    let copy_count = min([len(input_lines), target_lines - line('$')])
    call append(line('$'), input_lines[: copy_count - 1])
  endwhile

  let syntax_name = &l:filetype
  if empty(syntax_name)
    echoerr 'No filetype detected; cannot profile syntax.'
    qall!
  endif

  syntax clear
  unlet! b:current_syntax
  " Load through 'runtimepath' so compound filetypes, after/syntax and
  " :runtime! includes all resolve the way a normal session would.
  execute 'runtime! syntax/' . syntax_name . '.vim'
  if empty(get(b:, 'current_syntax', ''))
    echoerr 'Cannot load syntax for: ' . syntax_name
    qall!
  endif
  syntime on

  for lnum in range(1, line('$'))
    call synID(lnum, 1, 1)
  endfor

  let report_file = getcwd() .. '/output-' .. strftime('%Y%m%d-%H%M%S') .. '.txt'
  let saved_columns = &columns
  let &columns = max([saved_columns, 2000])
  let raw_report = execute('syntime report')
  let &columns = saved_columns

  let entries = []
  let total = []
  let name_width = strlen('NAME')
  for report_line in split(raw_report, "\n")
    if report_line =~# '^\s*TOTAL\s\+COUNT\>'
      continue
    endif
    let fields = matchlist(report_line,
          \ '^\s*\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\S\+\)\s\+\(.*\)$')
    if !empty(fields)
      call add(entries, fields[1:7])
      let name_width = max([name_width, strlen(fields[6])])
    else
      let fields = matchlist(report_line, '^\s*\(\S\+\)\s\+\(\d\+\)\s*$')
      if !empty(fields)
        let total = fields[1:2]
      endif
    endif
  endfor

    let aligned_report = [printf('Syntax: %s  Lines: %d', syntax_name, line('$')), '']
    call add(aligned_report, printf('%-13s %8s %7s %12s %12s %-*s %s',
        \ 'TOTAL', 'COUNT', 'MATCH', 'SLOWEST', 'AVERAGE', name_width,
      \ 'NAME', 'PATTERN'))
  for fields in entries
    call add(aligned_report, printf('%-13s %8s %7s %12s %12s %-*s %s',
          \ fields[0], fields[1], fields[2], fields[3], fields[4],
          \ name_width, fields[5], fields[6]))
  endfor
  if !empty(total)
    call add(aligned_report, '')
    call add(aligned_report, printf('TOTAL TIME: %s    TOTAL COUNT: %s',
          \ total[0], total[1]))
  endif
  call writefile(aligned_report, report_file)
  qall!
endfunction

autocmd VimEnter * call ProfileSyntax()

Running it on a source code file, like src/vim9script.c with vim -Nu profile_syntax.vim src/vim9script.c produces an output-$TIMESTAMP.txt file looking like this:

Syntax: c  Lines: 100000

TOTAL            COUNT   MATCH      SLOWEST      AVERAGE NAME               PATTERN
0.102609705      99328    9312  0.000011000  0.000001033 cString            \%(L\|U\|u8\)\="
0.092528889      90839    4198  0.000023291  0.000001019 cCppString         \%(L\|U\|u8\)\="
0.069483028      81272    6177  0.000032958  0.000000855 cNumbers           \<\d\|\.\d
0.062877236      91583       0  0.000010500  0.000000687 cString            \%(U\|u8\=\)"
0.057239944     102135   10552  0.000009083  0.000000560 cBracket           \[\|<::\@!
0.054717217      96789    5371  0.000015541  0.000000565 cCharacter         L\='[^\\]'
0.053602548      91583       0  0.000012208  0.000000585 cSpecialCharacter  L\='\\['\"?\\abfnrtv]'

From there, it's simply a matter of tweaking the regex trying make the numbers go down. Classic tricks include transforming things like A[BC]D into ABD and ACD, grouping common patterns together, forcing usage of the old regex engine, using plain text instead of regex, …

The script was also used to optimize the regex engines themselves, by running it in perf record via perf record -g --call-graph dwarf -- src/vim -Nu profile_syntax.vim --noplugin -N -X -n -i NONE --not-a-term a_big_file.c with its reporting part removed, calling perf script -i perf.data > perf.txt on the results, and dropping the resulting perf.txt file in speedscope. Tentative improvements were then verified by running perf stat -e instructions -- src/vim -Nu profile_syntax.vim --noplugin -N -X -n -i NONE --not-a-term a_big_file.c to see if the number of instructions went down, and validated in speedscope.

items.title: Shared standards, independent review: Fin's AI lesson
items.summary: Speed moved the bottleneck, not the work In episode 5 of The Next Commit , Kesha Mykhailov, Principal Engineer at Fin, describes a shift most engineering organizations now recognize. AI coding agents made implementation nearly free. The hard work didn't disappear. It moved. For Fin, adopting AI agents was not an experiment. Kesha frames it as competitive survival against younger, AI-first rivals that outship slower incumbents. That pressure makes speed attractive. It also exposes a problem that grows as agents improve—code can now move faster than the organization can think, verify, and learn. Ultimately, agents require less work to deliver the same outcome. An agent running at full speed, though, will generate more verification work if that verification isn't done efficiently. Fin's experience shows what that extra verification work looks like day to day. Why do AI coding agents create more review work instead of less? Before AI agents entered the workflow, any significant change at Fin started with a conversation. A developer explored an idea, talked to the people who understood the affected system, resolved open questions, and captured the approach in a technical plan. That plan was evidence the thinking had already happened. Agents collapsed that process, and Kesha has watched it happen in the Slack channel where Fin's engineers share technical plans. "With AI and how fast it is now to generate the code, there's a great temptation to skip that part," he says. "We see less and less of those tech plans shared in the channel. They almost disappeared." With them went the discussions that surfaced hidden constraints and taught newcomers why the system was built the way it was. The broader range of consequences is one we see across the industry: Reviewers reconstruct intent from a large implementation instead of reviewing against a known plan. Product teams learn about a change only after it merges and may find it works for one customer but can't scale, leaving rework or a revert as the only fix. The code is cheap to produce, yet integrating, verifying, and sometimes reverting it stays expensive. How do you verify AI-generated code at scale? Rather than lecturing developers about discipline, the response at Fin changed the economics of the workflow itself: A pull request above a certain size can't be approved automatically, while a small, safe change can. The size limit works as a guardrail and the auto-approval as a reward, so developers who ship smaller increments spend less time waiting for a human reviewer. Making the safer behavior the faster behavior means developers split their work into smaller pull requests on their own, because small changes get merged sooner. This workflow is imperfect, and Kesha says so: "No amount of code review will surface all the unknown unknowns that only could be surfaced in the only objective reality we have, which is production." Lines of code are a rough proxy for risk. That's why Fin layers additional reviews covering security, logical correctness, and the quality of the problem statement, with sensitive changes still routed to human approval. The principle holds regardless of the threshold: when code gets faster to write, the rest of the process has to keep the amount of new code within what your team can verify. Generation and verification need shared standards and independent judgment Fin's move from Ember.js to React illustrates what breaks when generation outpaces verification standards. React lets teams assemble very different stacks around the same library. Fin's experts chose specific patterns for forms, validation, and API access, but early agents produced large React changes that ignored those decisions entirely. A small group of senior engineers became the final verification layer, absorbing an unsustainable volume of pull request reviews. The team harvested comments on those reviews into a React skill, refining it against real pull requests until it captured what was useful. Then came the key architectural insight—that same skill now guides the coding agent when it writes React code and the review agent when it assesses the diff. One source of engineering judgment, applied on both sides. When the generator and the verifier draw from separate copies of the standards, those copies drift. A shared source eliminates that duplication, so improvements prompted by review shape the next generation attempt, instead of staying a downstream correction. A verifier is only useful if people can trust it Fin's developers relied heavily on their custom review agent, Shrek. They made it green before showing a change to a human, which made the verifier's quality a direct input to delivery itself. Every review runs many model calls, which Kesha calls "astronomically expensive." To cut costs, Fin tried moving one of Shrek's checks, the one that looks for logic errors, to a cheaper model. Before switching, the team ran the cheaper model against hundreds of historical pull requests, each labeled with the issues the agent should find, to confirm it would still catch them. It did. The recall looked identical, making the change appear safe when it was not. Because developers had built Shrek's approval into their workflow, the noise carried a real operational cost: delayed work, wasted attention, and eroding trust in automated feedback. Fin's evaluation checked whether the agent still caught real issues but never counted its wrong findings, so a far noisier model passed. Within a week, developers asked whether Shrek had become "a lot more picky." The lesson: a verifier has to be measured on its noise as well as its catches, because noise trains developers to ignore the signal. False positives also differ by model, so offline tests built from one model's mistakes won't catch a new model's. Fin now tracks three signals from real pull requests: Explicit thumbs up or down on review comments Soft resolution, where a final diff adopts a suggestion no one reacted to Merges that proceed with human approval despite an active agent flag, a reliable indicator of a false positive. As Kesha puts it, "We're building this agent for humans, ultimately. None of the evals will replace the real feedback from them." Each signal is closer to the reason the verifier exists, helping engineers ship safely without burning their attention. The takeaway Speed is only an advantage if verification keeps pace. Shared standards guide both generation and review. Independent, multilayered verification challenges the result. Production signals prove the verifier is genuinely helping the humans it serves. Kesha's candid account described what his team has solved and what they haven’t yet, making his interview with Tom Howlett one of the more honest conversations about agentic development you'll hear this year. Listen to episode 5 of The Next Commit to hear Kesha and Tom talk through the

  • Merges that proceed with human approval despite an active agent flag, a reliable indicator of a false positive. 

As Kesha puts it, "We're building this agent for humans, ultimately. None of the evals will replace the real feedback from them." Each signal is closer to the reason the verifier exists, helping engineers ship safely without burning their attention.

The takeaway

Speed is only an advantage if verification keeps pace. Shared standards guide both generation and review. Independent, multilayered verification challenges the result. Production signals prove the verifier is genuinely helping the humans it serves.

Kesha's candid account described what his team has solved and what they haven’t yet, making his interview with Tom Howlett one of the more honest conversations about agentic development you'll hear this year.

Listen to episode 5 of The Next Commit to hear Kesha and Tom  talk through the full story.

items.title: Attackers Reportedly Hack Supermarket Fridges and Raise Temperatures to 50°C
items.summary: French supermarket chains are dealing with a major cybersecurity incident after attackers reportedly changed refrigeration settings remotely, causing some chilled cabinets and freezers to heat up instead of cool down. The incident began overnight between October 11 and October 12 and affected stores linked to Intermarché, E.Leclerc, and Système U, according to early reports. The cyberattack is believed to have targeted refrigeration-control systems made by Danish industrial technology company Danfoss. These systems manage cooling equipment inside supermarkets, including freezers, chilled food displays, compressors, and temperature alerts. In the affected stores, attackers reportedly changed the settings to trigger continuous defrosting and set temperatures as high as 50°C. This meant refrigeration units designed to keep food cold reportedly operated like heaters for several hours. Fresh food, dairy items, meat, frozen products, and other temperature-sensitive goods may have become unsafe for sale. Stores were forced to inspect their stock and discard food that could no longer meet food-safety requirements. BFMTV reported that some locations could face losses reaching hundreds of thousands of euros, while around 150 Intermarché stores were reportedly affected. Supermarket Fridges Hacked The incident shows how a cyber incident can quickly become a physical and financial problem. Supermarkets depend on refrigeration around the clock. Even a short disruption can damage stock, interrupt deliveries, create food-safety concerns, and reduce customer trust. Reports indicate that the attackers may have abused a defrost feature built into the refrigeration-management software. Defrosting is a normal process that removes ice from cooling equipment. However, if it is enabled continuously or configured with unsafe values, the equipment cannot maintain the low temperatures needed to preserve food. Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of Coopérative U, confirmed that cybercriminal activity had affected refrigeration production systems in several stores in the group’s network. He said teams were working with refrigeration specialists to restore operations and that an investigation would be needed to establish how the incident occurred. Early reporting suggests older software versions may be involved. However, the exact intrusion method, the responsible group, and whether a known vulnerability was exploited have not been publicly confirmed. That distinction is important. A report that legacy software is present does not prove that a specific security flaw enabled the compromise. The event also places fresh attention on security issues affecting connected refrigeration equipment. Commercial cooling controllers are part of operational technology, or OT. Unlike ordinary office computers, OT systems directly control real-world equipment, including cooling units, pumps, manufacturing machines, and building controls. Cybersecurity News previously reported on 23 vulnerabilities in Copeland XWEB Pro refrigeration controllers used by supermarkets, warehouses, and hospitals. Researchers showed that compromised controllers could change temperature readings or silently stop cooling equipment. That research involved Copeland products, not the Danfoss systems named in the French incident, but it demonstrates the real-world impact of insecure refrigeration controls. Danfoss refrigeration products have also been subject to security advisories. CISA advisories discussed flaws affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers, including authentication weaknesses, command-injection risks, and settings-control issues in older versions. Danfoss released updates for affected software releases, and organizations should confirm that their equipment is running supported versions. Retailers using remotely managed refrigeration should urgently review every internet-connected controller, remote-access path, vendor account, and third-party maintenance connection. Systems should not be directly exposed to the public internet, and remote access should use a VPN, multi-factor authentication, and strict account controls. Security teams should also separate refrigeration networks from point-of-sale, corporate, and guest Wi-Fi networks . Temperature changes, repeated defrost commands, configuration edits, and unusual remote logins should create immediate alerts for both IT and facilities teams. The supermarket incident is still developing, but its lesson is already clear. When attackers gain control of systems that manage physical equipment, the impact can go far beyond stolen data. In this case, a change in software settings reportedly turned supermarket fridges into a costly food-waste event across France. Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min.
