items.title: What to Look for in a Cyber Deception Solution: 12 Capabilities That Matter
items.summary: Key Takeaways Decoys should look and behave like the environment around them, not just appear convincing on a dashboard. Placement matters more than decoy count. Deception is most useful when attackers encounter it along realistic attack paths. A high-confidence alert is only the starting point. The real value comes from knowing which endpoint or identity triggered it, what happened beforehand, and where the attacker tried to move next. Identity deception deserves as much attention as network deception. “Agentless” should not be treated as a checkbox. Buyers should look at what actually needs to be deployed, what touches production systems, how much maintenance is required, and whether the architecture works across cloud, OT, legacy, and unmanaged environments. Deception has to keep changing with the environment. Static decoys become easier to spot and harder to manage. Automated discovery and lifecycle management help keep the deception believable as infrastructure changes. Fidelis brings the pieces together rather than treating deception as an isolated trap. A cyber deception solution is easy to describe in a demo. Deploy a few decoys, scatter deceptive credentials around the environment, wait for an attacker to touch one, and generate an alert. Evaluating whether that deception will actually work across a large enterprise is considerably harder. The bigger question is: Will an attacker encounter the deception, believe it, and generate enough evidence for the SOC to act? Deception is no longer simply a honeypot at a larger scale. Modern deception can span endpoints, networks, identities, Active Directory, cloud infrastructure, OT environments, credentials, data, applications, and likely attack paths. The UK National Cyber Security Centre [1] has been testing that operational reality. Its cyber deception initiative involved 121 organizations, 14 commercial providers, and 10 product trials across environments ranging from cloud to operational technology. The NCSC found genuine potential for detecting novel threats and enriching threat intelligence, but also emphasized that deception is not plug-and-play. Its effectiveness depends on context, configuration, maintenance, and a clear strategy. For security leaders conducting a deception technology comparison, that is an important distinction. The decision should not come down to the number of decoys in a licensing tier or the longest feature list. It should come down to whether the platform can make deception believable, put it where attackers are likely to encounter it, keep it current, and turn an interaction into something the SOC can investigate. Here are 12 capabilities worth testing. 1. Deception That Remains Convincing Under Inspection Start with realism. A decoy may look perfectly legitimate on a product dashboard but fail the moment an attacker begins interrogating it. Reconnaissance can expose operating systems, open ports, service banners, applications, DNS information, naming conventions, directory relationships, files, and other characteristics. A fake SQL server that behaves nothing like the production SQL servers around it is not much of a trap. MITRE’s adversary-engagement [2] guidance points to the same problem. Traditional honeypots can be unrealistic, easily signatured, and overly generic. MITRE instead advocates engagement environments tailored to their surroundings and instrumented around the defender’s objective. Ask the vendor to demonstrate what happens when the decoy is interrogated more deeply. A mature deception solution should support the appropriate mix of emulated and higher-interaction systems. Lightweight emulation is useful when scale matters. More interactive environments may make sense when the objective is to observe attacker behavior in greater detail. The requirement is the right fidelity for the risk and use case. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis Deception ® builds decoys using context from the real environment. Its decoys can reproduce real operating systems and services, open ports, applications, files, folders, and other characteristics that an attacker would expect to see. Its deception architecture can include both actual and emulated operating systems and applications rather than forcing one interaction model everywhere. More importantly, Fidelis does not treat realism as a one-time configuration exercise. Its decoys can be automatically updated to mirror changes in the surrounding environment. For a buyer, that matters more than how convincing a decoy looks on deployment day. Advanced Deception Technology Comparison Real-World Performance Data Avoiding False Savings Why Fidelis Outperforms the Competition Download Now 2. High-Confidence Alerts with Enough Context to Investigate Deception has an inherent detection advantage: legitimate users and applications generally have little reason to interact with something deliberately created to be fake. A production administrator launching PowerShell may be legitimate. An unusual authentication could have an innocent explanation. An endpoint attempting to authenticate to a deceptive server using a credential that no legitimate user should possess is a different kind of signal. But there is an important distinction: High confidence does not automatically mean high context. An alert saying “Host 10.20.30.15 interacted with decoy server” gives the SOC a strong starting point, but the analyst still needs answers: Which endpoint initiated the interaction? Which identity or credential was involved? What did the system do before reaching the decoy? Was there reconnaissance or lateral movement ? What happened next? Good deception technology features should shorten the distance between the trigger and those answers. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis Deception generates alerts when attackers interact with decoys, fake credentials, deceptive data, fake accounts, or other deliberately planted assets. Fidelis deception events can be enriched with network, endpoint, sandbox, and threat context, allowing an analyst to move beyond the isolated decoy event and investigate the activity around it. That is the capability buyers should test: not simply whether the deception alert is accurate, but how much investigation remains after it fires. 3. Automated Discovery Before Decoy Deployment Good deception starts by understanding what is real. Before deciding what to fake, the platform should understand relevant assets, operating systems, services, applications, identities, communication relationships, and exposures. Otherwise, teams risk creating technically functional decoys that do not fit their surroundings. The challenge becomes more obvious six months after deployment. Servers have been added. Applications have moved. New cloud resources exist. Active Directory has changed. Older workloads have disappeared. If the deception layer still represents the environment as it looked during implementation, credibility gradually erodes. That is why buyers should distinguish between automated decoy deployment and environment-aware deception. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis Deception profiles and classifies assets, maps the cyber terrain , observes communication patterns, and uses that information to determine how deception should be deployed. Fidelis says the platform can then automatically create, deploy, test, and update decoys as the environment changes. It also automatically maps cyber terrain and identifies asset vulnerabilities before strategically deploying decoys based on real assets. With Fidelis, you can also deploy decoys at a scale that significantly expands your ability to detect attacker activity . 4. Attack-Path-Aware Placement Instead of Decoy Density A dashboard showing 5,000 deployed decoys looks impressive. It does not necessarily mean an attacker will encounter one. Attackers do not move evenly across an enterprise. They follow credentials, trust relationships, shared services, administrative paths, cloud permissions, accessible systems, and opportunities to gain privilege. Deception should therefore intersect likely attacker movement, not simply mirror the CMDB. Consider a domain controller. Protecting it does not necessarily mean placing another fake domain controller next to it. The stronger approach may be planting credentials, mapped drives, accounts, shares, or breadcrumbs at the points an attacker would investigate before reaching the real domain controller. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis Deception maps relationships between users, systems, and data to provide visibility into potential attack paths and movement patterns. Fidelis then uses that context to place deception where attackers are more likely to operate. Its approach also uses breadcrumbs to intentionally pull an attacker from something real toward something deceptive. Those breadcrumbs can include fake credentials, configuration information, connection artifacts, and other clues an adversary may encounter during reconnaissance or lateral movement. That makes the meaningful metric less about decoy density and more about attacker encounter probability. 5. Identity and Credential Deception A deception strategy focused only on network assets leaves a major part of the attack surface untouched. MITRE ATT&CK documents [3] the use of valid accounts across domain, local, cloud, and other account types. Once an adversary has legitimate credentials, authentication activity can become considerably harder to separate from normal behavior. Deceptive identities change that equation. Buyers should look for the ability to create or place artifacts such as: deceptive privileged accounts, honey credentials, fake service accounts, deceptive AD users and computer objects, tokens and keys, cached credentials, misleading directory relationships, and other identity artifacts appropriate to the environment. If an adversary retrieves and uses a credential that should never have been used by anyone, intent becomes much clearer. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis has extended deception specifically into Active Directory through Fidelis Active Directory Intercept . It detects reconnaissance and enumeration, Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, DCSync, DCShadow, Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket, GPO abuse, and other identity-related attack techniques. Fidelis combines AD-aware network inspection with deceptive objects and credentials designed to expose suspicious identity use. Fidelis seeds environments with fake high-privilege accounts, ghost users, and honey credentials, while breadcrumbs on real assets can draw attackers toward the deception layer. For organizations where AD is central to lateral movement and privilege escalation , identity deception should therefore be treated as a core platform requirement rather than an optional add-on. 6. Coverage Across Endpoint, Network, Cloud, Identity, and OT Attackers do not respect product boundaries. An intrusion can begin on an endpoint, discover credentials, query Active Directory, move across the network, authenticate to a cloud workload, and eventually approach OT or IoT systems. Deception should be able to follow that path. That means assessing coverage against the attack surfaces such as endpoint, identity, network, cloud, and OT/IoT rather than against a collection of individual product SKUs. Endpoint → Identity → Network → Cloud → OT/IoT. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis Deception is designed for deception across on-premises and cloud environments , and Fidelis also provides coverage for enterprise networks, endpoints, Active Directory, OT, IoT, SCADA, cloud, and hybrid environments. For cloud deception specifically, Fidelis provides deceptive resources across AWS, Azure, Kubernetes, and hybrid infrastructure, including realistic workloads, storage, containers, endpoints, credentials, and identity services. The platform also tracks infrastructure changes so deception can adapt as cloud resources change. This helps because cloud deception cannot simply be an on-premises honeypot moved into a VPC. Cloud environments are highly dynamic and increasingly identity-driven. Similarly, Fidelis’ OT-focused deception can use protocol-aware decoys and an off-path architecture designed to avoid sitting inline with production control traffic. 7. Multiple Levels and Types of Deception A modern deception solution should not reduce the category to fake servers. Different attack stages create different opportunities to deceive. An endpoint breadcrumb may expose credential discovery. A fake AD object may become visible during directory enumeration. A deceptive share may attract an adversary searching for valuable data. An emulated network service may reveal reconnaissance. A higher-interaction operating system may provide more detail once the attacker commits. That means buyers should consider both the breadth of deceptive assets and the depth of interaction available. MITRE Engage provides a useful framework here because deception is treated as more than an alarm. The objective can include exposing an adversary, eliciting information about their methods, affecting their decisions, and ultimately understanding how they operate. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis supports multiple forms of deception rather than relying on one decoy type. For example: real or emulated operating systems and services, servers and workstations, applications and databases, cloud workloads and containers, network and IoT assets, fake credentials, deceptive data, Active Directory objects, files and other breadcrumbs. That gives security teams the ability to use lightweight deception at scale while reserving richer interactions for places where observing the attacker in greater detail provides additional value. The goal is enough realism, in enough places, that an attacker cannot safely assume what is real. 8. Useful Evidence After the Attacker Takes the Bait Too many descriptions of deception end here: Attacker touches decoy → Alert fires. Decision-makers should keep going. What does the security team learn once the interaction occurs? Depending on the deployment, useful evidence might include: reconnaissance activity, identities and credentials used, commands attempted, services accessed, tools or files introduced, lateral movement attempts, protocols used, and the sequence of actions around the deception event. This matters because the larger threat environment is moving quickly. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report [4] found that 31% of breaches started with software vulnerability exploitation and 48% involved ransomware. Verizon also found generative AI augmenting multiple attack techniques. Deception does not replace vulnerability management , EDR, NDR, or incident response. Its value is that it can provide an unusually strong point of evidence once an adversary begins operating where they should not. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis positions deception as more than a tripwire. Interactions with decoys, breadcrumbs, and deceptive credentials can reveal reconnaissance, attempted movement, credential use, attacker preferences, and other TTPs. Fidelis visually maps attacker movement and uses attack timelines to understand how the activity progressed. That deception evidence can be correlated with endpoint, network, identity, cloud, sandbox , and threat context. 9. Agentless Deception or Lightweight Deployment Where It Makes Sense Deployment architecture deserves careful scrutiny. But buyers should avoid reducing the decision to agentless deception being good and agent deception as bad. Real architectures are more nuanced. A platform may avoid installing software on production endpoints while still using sensors, virtual appliances, containers, integrations, or centralized deception infrastructure. Another platform may use endpoint components because a particular form of deception requires local placement or interaction. The decision depends on what exactly must be deployed and where. Evaluate: software installed on production assets, required privileges, CPU and memory impact, sensors or appliances required per site or network segment, remote-site architecture, legacy and unmanaged asset coverage, upgrade requirements, failure behavior, and day-to-day administration. This is especially important for OT, IoT, legacy systems, and other environments where another endpoint agent may be difficult or unacceptable. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis’ passive environment discovery techniques can build asset and communication context without endpoint modification. For OT-focused network deception , Fidelis uses lightweight virtual images and containerized services running off-path rather than inline with production traffic. Fidelis has a centralized deception server to manage decoy deployment and monitoring. These characteristics reduce deployment disruption in environments where touching production systems is undesirable. However, buyers should still validate the exact architecture for their endpoint, network, cloud, and identity use cases rather than assuming every deceptive artifact is delivered the same way. 10. Safe Isolation and Controlled Attacker Interaction Deception deliberately encourages an adversary to interact with something. That means containment is part of the product evaluation. Security teams should understand: how decoys are separated from production, whether attackers can move from deception back into real systems, what outbound communication is allowed, how higher-interaction systems are controlled, and what prevents the deception infrastructure itself from creating additional risk. The NCSC’s trials explicitly warned that poorly configured deception can create new vulnerabilities or a false sense of security. The issue becomes more important as interaction depth increases. A basic token provides little functionality to abuse. A real operating system gives the defender richer observations but also needs tighter controls. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis Deception capabilities are designed to operate without impacting users or normal operations. Its OT deployment model is particularly relevant: decoys can run off-path and outside the production traffic path, rather than being inserted inline with industrial systems. That is useful in availability-sensitive environments, but buyers should still make isolation testing part of a proof of value. Ask the vendor to demonstrate what prevents a compromised high-interaction decoy from becoming a bridge back toward production. 11. SIEM, SOAR, EDR, NDR, and XDR Integration That Changes the Workflow Almost every enterprise security product has an integration page. But ask the vendor to demonstrate the complete workflow: Decoy interaction → enriched detection → investigation → endpoint or identity identified → additional evidence retrieved → response initiated Then ask: Does the SIEM receive context or only another alert? Can network evidence show what happened around the interaction? Can endpoint telemetry explain what occurred on the originating host? Can SOAR initiate containment? Can identity controls act when a deceptive credential is used? Can an analyst pivot between evidence without manually rebuilding the attack? How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis Deception can operate as a standalone product, so organizations do not have to adopt Fidelis Elevate to use the deception capability. When integrated with Fidelis Elevate, however, deception becomes part of a broader investigation layer alongside Fidelis Network ® , Fidelis Endpoint ® , sandbox, identity, and threat context. Fidelis also supports integrations with external security tooling. Its deception intelligence feeds SIEM, SOAR, XDR, threat-hunting , and incident-response workflows. It also supports integrations across third-party SIEM, SOAR, EDR, threat intelligence, and network tools. 12. Automated Lifecycle Management and Measurable Operational Value Deploying decoys is only the beginning. A deception platform may automatically create hundreds of fake assets on day one and still become operationally expensive by month six. Production environments change constantly: workloads appear and disappear, users move, applications change, cloud resources are ephemeral, credentials rotate, network segments are reorganized, and attack paths evolve. The deception layer has to keep pace. That means buyers should assess whether the system can automatically discover change, refresh deceptive assets, retire stale artifacts, adjust placement, and maintain credibility without constant manual tuning. How Fidelis addresses this Fidelis Deception’s automated lifecycle capabilities are worth testing. Fidelis platform profiles assets, maps cyber terrain and communication patterns, then can create, deploy, test, and update decoys automatically. It also continuously adjusts deception so that fake systems remain representative of the enterprise around them. Fidelis Deception: Study Attacker’s Every Move and Turn Them into a Target Trust Your Alerts Maintain Cyber Resiliency Active Deception Read Datasheet What Should You Look for in a Cyber Deception Solution? A strong deception solution should do four things well. It should make deception discoverable by placing it where attackers actually move. It should make deception believable by reflecting the systems, identities, applications, and services around it. It should make every interaction actionable by giving the SOC enough evidence to understand what happened and investigate further. And it should remain manageable as the enterprise changes. Fidelis Deception maps particularly well to those requirements because it combines cyber-terrain discovery, realistic and adaptive decoys, attack-path-aware breadcrumbs, identity deception, hybrid and OT coverage, and high-confidence detection. When used with Fidelis Elevate, those deception events can also be connected with network, endpoint, identity, sandbox, and other security context rather than remaining isolated alerts. Frequently Asked Questions What is a cyber deception solution? A cyber deception solution creates deliberately false but believable assets, identities, credentials, services, applications, data, or other artifacts designed to attract or misdirect an adversary. Because legitimate users generally have no reason to interact with these assets, an interaction can provide a high-confidence indication of suspicious activity and additional evidence about attacker behavior. What are the most important deception technology features? Security teams should evaluate realistic and adaptive decoys, automated environment discovery, attack-path-aware placement, identity and credential deception, endpoint and network deception, cloud deception, multiple interaction levels, investigation evidence, safe isolation, flexible deployment architecture, integrations, automated lifecycle management. How does Fidelis Deception differ from a basic honeypot? Fidelis Deception goes beyond placing standalone fake systems in the network. It maps cyber terrain, profiles assets and relationships, uses breadcrumbs and deceptive credentials, supports multiple decoy types across on-premises and cloud environments, and can automatically create and update deception based on the surrounding environment. When integrated with Fidelis Elevate, deception evidence can also be correlated with network, endpoint, sandbox, identity, and threat context. Is agentless deception better than agent-based deception? Not automatically. Agentless deception can be attractive where organizations want to limit additional endpoint software or where endpoints cannot support an agent. Agent deception or locally delivered artifacts can provide different capabilities depending on the architecture. The better evaluation is to determine exactly which components need to be deployed, what privileges and resources they require, how they are updated, and how much operational work they create. Fidelis, for example, supports passive discovery approaches that do not require endpoint modification for that discovery process, while its OT deception can use lightweight virtual images and containerized services deployed off-path. The exact architecture should still be validated against the intended use case. How should organizations conduct a deception technology comparison? Use the same attack scenario and success criteria for every vendor. Test whether the attacker encounters the deception, Whether the deception remains believable under inspection, What context the SOC receives after an interaction, How much effort is required to deploy and maintain the environment. An alert saying “Host 10.20.30.15 interacted with decoy server” gives the SOC a strong starting point, but the analyst still needs answers:

  • Which endpoint initiated the interaction?
  • Which identity or credential was involved?
  • What did the system do before reaching the decoy?
  • Was there reconnaissance or lateral movement?
  • What happened next?

Good deception technology features should shorten the distance between the trigger and those answers.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception generates alerts when attackers interact with decoys, fake credentials, deceptive data, fake accounts, or other deliberately planted assets.

Fidelis deception events can be enriched with network, endpoint, sandbox, and threat context, allowing an analyst to move beyond the isolated decoy event and investigate the activity around it.

That is the capability buyers should test: not simply whether the deception alert is accurate, but how much investigation remains after it fires.

3. Automated Discovery Before Decoy Deployment

Good deception starts by understanding what is real.

Before deciding what to fake, the platform should understand relevant assets, operating systems, services, applications, identities, communication relationships, and exposures.

Otherwise, teams risk creating technically functional decoys that do not fit their surroundings. The challenge becomes more obvious six months after deployment.

Servers have been added. Applications have moved. New cloud resources exist. Active Directory has changed. Older workloads have disappeared.

If the deception layer still represents the environment as it looked during implementation, credibility gradually erodes.

That is why buyers should distinguish between automated decoy deployment and environment-aware deception.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception profiles and classifies assets, maps the cyber terrain, observes communication patterns, and uses that information to determine how deception should be deployed. Fidelis says the platform can then automatically create, deploy, test, and update decoys as the environment changes.

It also automatically maps cyber terrain and identifies asset vulnerabilities before strategically deploying decoys based on real assets. With Fidelis, you can also deploy decoys at a scale that significantly expands your ability to detect attacker activity.

4. Attack-Path-Aware Placement Instead of Decoy Density

A dashboard showing 5,000 deployed decoys looks impressive. It does not necessarily mean an attacker will encounter one.

Attackers do not move evenly across an enterprise. They follow credentials, trust relationships, shared services, administrative paths, cloud permissions, accessible systems, and opportunities to gain privilege.

Deception should therefore intersect likely attacker movement, not simply mirror the CMDB.

Consider a domain controller.

Protecting it does not necessarily mean placing another fake domain controller next to it. The stronger approach may be planting credentials, mapped drives, accounts, shares, or breadcrumbs at the points an attacker would investigate before reaching the real domain controller.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception maps relationships between users, systems, and data to provide visibility into potential attack paths and movement patterns. Fidelis then uses that context to place deception where attackers are more likely to operate.

Its approach also uses breadcrumbs to intentionally pull an attacker from something real toward something deceptive. Those breadcrumbs can include fake credentials, configuration information, connection artifacts, and other clues an adversary may encounter during reconnaissance or lateral movement.

That makes the meaningful metric less about decoy density and more about attacker encounter probability.

5. Identity and Credential Deception

A deception strategy focused only on network assets leaves a major part of the attack surface untouched.

MITRE ATT&CK documents[3] the use of valid accounts across domain, local, cloud, and other account types. Once an adversary has legitimate credentials, authentication activity can become considerably harder to separate from normal behavior.

Deceptive identities change that equation.

Buyers should look for the ability to create or place artifacts such as:

  • deceptive privileged accounts,
  • honey credentials,
  • fake service accounts,
  • deceptive AD users and computer objects,
  • tokens and keys,
  • cached credentials,
  • misleading directory relationships,
  • and other identity artifacts appropriate to the environment.

If an adversary retrieves and uses a credential that should never have been used by anyone, intent becomes much clearer.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis has extended deception specifically into Active Directory through Fidelis Active Directory Intercept.

It detects reconnaissance and enumeration, Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, DCSync, DCShadow, Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket, GPO abuse, and other identity-related attack techniques. Fidelis combines AD-aware network inspection with deceptive objects and credentials designed to expose suspicious identity use.

Fidelis seeds environments with fake high-privilege accounts, ghost users, and honey credentials, while breadcrumbs on real assets can draw attackers toward the deception layer.

For organizations where AD is central to lateral movement and privilege escalation, identity deception should therefore be treated as a core platform requirement rather than an optional add-on.

6. Coverage Across Endpoint, Network, Cloud, Identity, and OT

Attackers do not respect product boundaries.

An intrusion can begin on an endpoint, discover credentials, query Active Directory, move across the network, authenticate to a cloud workload, and eventually approach OT or IoT systems. Deception should be able to follow that path.

That means assessing coverage against the attack surfaces such as endpoint, identity, network, cloud, and OT/IoT rather than against a collection of individual product SKUs.

Endpoint → Identity → Network → Cloud → OT/IoT.
How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception is designed for deception across on-premises and cloud environments, and Fidelis also provides coverage for enterprise networks, endpoints, Active Directory, OT, IoT, SCADA, cloud, and hybrid environments.

For cloud deception specifically, Fidelis provides deceptive resources across AWS, Azure, Kubernetes, and hybrid infrastructure, including realistic workloads, storage, containers, endpoints, credentials, and identity services. The platform also tracks infrastructure changes so deception can adapt as cloud resources change.

This helps because cloud deception cannot simply be an on-premises honeypot moved into a VPC. Cloud environments are highly dynamic and increasingly identity-driven.

Similarly, Fidelis’ OT-focused deception can use protocol-aware decoys and an off-path architecture designed to avoid sitting inline with production control traffic.

7. Multiple Levels and Types of Deception

A modern deception solution should not reduce the category to fake servers. Different attack stages create different opportunities to deceive.

An endpoint breadcrumb may expose credential discovery. A fake AD object may become visible during directory enumeration. A deceptive share may attract an adversary searching for valuable data. An emulated network service may reveal reconnaissance. A higher-interaction operating system may provide more detail once the attacker commits.

That means buyers should consider both the breadth of deceptive assets and the depth of interaction available.

MITRE Engage provides a useful framework here because deception is treated as more than an alarm. The objective can include exposing an adversary, eliciting information about their methods, affecting their decisions, and ultimately understanding how they operate.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis supports multiple forms of deception rather than relying on one decoy type. For example:

  • real or emulated operating systems and services,
  • servers and workstations,
  • applications and databases,
  • cloud workloads and containers,
  • network and IoT assets,
  • fake credentials,
  • deceptive data,
  • Active Directory objects,
  • files and other breadcrumbs.

That gives security teams the ability to use lightweight deception at scale while reserving richer interactions for places where observing the attacker in greater detail provides additional value.

The goal is enough realism, in enough places, that an attacker cannot safely assume what is real.

8. Useful Evidence After the Attacker Takes the Bait

Too many descriptions of deception end here: Attacker touches decoy → Alert fires.

Decision-makers should keep going. What does the security team learn once the interaction occurs?

Depending on the deployment, useful evidence might include:

  • reconnaissance activity,
  • identities and credentials used,
  • commands attempted,
  • services accessed,
  • tools or files introduced,
  • lateral movement attempts,
  • protocols used,
  • and the sequence of actions around the deception event.

This matters because the larger threat environment is moving quickly. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report[4] found that 31% of breaches started with software vulnerability exploitation and 48% involved ransomware. Verizon also found generative AI augmenting multiple attack techniques.

Deception does not replace vulnerability management, EDR, NDR, or incident response. Its value is that it can provide an unusually strong point of evidence once an adversary begins operating where they should not.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis positions deception as more than a tripwire.

Interactions with decoys, breadcrumbs, and deceptive credentials can reveal reconnaissance, attempted movement, credential use, attacker preferences, and other TTPs. Fidelis visually maps attacker movement and uses attack timelines to understand how the activity progressed.

That deception evidence can be correlated with endpoint, network, identity, cloud, sandbox, and threat context.

9. Agentless Deception or Lightweight Deployment Where It Makes Sense

Deployment architecture deserves careful scrutiny. But buyers should avoid reducing the decision to agentless deception being good and agent deception as bad. Real architectures are more nuanced.

A platform may avoid installing software on production endpoints while still using sensors, virtual appliances, containers, integrations, or centralized deception infrastructure. Another platform may use endpoint components because a particular form of deception requires local placement or interaction.

The decision depends on what exactly must be deployed and where.

Evaluate:

  • software installed on production assets,
  • required privileges,
  • CPU and memory impact,
  • sensors or appliances required per site or network segment,
  • remote-site architecture,
  • legacy and unmanaged asset coverage,
  • upgrade requirements,
  • failure behavior,
  • and day-to-day administration.

This is especially important for OT, IoT, legacy systems, and other environments where another endpoint agent may be difficult or unacceptable.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis’ passive environment discovery techniques can build asset and communication context without endpoint modification.

For OT-focused network deception, Fidelis uses lightweight virtual images and containerized services running off-path rather than inline with production traffic. Fidelis has a centralized deception server to manage decoy deployment and monitoring.

These characteristics reduce deployment disruption in environments where touching production systems is undesirable.

However, buyers should still validate the exact architecture for their endpoint, network, cloud, and identity use cases rather than assuming every deceptive artifact is delivered the same way.

10. Safe Isolation and Controlled Attacker Interaction

Deception deliberately encourages an adversary to interact with something. That means containment is part of the product evaluation.

Security teams should understand:

  • how decoys are separated from production,
  • whether attackers can move from deception back into real systems,
  • what outbound communication is allowed,
  • how higher-interaction systems are controlled,
  • and what prevents the deception infrastructure itself from creating additional risk.

The NCSC’s trials explicitly warned that poorly configured deception can create new vulnerabilities or a false sense of security.

The issue becomes more important as interaction depth increases. A basic token provides little functionality to abuse. A real operating system gives the defender richer observations but also needs tighter controls.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception capabilities are designed to operate without impacting users or normal operations. Its OT deployment model is particularly relevant: decoys can run off-path and outside the production traffic path, rather than being inserted inline with industrial systems.

That is useful in availability-sensitive environments, but buyers should still make isolation testing part of a proof of value.

Ask the vendor to demonstrate what prevents a compromised high-interaction decoy from becoming a bridge back toward production.

11. SIEM, SOAR, EDR, NDR, and XDR Integration That Changes the Workflow

Almost every enterprise security product has an integration page. But ask the vendor to demonstrate the complete workflow:

Decoy interaction → enriched detection → investigation → endpoint or identity identified → additional evidence retrieved → response initiated

Then ask:

  • Does the SIEM receive context or only another alert?
  • Can network evidence show what happened around the interaction?
  • Can endpoint telemetry explain what occurred on the originating host?
  • Can SOAR initiate containment?
  • Can identity controls act when a deceptive credential is used?
  • Can an analyst pivot between evidence without manually rebuilding the attack?
How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception can operate as a standalone product, so organizations do not have to adopt Fidelis Elevate to use the deception capability.

When integrated with Fidelis Elevate, however, deception becomes part of a broader investigation layer alongside Fidelis Network®, Fidelis Endpoint®, sandbox, identity, and threat context.

Fidelis also supports integrations with external security tooling. Its deception intelligence feeds SIEM, SOAR, XDR, threat-hunting, and incident-response workflows. It also supports integrations across third-party SIEM, SOAR, EDR, threat intelligence, and network tools.

12. Automated Lifecycle Management and Measurable Operational Value

Deploying decoys is only the beginning. A deception platform may automatically create hundreds of fake assets on day one and still become operationally expensive by month six.

Production environments change constantly:

  • workloads appear and disappear,
  • users move,
  • applications change,
  • cloud resources are ephemeral,
  • credentials rotate,
  • network segments are reorganized,
  • and attack paths evolve.

The deception layer has to keep pace.

That means buyers should assess whether the system can automatically discover change, refresh deceptive assets, retire stale artifacts, adjust placement, and maintain credibility without constant manual tuning.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception’s automated lifecycle capabilities are worth testing. Fidelis platform profiles assets, maps cyber terrain and communication patterns, then can create, deploy, test, and update decoys automatically. It also continuously adjusts deception so that fake systems remain representative of the enterprise around them.

What Should You Look for in a Cyber Deception Solution?

A strong deception solution should do four things well.

  • It should make deception discoverable by placing it where attackers actually move.
  • It should make deception believable by reflecting the systems, identities, applications, and services around it.
  • It should make every interaction actionable by giving the SOC enough evidence to understand what happened and investigate further.
  • And it should remain manageable as the enterprise changes.

Fidelis Deception maps particularly well to those requirements because it combines cyber-terrain discovery, realistic and adaptive decoys, attack-path-aware breadcrumbs, identity deception, hybrid and OT coverage, and high-confidence detection. When used with Fidelis Elevate, those deception events can also be connected with network, endpoint, identity, sandbox, and other security context rather than remaining isolated alerts.

Frequently Asked Questions
What is a cyber deception solution?

A cyber deception solution creates deliberately false but believable assets, identities, credentials, services, applications, data, or other artifacts designed to attract or misdirect an adversary. Because legitimate users generally have no reason to interact with these assets, an interaction can provide a high-confidence indication of suspicious activity and additional evidence about attacker behavior.

What are the most important deception technology features?

Security teams should evaluate

  1. realistic and adaptive decoys,
  2. automated environment discovery,
  3. attack-path-aware placement,
  4. identity and credential deception,
  5. endpoint and network deception,
  6. cloud deception,
  7. multiple interaction levels,
  8. investigation evidence,
  9. safe isolation,
  10. flexible deployment architecture,
  11. integrations,
  12. automated lifecycle management.
How does Fidelis Deception differ from a basic honeypot?

Fidelis Deception goes beyond placing standalone fake systems in the network. It maps cyber terrain, profiles assets and relationships, uses breadcrumbs and deceptive credentials, supports multiple decoy types across on-premises and cloud environments, and can automatically create and update deception based on the surrounding environment. When integrated with Fidelis Elevate, deception evidence can also be correlated with network, endpoint, sandbox, identity, and threat context.

Is agentless deception better than agent-based deception?

Not automatically.

Agentless deception can be attractive where organizations want to limit additional endpoint software or where endpoints cannot support an agent. Agent deception or locally delivered artifacts can provide different capabilities depending on the architecture.

The better evaluation is to determine exactly which components need to be deployed, what privileges and resources they require, how they are updated, and how much operational work they create.

Fidelis, for example, supports passive discovery approaches that do not require endpoint modification for that discovery process, while its OT deception can use lightweight virtual images and containerized services deployed off-path. The exact architecture should still be validated against the intended use case.

How should organizations conduct a deception technology comparison?
  • Use the same attack scenario and success criteria for every vendor.
  • Test whether the attacker encounters the deception,
  • Whether the deception remains believable under inspection,
  • What context the SOC receives after an interaction,
  • How much effort is required to deploy and maintain the environment.

items.title: How “123456” became the key to almost 9 million personal records
items.summary: An attacker reportedly used a leaked password to abuse a company’s legitimate access to Denmark’s population register (CPR). The weak password is remarkable, but the failure to spot millions of unusual searches made the breach worse. The CPR administration states it identified a serious security incident. By abusing a Danish company’s authorized access to the CPR system, unauthorized people gained access to the names, addresses, CPR numbers, and other information belonging to around 8.8 million people registered in the system. CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. How could a password so weak that it should have been rejected by the system open the door to so much personal information ? The attacker reportedly gained access through Pays ApS, an IT company based in Odense. According to TV 2 , Pays has confirmed that its authorized access to search the CPR system was abused. Pays offers services including data updates and “CPR cleansing,” allowing customers to check records against the register to update addresses, identify people who have died, and obtain information about changes of address. The attacker reportedly used a leaked password associated with a former Pays employee. TV 2 says an email containing the password 123456 had appeared in a larger data leak, and that this account of the initial access matches its own research. The attackers had access for 21 days before it was shut down on October 2, although the suspicious activity appears to have stopped on September 20. An unusually large bill for around 14 million searches drew attention to the breach. Politiken reports that the data stolen in those searches belonged to approximately 5.5 million living and 3.3 million deceased people. A weak, leaked password opened an authorized route into a sensitive register. That access allowed millions of searches, and the activity was discovered only after an unusually large bill drew attention to it. How to stay safe If your organization handles sensitive data: Don’t reuse passwords or use personal passwords for work accounts. Use a password manager to create and remember strong, unique passwords for you. For systems that give access to sensitive data, enforce authentication that would reject weak passwords and make multi-factor authentication mandatory. Monitor for unusual activity. That many searches from one account should have been noticed earlier. If your data may have been exposed in this breach: Keep an eye on official updates about the incident. Be alert to phishing and other scams. Scammers could use personal details to make their messages more convincing. Read our blog Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know . items.title: IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws, Including Critical Remote Code Execution Bugs
items.summary: IBM patched 22 vulnerabilities in Verify Identity Access and Security Verify Access, including two critical flaws allowing unauthenticated remote code execution across appliance and container deployments. The most severe bugs, CVE-2026-78401 and CVE-2026-78406, each carry a CVSS score of 9.8. Both involve deserializing untrusted data, a process where software rebuilds stored or transmitted data into objects without properly checking whether it is safe. The publicly listed advisory for CVE-2026-78401 confirms the risk of unauthenticated remote code execution . IBM rates both deserialization bugs as network-accessible attacks with low complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction.IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws, Including Critical Remote Code Execution Bugs. Successful exploitation could seriously affect data confidentiality, integrity, and service availability. However, the supplied bulletin does not identify vulnerable endpoints, describe an exploit chain, or report confirmed attacks. These critical flaws deserve close attention because attackers do not need a valid account to reach the vulnerable code. Their severity reflects potential impact and ease of attack, not evidence that exploitation has already occurred. IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws Three additional vulnerabilities carry scores of 9.1. CVE-2026-16916 allows an authenticated, high-privilege remote attacker to execute arbitrary code because a protection mechanism fails. CVE-2026-16823 enables attackers to bypass security restrictions, while CVE-2026-19491 allows authentication bypass. Unlike the deserialization bugs, these issues require different access and have different outcomes. The update follows earlier IBM Identity and Verify Access vulnerabilities reported by Cyber Security News, which covered request smuggling, privilege escalation, and other security weaknesses in the same product family. Do not confuse those earlier fixes with this October patch release. The bulletin also addresses CVE-2026-18740 and CVE-2026-19482, both rated 8.8. These argument injection flaws let authenticated remote attackers perform unauthorized actions or execute arbitrary commands. CVE-2026-19493, rated 7.5, allows a remote attacker to write files through path traversal. Other vulnerabilities include cross-site scripting that could expose credentials within trusted sessions, SQL injection that could modify data or disrupt services, and cross-site request forgery that could trigger unauthorized actions . Additional fixes address audit log forgery, incorrect authorization checks, authentication workflow bypass, and information disclosure in the Snapshot Manager Container. Several denial-of-service flaws affect resource allocation, recursive processing, and memory reads. IBM also patched a stack buffer write issue that requires administrative privileges and access to the local management interface. Earlier IBM Security Verify command execution coverage provides related background on previously patched appliance flaws. Affected releases include IBM Security Verify Access and its Container edition from 10.0 through 10.0.9.2. IBM Verify Identity Access and its Container edition are affected from 11.0 through 11.0.3. IBM directs appliance customers to install Verify Identity Access 11.0.3.1 or Security Verify Access 10.0.9.3 through its Fix Central download links. Container customers should follow IBM’s container download guidance , which identifies product images and registry locations. IBM renamed Security Verify Access to Verify Identity Access starting with version 11.0.0. The bulletin lists no workarounds or mitigations. IBM encourages customers to update promptly, and the bulletin lists the supplied fixes as the stated remediation for these vulnerabilities across affected supported deployments. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. Integrate ANYRUN’s Sandbox in your SOC

items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Webshells and XMRig Miners
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting two flaws in AhsayCBS backup servers to run commands, plant webshells, and install XMRig cryptocurrency miners disguised as Microsoft Edge. Huntress first observed exploitation on October 7, 2026, at 23:20:15 UTC. By October 8, its researchers had seen five organizations targeted, with attackers checking systems and setting up tools to maintain access. The campaign targets Ahsay Cloud Backup Server, a management platform used by managed service providers and system integrators. Administrators use it to manage backup users, policies, and operations. According to Huntress’s investigation , versions up to 10.3.4 are affected, including a release previously described as safe. The attack chains CVE-2026-105133, a medium-severity authentication flaw in the checkSysPwd function, with CVE-2026-105134, a critical flaw in the Replication Receiver endpoint at /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Together, they let attackers bypass login checks and execute commands as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, giving them broad control over the Windows host. Hackers Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws The NVD entry for CVE-2026-105134, published October 4, lists a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and describes remote command injection. It still identifies version 10.3.4 as a fix. However, Huntress’s October 8 update says that the version remains vulnerable, making the conflicting guidance important for administrators assessing exposure. VirusTotal results for msedge.exe (source: Huntress ) After gaining access, attackers configured a malicious replication receiver and placed Java Server Page webshells inside the application’s web directory. Huntress also detected suspicious commands launched by cbssvcX64.exe, the AhsayCBS service executable. This pattern resembles earlier z0Miner attacks against WebLogic servers , where attackers used JSP webshells to maintain access before deploying mining tools. That similarity describes a shared method, not evidence that the campaigns involve the same operators. Attackers downloaded Taskgmr.ps1, edge.exe, msedge.exe, and config.json into temporary folders from an Alibaba Cloud Object Storage endpoint. The file edge.exe was XMRig, while msedge.exe was a modified copy of NSSM, a legitimate utility that keeps other programs running. Hackers are exploiting two flaws in AhsayCBS backup servers to run commands, plant webshells, and install XMRig cryptocurrency miners disguised as Microsoft Edge.

Huntress first observed exploitation on October 7, 2026, at 23:20:15 UTC. By October 8, its researchers had seen five organizations targeted, with attackers checking systems and setting up tools to maintain access.

The campaign targets Ahsay Cloud Backup Server, a management platform used by managed service providers and system integrators. Administrators use it to manage backup users, policies, and operations. According to Huntress’s investigation, versions up to 10.3.4 are affected, including a release previously described as safe.

The attack chains CVE-2026-105133, a medium-severity authentication flaw in the checkSysPwd function, with CVE-2026-105134, a critical flaw in the Replication Receiver endpoint at /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do.

Together, they let attackers bypass login checks and execute commands as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, giving them broad control over the Windows host.

Hackers Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws

The NVD entry for CVE-2026-105134, published October 4, lists a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and describes remote command injection. It still identifies version 10.3.4 as a fix.

However, Huntress’s October 8 update says that the version remains vulnerable, making the conflicting guidance important for administrators assessing exposure.

VirusTotal results for msedge.exe (source: Huntress )

After gaining access, attackers configured a malicious replication receiver and placed Java Server Page webshells inside the application’s web directory. Huntress also detected suspicious commands launched by cbssvcX64.exe, the AhsayCBS service executable.

This pattern resembles earlier z0Miner attacks against WebLogic servers, where attackers used JSP webshells to maintain access before deploying mining tools. That similarity describes a shared method, not evidence that the campaigns involve the same operators.

Attackers downloaded Taskgmr.ps1, edge.exe, msedge.exe, and config.json into temporary folders from an Alibaba Cloud Object Storage endpoint. The file edge.exe was XMRig, while msedge.exe was a modified copy of NSSM, a legitimate utility that keeps other programs running.

items.title: FBI Arrests Cybersecurity Executive in ShinyHunters-Linked Extortion Investigation
items.summary: The FBI arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky in Pennsylvania on October 8, 2026, as part of its investigation into the hacking group ShinyHunters . The arrest links a professional involved in ransomware response to an alleged cyber extortion conspiracy. However, the evidence behind the charges remains largely sealed, and the allegations have not been proven in court. According to KrebsOnSecurity, Dubrovsky was associated with Canadian security firm CyberSteward and had planned to attend a cyber insurance conference in Philadelphia. Sources told the publication that the arrested Canadian was visiting Pennsylvania for the event. The Cyber Risk Summit ran from October 5 through October 7 at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel. The public court docket lists the defendant as Edward Dobrovsky, a slightly different spelling. FBI Arrests Cybersecurity Executive in ShinyHunters KrebsOnSecurity reported charges involving conspiracy to threaten the confidentiality of information to extort money and interference with commerce through threats. With the main complaint sealed, the public record does not explain what actions prosecutors allege Dobrovsky took. An October 9 court order committed the defendant to the Eastern District of Texas. Records also show that a judge appointed federal defenders and ordered detention pending a hearing in the charging district. This updates an important detail in the initial reporting, which said Dubrovsky had not yet received appointed counsel. Cypfer, another Canadian cybersecurity company, disputed Dubrovsky’s claim that he was a former founder. In an October 10 update, a company spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity that he had served as managing director, not founder or co-founder, and resigned in November 2025. The distinction prevents his arrest from being wrongly presented as the arrest of Cypfer’s founder. Indexed at Courtlistener (source : krebsonsecurity ) ShinyHunters typically steals login details through phishing and uses compromised accounts to take data from cloud software services. The group then threatens to publish stolen records unless victims pay. KrebsOnSecurity, citing the FBI, reported that the group had extorted more than $70 million from victims during 2026. The investigation also covers the theft of sensitive information from the FBI’s recruitment portal. The New York Times reported that stolen records included home addresses, Social Security numbers , and sensitive job assignments. KrebsOnSecurity said the exposed material included medical and psychiatric information. Such records create concerns beyond financial loss because they reveal deeply personal details about bureau personnel. The case follows the arrest of an alleged ShinyHunters leader in the Netherlands . Dutch police detained a 24-year-old Amsterdam suspect on September 15 with FBI support. A security company executive identified him as Pepijn van der Stap, although Dutch authorities did not publicly name him. His alleged role remains unproven. Another development involved Saif al-Din Khader, reportedly known online as Rey. Cybersecurity News previously reported that the suspected ShinyHunters member helped FBI investigators after detention in Jordan. That reported cooperation does not establish his role in the FBI breach or validate every claim made by the hacking group. For readers following the case, the key gap remains Dubrovsky’s alleged conduct. Public reporting establishes an arrest and allegations of extortion, but the sealed complaint limits scrutiny of the evidence. Further court filings may clarify how prosecutors connect his work to ShinyHunters. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. Integrate ANYRUN’s Sandbox in your SOC

items.title: DTX + UCX 2026: Ingram Micro on Unlocking AI and Cloud Without Losing Control
items.summary: Ahead of their participation at DTX + UCX London 2026 , Lee Robson, AWS Greenfield Practice Lead at Ingram Micro shares what the company will be showcasing at the event and explains what trends will impact the channel in the year ahead. How is Ingram Micro participating in DTX + UCX 2026? Ingram Micro will be showcasing how organisations can accelerate innovation with AWS. Our team will be demonstrating practical AI, cloud and security solutions, including AWS Quick , Claude via Amazon Bedrock , FinOps-led cloud optimisation and AWS security assessments . We’ll be connecting customers with specialist partners that can help turn strategy into measurable business outcomes. What are the key messages you will be promoting to delegates of the show? Our message is simple: unlock the value of AI and cloud while maintaining control of cost, security and governance. We’ll be highlighting how AWS enables organisations to innovate faster, connect apps, data, and teams so answers turn into action instantly with AWS Quick, adopt generative AI through Claude via Bedrock, optimise cloud spend through FinOps, and strengthen their security posture. What are the biggest challenges organisations face when purchasing technology through the channel? Many organisations are overwhelmed by the pace of technology change, particularly around AI and cloud. Common challenges include understanding where to start, selecting the right solutions, managing cloud costs, ensuring security and compliance, and finding the skills required to implement and support new technologies successfully. How can dedicated, experienced partners solve these challenges? Experienced partners help customers move from technology discussions to business outcomes. With Ingram Micro, they remove the barrier to entry for a lot of businesses and provide strategic guidance, technical expertise and proven delivery frameworks that reduce risk and accelerate adoption. Partners can also help organisations optimise AWS investments, implement AI responsibly, improve security and create clear roadmaps for long-term success. What trends do you believe will impact the channel in the year ahead? Generative AI adoption will continue to accelerate, but organisations will increasingly focus on governance, security and achieving measurable ROI. We also expect greater emphasis on FinOps as cloud estates mature, alongside growing demand for cybersecurity services. Partners that combine AI expertise, cloud optimisation and security capabilities will be best positioned for growth.

items.title: Pluralistic: How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist (12 Oct 2026)
items.summary: Today's links How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist : If you care about labor justice and artists' rights, stop focusing on copyright. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : China unblocks Wikipedia; CCC cracks the Bundestrojaner; "Children of the Sky"; "Messy"; Every top Icelandic banker is guilty; Climate activism x digital activism; Gene Kan on P2P's future; Larry Ellison x mass surveillance; W3C v patents; "Work from home" in the cybercrime supply-chain; "Nursery Rhyme Comics"; Glitchy tea-set; Tourist Guy; Vista v reinstallation; Ryanair v your bladder; Wells Fargo CEO loves "sales culture"; "Attention Merchants"; Orban v free press; AI v GIGO; Dylan wins the Nobel; India's starving kids app; Adobe's spyware copyfraud; Charter blackmails customers with bad credit threats; Fix UK housing. Upcoming appearances : Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Kilkenny, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist ( permalink ) If you work in the media, you have doubtless had a lifetime of encouragement to treat copyright as your primary source of economic protection, and doubtless you've been told that this protection arises from the fact that copyright is a property right – specifically, it's a subspecies of "intellectual property": https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-ip/ Property rights are capitalism's holy sacrament, so of course, it's natural to treasure any property right you can lay claim to. But this is a trap. Creative workers aren't asset speculators , we're workers . When we bargain with a media company to sell them our copyright, we're just bargaining to sell our labor , not our property . This is a distinction with a difference. Property rights are alienable . When you negotiate to sell your property to someone else, you propose to transfer the title to that property. If you sell your house, you don't get to move back in if you change your mind later. Sell your car, and you must not get in and drive it away. Nominally, creative workers only bargain away some of their copyright, because copyright is also divisible . You can sell US English print rights to a novel, a one-month license to synch a song to an advertisement, or the right to display a painting for a year. But here's the thing about property rights: the most reliable predictor of how many property rights you must give up in a sale isn't how many property rights you started with – it's how much bargaining power you have. For 50 years, governments have expanded copyright in every way, making it last longer, cover more works and restrict more uses, all backstopped by ever-steepening penalties. 50 years later, media companies – our bosses – are larger and more profitable than they've ever been, and we're poorer than we've ever been. The share of the money generated by our labor has declined, even as our rights over the product of that labor have expanded. How to make sense of this? It's easy, once you factor in power . In a world of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies and a single ebook/audiobook company, getting more copyright to bargain with just means getting more copyright to bargain away . When copyright's term expanded from "life plus 50 years" to "life plus 70 years," our bosses simply demanded the entirety of the new term, and didn't offer us a dime more. This is the thesis of Chokepoint Capitalism , the book on Big Tech, Big Media, and creative labor markets Rebecca Giblin and I published in 2022: https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx Chokepoint Capitalism is broken into two parts: the first half of the book is a series of pitiless, plain-language dissections of the baroque scams that media companies have used to make themselves richer from our work, from Spotify to Amazon to Livenation and beyond. From reader feedback, I can tell you that these chapters will make you very angry, because once you strip away all the deliberate obfuscation, all you're left with is one screw-job after another, each of which makes the creators you love poorer even as you pay more for their work. But then there's the second half of the book. This section is devoted to "shovel-ready" policy solutions, each of which is designed to change the "distribution" of the spoils of the media industry, putting more money in workers' pockets at the expense of our bosses. None of these are things you can do as a "conscious consumer." The monopolistic destruction of creators' livelihoods is a systemic problem and you can't solve it by shopping better. The point of these chapters is to lay out what we must demand from our policymakers when (inevitably), they propose to "solve" the problem of worsening straits for creative workers – and to help creative workers understand that when our bosses demand more copyright, that's not there to benefit us . One of these systemic solutions is "termination of transfer," a simple and radical idea that has a proven track-record of making creative workers richer at our bosses' expense. Simply put, "termination of transfer" is the statutory right to void any contract you've signed to transfer your copyright to someone else. In the USA, the 1976 Copyright Act introduced a 35-year termination right. 35 years after you sign any copyright contract, you can file some paperwork with the US Copyright Office and get that copyright back, no matter what your contract says . Now, most creative works don't have a commercial life after 35 years (very few works are commercially viable even after the original US copyright term of 14 years), but for those that do, termination of transfer is a reliable way to address the extremely common situation in which a creator signs away their rights for a low price, not knowing that it will become a lasting hit. Once you've scored that hit, you can probably get a better deal from your next work, but the deal for that hit is done and can't be altered. Termination solves this. From The Babysitters Club to the early Stephen King novels to George Clinton's entire catalog, termination of transfer has put lots of money into creative workers' pockets at the expense of corporations that ripped them off at the start of their careers. From the start, there was no question whether termination of transfer would make it into Chokepoint Capitalism . Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject, having co-authored the definitive study of termination: https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/ In the book, we note that – unlike longer copyright terms – termination has a proven track record of putting groceries on creators' tables, braces on their kids' teeth, and a roof over their heads. We go over the legislative history of termination in the 1976 Act, noting that it was originally supposed to be automatic and kick in after just 20 years. If we want to make creative workers richer, changing the 35-year administrative right into an automatic 20-year termination right is a no-brainer amendment to copyright law. How did an automatic right that kicked in after 20 years turn into a right you have to apply for after 35 years? Simple: our bosses hate termination. How much do they hate it? Well, take Mitch Glazier, the head of the Recording Industry Association of America, where he draws a $1.3m annual salary to represent the record labels. Before Glazier got the RIAA gig, he was an obscure Congressional staffer, but he was forced out of the job after he snuck a clause into an otherwise unrelated bill that killed termination of transfer for recording artists. This was so outrageous that Congress actually convened a special session so they could rip out Glazier's amendment, and Glazier got a new job as a millionaire lobbyist for the recording industry: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation Termination is hugely useful and quite radical. Last year saw Gary K Wolf, creator of the novel Who Censored Roger Rabbit? (later adapted by Disney as Who Framed Roger Rabbit? ) claw back his rights to the book and its characters, in order to continue the series: https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way In 2023, Bill Willingham terminated the transfer of his wildly successful graphic novel series Fables from DC and released the copyright into the public domain: https://pluralistic.net/2023/09/15/fairy-use-tales/#sampling-license And now, Richard Garriott, AKA "Lord British," has claimed back the rights to the groundbreaking Ultima series of computer role-playing games, which he sold to Electronic Arts in 1992: https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/richard-garriott-is-officially-regaining-control-of-the-ultima-series/ On the Techjess podcast, Garriott marveled at how easy the process was: "there’s a really weird United States copyright law that says if you are the original holder of a copyright and you assign it or sell it to any publisher or any other entity, after 35 years, you can just take it back": https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2El7VtPuSzs EA killed off Ultima in 2000, and it has languished since, despite an ardent fandom. Garriott has vowed to reissue the old games and is mulling new ones. All this brings me back to property rights. Property rights are uniquely unsuitable to this kind of arrangement. You don't get to move back into the house your parents sold 35 years ago, and if you did, the photographer who took the family portrait in the hallway wouldn't be allowed to break in and take it away 35 years after you sat for it. Termination of transfer isn't an "IP right" – it's a labor right . It belongs to the large class of rights that are far more important and useful than mere property rights, such as privacy rights and human rights: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/28/cost-of-everything/#value-of-nothing If copyright were just about property rights, then termination of transfer would be inconceivable. Termination is a vestigial labor right at the very periphery of copyright. It protects artists, and it can only do so because it is not a property right. This is one of the themes in The Bezzle , my 2024 historical technothriller, starring my two-fisted forensic accountant hero Martin Hench who uses termination to help an artist claw back his rights from an unscrupulous former manager who forged his signature decades before (this plotline is based on the true story of Parliament/Funkadelic's George Clinton!): https://craphound.com/bezzle/ If you signed away your rights 35 years ago and want to get them back, check out the Authors Alliance, a nonprofit whose advisory board I volunteer for. We produced a tool that automates all the hardest parts of terminating your transfers and getting your rights back: https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/ Some of our most ardent fans are academics, whose publicly funded papers are published in journals dominated by a cartel of giant companies that do not pay the authors, nor the editors, nor the reviewers, but still claim all rights and charge the institutions that funded the research they publish tens of thousands of dollars per journal to access that research: https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/16/the-public-sphere/#not-the-elsevier But it's not just academics who have an interest in termination of transfer. It's video game authors, novelists, musicians – and maybe you, someday!
