How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist (permalink)

If you work in the media, you have doubtless had a lifetime of encouragement to treat copyright as your primary source of economic protection, and doubtless you've been told that this protection arises from the fact that copyright is a property right – specifically, it's a subspecies of "intellectual property":

https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-ip/

Property rights are capitalism's holy sacrament, so of course, it's natural to treasure any property right you can lay claim to. But this is a trap. Creative workers aren't asset speculators, we're workers. When we bargain with a media company to sell them our copyright, we're just bargaining to sell our labor, not our property.

This is a distinction with a difference. Property rights are alienable. When you negotiate to sell your property to someone else, you propose to transfer the title to that property. If you sell your house, you don't get to move back in if you change your mind later. Sell your car, and you must not get in and drive it away.

Nominally, creative workers only bargain away some of their copyright, because copyright is also divisible. You can sell US English print rights to a novel, a one-month license to synch a song to an advertisement, or the right to display a painting for a year.

But here's the thing about property rights: the most reliable predictor of how many property rights you must give up in a sale isn't how many property rights you started with – it's how much bargaining power you have. For 50 years, governments have expanded copyright in every way, making it last longer, cover more works and restrict more uses, all backstopped by ever-steepening penalties. 50 years later, media companies – our bosses – are larger and more profitable than they've ever been, and we're poorer than we've ever been. The share of the money generated by our labor has declined, even as our rights over the product of that labor have expanded.

How to make sense of this? It's easy, once you factor in power. In a world of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies and a single ebook/audiobook company, getting more copyright to bargain with just means getting more copyright to bargain away. When copyright's term expanded from "life plus 50 years" to "life plus 70 years," our bosses simply demanded the entirety of the new term, and didn't offer us a dime more.

This is the thesis of Chokepoint Capitalism, the book on Big Tech, Big Media, and creative labor markets Rebecca Giblin and I published in 2022:

https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx

Chokepoint Capitalism is broken into two parts: the first half of the book is a series of pitiless, plain-language dissections of the baroque scams that media companies have used to make themselves richer from our work, from Spotify to Amazon to Livenation and beyond. From reader feedback, I can tell you that these chapters will make you very angry, because once you strip away all the deliberate obfuscation, all you're left with is one screw-job after another, each of which makes the creators you love poorer even as you pay more for their work.

But then there's the second half of the book. This section is devoted to "shovel-ready" policy solutions, each of which is designed to change the "distribution" of the spoils of the media industry, putting more money in workers' pockets at the expense of our bosses. None of these are things you can do as a "conscious consumer." The monopolistic destruction of creators' livelihoods is a systemic problem and you can't solve it by shopping better.

The point of these chapters is to lay out what we must demand from our policymakers when (inevitably), they propose to "solve" the problem of worsening straits for creative workers – and to help creative workers understand that when our bosses demand more copyright, that's not there to benefit us.

One of these systemic solutions is "termination of transfer," a simple and radical idea that has a proven track-record of making creative workers richer at our bosses' expense. Simply put, "termination of transfer" is the statutory right to void any contract you've signed to transfer your copyright to someone else. In the USA, the 1976 Copyright Act introduced a 35-year termination right. 35 years after you sign any copyright contract, you can file some paperwork with the US Copyright Office and get that copyright back, no matter what your contract says.

Now, most creative works don't have a commercial life after 35 years (very few works are commercially viable even after the original US copyright term of 14 years), but for those that do, termination of transfer is a reliable way to address the extremely common situation in which a creator signs away their rights for a low price, not knowing that it will become a lasting hit. Once you've scored that hit, you can probably get a better deal from your next work, but the deal for that hit is done and can't be altered.

Termination solves this. From The Babysitters Club to the early Stephen King novels to George Clinton's entire catalog, termination of transfer has put lots of money into creative workers' pockets at the expense of corporations that ripped them off at the start of their careers.

From the start, there was no question whether termination of transfer would make it into Chokepoint Capitalism. Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject, having co-authored the definitive study of termination:

https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/

In the book, we note that – unlike longer copyright terms – termination has a proven track record of putting groceries on creators' tables, braces on their kids' teeth, and a roof over their heads. We go over the legislative history of termination in the 1976 Act, noting that it was originally supposed to be automatic and kick in after just 20 years. If we want to make creative workers richer, changing the 35-year administrative right into an automatic 20-year termination right is a no-brainer amendment to copyright law.

How did an automatic right that kicked in after 20 years turn into a right you have to apply for after 35 years? Simple: our bosses hate termination. How much do they hate it? Well, take Mitch Glazier, the head of the Recording Industry Association of America, where he draws a $1.3m annual salary to represent the record labels.

Before Glazier got the RIAA gig, he was an obscure Congressional staffer, but he was forced out of the job after he snuck a clause into an otherwise unrelated bill that killed termination of transfer for recording artists. This was so outrageous that Congress actually convened a special session so they could rip out Glazier's amendment, and Glazier got a new job as a millionaire lobbyist for the recording industry:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation

Termination is hugely useful and quite radical. Last year saw Gary K Wolf, creator of the novel Who Censored Roger Rabbit? (later adapted by Disney as Who Framed Roger Rabbit?) claw back his rights to the book and its characters, in order to continue the series:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way

In 2023, Bill Willingham terminated the transfer of his wildly successful graphic novel series Fables from DC and released the copyright into the public domain:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/09/15/fairy-use-tales/#sampling-license

And now, Richard Garriott, AKA "Lord British," has claimed back the rights to the groundbreaking Ultima series of computer role-playing games, which he sold to Electronic Arts in 1992:

https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/richard-garriott-is-officially-regaining-control-of-the-ultima-series/

On the Techjess podcast, Garriott marveled at how easy the process was: "there’s a really weird United States copyright law that says if you are the original holder of a copyright and you assign it or sell it to any publisher or any other entity, after 35 years, you can just take it back":

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2El7VtPuSzs

EA killed off Ultima in 2000, and it has languished since, despite an ardent fandom. Garriott has vowed to reissue the old games and is mulling new ones.

All this brings me back to property rights. Property rights are uniquely unsuitable to this kind of arrangement. You don't get to move back into the house your parents sold 35 years ago, and if you did, the photographer who took the family portrait in the hallway wouldn't be allowed to break in and take it away 35 years after you sat for it.

Termination of transfer isn't an "IP right" – it's a labor right. It belongs to the large class of rights that are far more important and useful than mere property rights, such as privacy rights and human rights:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/28/cost-of-everything/#value-of-nothing

If copyright were just about property rights, then termination of transfer would be inconceivable. Termination is a vestigial labor right at the very periphery of copyright. It protects artists, and it can only do so because it is not a property right.

This is one of the themes in The Bezzle, my 2024 historical technothriller, starring my two-fisted forensic accountant hero Martin Hench who uses termination to help an artist claw back his rights from an unscrupulous former manager who forged his signature decades before (this plotline is based on the true story of Parliament/Funkadelic's George Clinton!):

https://craphound.com/bezzle/

If you signed away your rights 35 years ago and want to get them back, check out the Authors Alliance, a nonprofit whose advisory board I volunteer for. We produced a tool that automates all the hardest parts of terminating your transfers and getting your rights back:

https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/

Some of our most ardent fans are academics, whose publicly funded papers are published in journals dominated by a cartel of giant companies that do not pay the authors, nor the editors, nor the reviewers, but still claim all rights and charge the institutions that funded the research they publish tens of thousands of dollars per journal to access that research:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/16/the-public-sphere/#not-the-elsevier

But it's not just academics who have an interest in termination of transfer. It's video game authors, novelists, musicians – and maybe you, someday!

items.title: From zero to agent builder: Running kagent on your laptop
items.summary: If you have seen a demo of a no-code agent builder, you know the moment. Someone types one sentence, waits a minute, and there it is: a new agent, running, with tools. It is impressive. For about ten seconds. Then the questions start. Where does it run? What can it touch? Who approved it? This post is about the first part, the ten impressive seconds. I want to show that it is not magic and that you can build it yourself, in an afternoon, with open source and spending a minimum on tokens. The tool is kagent , a CNCF Sandbox project that runs AI agents as Kubernetes resources. The questions come back at the end, because they are the real work. Why kagent makes this almost boring In kagent, an agent is not a process you start by hand. It is a custom resource. You write an Agent with a system prompt, a model, and a list of tools. You apply it, and the controller turns it into a running pod that speaks A2A . Once agents are just YAML, an agent that builds agents is simply an agent that can write one kind of YAML. No new framework, no plugin. One Agent , three tools, and a prompt that knows what an Agent looks like. Figure 1: An agent that builds agents, on kagent. Before you start: What this lab is not The goal here is the builder. Security is out of scope, on purpose, and I want to be upfront about what that means: kagent runs in its default unsecure auth mode, so every request acts as the same user. The chart’s bundled PostgreSQL uses its built-in password. The UI and API are reachable only through kubectl port-forward on 127.0.0.1. That is fine for a laptop. It is not fine for a shared cluster, and I will come back to why that gap matters. You need Docker, kind, kubectl, helm, jq and Ollama (alternatively, you can use your API Key for Claude, OpenAI, or any other provider, but we wanted to make it as cheap as possible). There is nothing to clone: you create every file as you go. Start in an empty folder: mkdir kagent-agent-builder && cd kagent-agent-builder Step 1: Pick a local model that can actually do it This is the part that surprised me. Writing a valid Kubernetes manifest through a tool call is harder than chatting, and small models show it. In my runs, qwen2.5:7b-instruct invented its own tool block format, and qwen2.5:14b-instruct sometimes answered politely without ever calling the apply tool. qwen3-coder:30b-a3b got it right on every run, so that is the model this post uses: ollama pull qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q4_K_M # about 18 GB on disk The cluster reaches Ollama at host.docker.internal:11434, which works out of the box with Docker Desktop. On Linux you have to change that host in the values file below to an address the kind node can reach. I have not tested that path. If you prefer a hosted model, kagent’s Helm chart also has provider blocks for OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI and Gemini. Then it is no longer free, of course. Step 2: Install kagent with a tool server that can only write Agents Create the cluster: kind create cluster --name kagent-builder kagent ships a tool server with Kubernetes tools, and by default the chart gives its ServiceAccount cluster-admin. A builder backed by cluster-admin is a bad idea even on a laptop, so the values file changes that. Create it: providers: default: ollama ollama: provider: Ollama model: "qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q4_K_M" config: host: host.docker.internal:11434 options: num_ctx: "32768" kagent-tools: tools: enabledTools: - k8s rbac: readOnly: true additionalRules: - apiGroups: ["kagent.dev"] resources: ["agents"] verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"] grafana-mcp: {enabled: false} k8s-agent: {enabled: false} kgateway-agent: {enabled: false} istio-agent: {enabled: false} promql-agent: {enabled: false} observability-agent: {enabled: false} argo-rollouts-agent: {enabled: false} helm-agent: {enabled: false} cilium-policy-agent: {enabled: false} cilium-manager-agent: {enabled: false} cilium-debug-agent: {enabled: false} The model becomes the default ModelConfig . The tool server loads only its Kubernetes tools (22 of them). And it gets a read-only role plus one extra rule: it may write agents.kagent.dev, nothing else. The last block turns off the sample agents the chart installs by default, so the UI only shows yours. Install the CRDs and kagent 0.10.2 with that file, and wait for the pods: helm upgrade --install kagent-crds oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent-crds \ --kube-context kind-kagent-builder \ --version 0.10.2 --namespace kagent --create-namespace helm upgrade --install kagent oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent \ --kube-context kind-kagent-builder \ --version 0.10.2 --namespace kagent --values kagent-values.yaml for d in kagent-controller kagent-ui kagent-tools; do kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent rollout status deploy/$d --timeout=300s done Step 3: The builder is just an agent This is the whole builder. Create the file: apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2 kind: Agent metadata: name: agent-builder namespace: kagent spec: description: Builds new kagent agents from a plain-language description and deploys them. type: Declarative declarative: modelConfig: default-model-config stream: false systemMessage: | You build kagent agents. The user describes, in plain language, an agent they want. You turn that into ONE Kubernetes manifest and apply it. Do not ask follow-up questions: pick sensible defaults and go. How you work, in this order: 1. List the existing agents with k8s_get_resources (resource_type agents.kagent.dev, namespace kagent). Pick a name that is not taken; never overwrite an existing agent. 2. Write the manifest in exactly the shape below and apply it with k8s_apply_manifest. The user confirms the apply in the UI; that is expected. 3. Read it back with k8s_get_resource_yaml (resource_type agents.kagent.dev, namespace kagent) and look at the Accepted and Ready conditions in its status. Ready can take a few seconds. The manifest must be exactly this shape, and nothing else: apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2 kind: Agent metadata: name: namespace: kagent labels: app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: agent-builder spec: description: |- type: Declarative declarative: modelConfig: default-model-config stream: false systemMessage: | tools: - type: McpServer mcpServer: apiGroup: kagent.dev kind: RemoteMCPServer name: kagent-tool-server toolNames: [ ] Read-only tools you may give it: k8s_get_resources, k8s_get_resource_yaml, k8s_describe_resource, k8s_get_events, k8s_get_pod_logs. Never another kind, never another namespace, never write or delete tools, never more than one document. YAML that does not break: free text always goes in a block scalar, as in the shape above (description with |-, systemMessage with |). In a plain scalar, a colon followed by a space makes the YAML invalid, and a space followed by # silently cuts the value short. When something goes wrong: - If the user rejects the apply, do not retry it and do not read the agent back. Say it was not applied, and stop. - Never create a second resource with another name (-test, -check, -v2) to find out what failed. It tells you nothing and leaves clutter. - Do not name a cause you have not checked. An opaque error is not proof of a name clash, a permission problem or a network issue. - Report the error exactly as the tool returned it, and stop. When it is done, answer in three short lines: the agent's name, what it does, and which tools it can use. Then one more line with its real state from step 3 (Accepted, Ready). Never claim it is ready if it is not. tools: - type: McpServer mcpServer: apiGroup: kagent.dev kind: RemoteMCPServer name: kagent-tool-server toolNames: - k8s_apply_manifest - k8s_get_resources - k8s_get_resource_yaml requireApproval: - k8s_apply_manifest a2aConfig: skills: - id: build-agent name: Build an agent description: Turns a plain-language description into a deployed kagent agent. tags: [builder, agents] examples: - "Create an agent for the support team that answers questions about the state of the services in the cluster" Apply it and wait until kagent reports it Ready: kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder apply -f agent-builder.yaml kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent wait --for=condition=Ready \ agent/agent-builder --timeout=300s The tools block at the end is where the builder gets its limits. toolNames is an allowlist: of the 22 tools on the server, the model sees three. requireApproval is kagent’s human-in-the-loop switch. When the agent calls a tool on that list, the run pauses and the user has to approve or reject the call. The system prompt does the rest. It tells the model to list existing agents first, so it never overwrites one, and then gives it the exact manifest shape it may produce: one Agent , in the kagent namespace, with a label that marks it as built by the builder, and only read-only tools. It also carries a few lessons I learned the hard way. Free text goes in YAML block scalars, because a colon followed by a space inside a plain string breaks the manifest. And when something fails, the model must report the error and stop, not create my-agent-v2 to see what happens. Keep in mind that the prompt is a request, not a guarantee. The guarantees are the allowlist, the approval and RBAC. Step 4: Ask for an agent Open the UI: kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent port-forward \ --address 127.0.0.1 svc/kagent-ui 8080:8080 Go to http://localhost:8080 , pick agent-builder and ask for something: Create an agent for the support team that answers questions about the state of the services in the cluster After half a minute or so the run stops. The UI shows the manifest the model wants to apply and two buttons. Figure 2: The UI showing the manifest requiring user approval before applying. Read it before you click. This is the one moment where a human sees exactly what is about to land in the cluster. Approve, and the builder applies it, reads it back and reports the real state: Figure 3: The UI showing the result and real state after applying the manifest. The new agent shows up in the agent list and you can chat with it straight away. Ask it which services exist in the kagent namespace. It answers with read-only tools, because those are the only ones the builder was allowed to give it. Step 5: The same thing without the UI Every kagent agent is an A2A endpoint on the controller, so you can script the whole flow. Forward the controller port and send the request: kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent port-forward \ --address 127.0.0.1 svc/kagent-controller 8083:8083 & sleep 3 # give the port-forward a moment to listen curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/api/a2a/kagent/agent-builder/ \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"1","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"Create an agent that lists the pods that are not running in the kagent namespace"}]}}}' \ > build.json jq -r '.result.status.state' build.json # input-required input-required means the apply is waiting for you. The pending manifest is in a data part of the status message. To answer, send a message on the same task and context with a decision: TASK=$(jq -r .result.id build.json); CTX=$(jq -r .result.contextId build.json) curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/api/a2a/kagent/agent-builder/ \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":\"2\",\"method\":\"message/send\",\"params\":{\"message\":{\"role\":\"user\",\"messageId\":\"2\",\"taskId\":\"$TASK\",\"contextId\":\"$CTX\",\"parts\":[{\"kind\":\"data\",\"data\":{\"decision_type\":\"approve\"}}]}}}" \ | jq -r '.result.status.state' # completed Use “ reject ” instead of “ approve ” and nothing is created. Either way, the cluster tells you what really happened: kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent get agents Why three guardrails and not one Figure 4: Three guardrails that do not depend on the prompt. It is tempting to think the prompt is enough. It is not, and not because the model is malicious. Models get YAML wrong, retry in creative ways and misunderstand requests. It happened to me while checking the commands for this post. The prompt spells out the tool server name, kagent-tool-server , and one run still produced an Agent pointing at kagent-tools . My curl approved it blindly, as scripts do. The controller refused it: Accepted=False, RemoteMCPServer "kagent-tools" not found . Nothing broke, but it is a good reminder of where the real checks live. Each layer catches what the previous one lets through: The allowlist. If the model reaches for k8s_delete_resource , the tool simply is not there. The approval. If it writes a manifest you did not expect, you see it before it exists. RBAC. If you approve something you should not have, the API server still refuses anything that is not an Agent . You can check that last one yourself: SA=system:serviceaccount:kagent:kagent-tools kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder auth can-i create agents.kagent.dev --as=$SA -n kagent # yes kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder auth can-i create deployments --as=$SA -n kagent # no kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder auth can-i get secrets --as=$SA -n kagent # no The part this lab leaves open So building the agent took one YAML file and a couple of Helm installs. That was the easy part, and it is exactly why I do not think it is the interesting part anymore. Look again at the box at the bottom of Figure 4 . On this laptop nobody knows who asked for the agent, because everyone is the same user. Nobody knows what its model calls cost, or for which team. And nobody decided whether the agent should exist, beyond one click by whoever happened to be in the chat. Now imagine a company with a builder like this, a few frameworks, a hosted agent platform and a couple of assistants on developers’ machines. Each one answers those questions differently, if it answers them at all. That is the argument for a governance layer that sits in front of the agents, wherever they come from, instead of inside each one. In the open source world one option is agentgateway , a Linux Foundation project. It proxies LLM, MCP and A2A traffic, with authentication (JWT, API keys), fine-grained authorization with CEL, and OpenTelemetry metrics, logs and traces for every call. Wiring it in front of this lab is a good next exercise, and probably my next post. Clean up Everything lives in the kind cluster, so one command removes it: kind delete cluster --name kagent-builder Where to go from here The kagent docs cover more tool servers, other model providers and agents written in code, and the project lives at github.com/kagent-dev/kagent . If you build something on top of this, or you find a smaller local model that handles the builder well, I would really like to hear about it.

  default: ollama
  ollama:
    provider: Ollama
    model: "qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q4_K_M"
    config:
      host: host.docker.internal:11434
      options:
        num_ctx: "32768"
kagent-tools:
  tools:
    enabledTools:
      - k8s
  rbac:
    readOnly: true
    additionalRules:
      - apiGroups: ["kagent.dev"]
        resources: ["agents"]
        verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
grafana-mcp: {enabled: false}
k8s-agent: {enabled: false}
kgateway-agent: {enabled: false}
istio-agent: {enabled: false}
promql-agent: {enabled: false}
observability-agent: {enabled: false}
argo-rollouts-agent: {enabled: false}
helm-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-policy-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-manager-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-debug-agent: {enabled: false}

The model becomes the default ModelConfig. The tool server loads only its Kubernetes tools (22 of them). And it gets a read-only role plus one extra rule: it may write agents.kagent.dev, nothing else. The last block turns off the sample agents the chart installs by default, so the UI only shows yours.

Install the CRDs and kagent 0.10.2 with that file, and wait for the pods:

helm upgrade --install kagent-crds oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent-crds \
  --kube-context kind-kagent-builder \
  --version 0.10.2 --namespace kagent --create-namespace
helm upgrade --install kagent oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent \
  --kube-context kind-kagent-builder \
  --version 0.10.2 --namespace kagent --values kagent-values.yaml
for d in kagent-controller kagent-ui kagent-tools; do
  kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent rollout status deploy/$d --timeout=300s
done
Step 3: The builder is just an agent

This is the whole builder. Create the file:

apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: agent-builder
  namespace: kagent
spec:
  description: Builds new kagent agents from a plain-language description and deploys them.
  type: Declarative
  declarative:
    modelConfig: default-model-config
    stream: false
    systemMessage: |
      You build kagent agents. The user describes, in plain language, an agent
      they want. You turn that into ONE Kubernetes manifest and apply it. Do not
      ask follow-up questions: pick sensible defaults and go.
      How you work, in this order:
      1. List the existing agents with k8s_get_resources (resource_type
         agents.kagent.dev, namespace kagent). Pick a name that is not taken;
         never overwrite an existing agent.
      2. Write the manifest in exactly the shape below and apply it with
         k8s_apply_manifest. The user confirms the apply in the UI; that is
         expected.
      3. Read it back with k8s_get_resource_yaml (resource_type
         agents.kagent.dev, namespace kagent) and look at the Accepted and
         Ready conditions in its status. Ready can take a few seconds.
      The manifest must be exactly this shape, and nothing else:
        apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2
        kind: Agent
        metadata:
          name: 
          namespace: kagent
          labels:
            app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: agent-builder
        spec:
          description: |-
            
          type: Declarative
          declarative:
            modelConfig: default-model-config
            stream: false
            systemMessage: |
              
            tools:
              - type: McpServer
                mcpServer:
                  apiGroup: kagent.dev
                  kind: RemoteMCPServer
                  name: kagent-tool-server
                  toolNames: []
      Read-only tools you may give it: k8s_get_resources, k8s_get_resource_yaml,
      k8s_describe_resource, k8s_get_events, k8s_get_pod_logs.
      Never another kind, never another namespace, never write or delete tools,
      never more than one document.
      YAML that does not break: free text always goes in a block scalar, as in
      the shape above (description with |-, systemMessage with |). In a plain
      scalar, a colon followed by a space makes the YAML invalid, and a space
      followed by # silently cuts the value short.
      When something goes wrong:
      - If the user rejects the apply, do not retry it and do not read the
        agent back. Say it was not applied, and stop.
      - Never create a second resource with another name (-test, -check, -v2)
        to find out what failed. It tells you nothing and leaves clutter.
      - Do not name a cause you have not checked. An opaque error is not proof
        of a name clash, a permission problem or a network issue.
      - Report the error exactly as the tool returned it, and stop.
      When it is done, answer in three short lines: the agent's name, what it
      does, and which tools it can use. Then one more line with its real state
      from step 3 (Accepted, Ready). Never claim it is ready if it is not.
    tools:
      - type: McpServer
        mcpServer:
          apiGroup: kagent.dev
          kind: RemoteMCPServer
          name: kagent-tool-server
          toolNames:
            - k8s_apply_manifest
            - k8s_get_resources
            - k8s_get_resource_yaml
          requireApproval:
            - k8s_apply_manifest
    a2aConfig:
      skills:
        - id: build-agent
          name: Build an agent
          description: Turns a plain-language description into a deployed kagent agent.
          tags: [builder, agents]
          examples:
            - "Create an agent for the support team that answers questions about the state of the services in the cluster"

Apply it and wait until kagent reports it Ready:

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder apply -f agent-builder.yaml
kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent wait --for=condition=Ready \
  agent/agent-builder --timeout=300s

The tools block at the end is where the builder gets its limits. toolNames is an allowlist: of the 22 tools on the server, the model sees three. requireApproval is kagent’s human-in-the-loop switch. When the agent calls a tool on that list, the run pauses and the user has to approve or reject the call.

The system prompt does the rest. It tells the model to list existing agents first, so it never overwrites one, and then gives it the exact manifest shape it may produce: one Agent, in the kagent namespace, with a label that marks it as built by the builder, and only read-only tools. It also carries a few lessons I learned the hard way. Free text goes in YAML block scalars, because a colon followed by a space inside a plain string breaks the manifest. And when something fails, the model must report the error and stop, not create my-agent-v2 to see what happens.

Keep in mind that the prompt is a request, not a guarantee. The guarantees are the allowlist, the approval and RBAC.

Step 4: Ask for an agent

Open the UI:

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent port-forward \
  --address 127.0.0.1 svc/kagent-ui 8080:8080

Go to http://localhost:8080, pick agent-builder and ask for something:

Create an agent for the support team that answers questions
about the state of the services in the cluster

After half a minute or so the run stops. The UI shows the manifest the model wants to apply and two buttons.

Figure 2: The UI showing the manifest requiring user approval before applying.

Read it before you click. This is the one moment where a human sees exactly what is about to land in the cluster. Approve, and the builder applies it, reads it back and reports the real state:

Figure 3: The UI showing the result and real state after applying the manifest.

The new agent shows up in the agent list and you can chat with it straight away. Ask it which services exist in the kagent namespace. It answers with read-only tools, because those are the only ones the builder was allowed to give it.

Step 5: The same thing without the UI

Every kagent agent is an A2A endpoint on the controller, so you can script the whole flow. Forward the controller port and send the request:

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent port-forward \
  --address 127.0.0.1 svc/kagent-controller 8083:8083 &
sleep 3   # give the port-forward a moment to listen

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/api/a2a/kagent/agent-builder/ \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"1","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"Create an agent that lists the pods that are not running in the kagent namespace"}]}}}' \
  > build.json

jq -r '.result.status.state' build.json    # input-required

input-required means the apply is waiting for you. The pending manifest is in a data part of the status message. To answer, send a message on the same task and context with a decision:

TASK=$(jq -r .result.id build.json); CTX=$(jq -r .result.contextId build.json)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/api/a2a/kagent/agent-builder/ \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":\"2\",\"method\":\"message/send\",\"params\":{\"message\":{\"role\":\"user\",\"messageId\":\"2\",\"taskId\":\"$TASK\",\"contextId\":\"$CTX\",\"parts\":[{\"kind\":\"data\",\"data\":{\"decision_type\":\"approve\"}}]}}}" \
  | jq -r '.result.status.state'            # completed

Use “reject” instead of “approve” and nothing is created. Either way, the cluster tells you what really happened:

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent get agents
Why three guardrails and not one

Figure 4: Three guardrails that do not depend on the prompt.

It is tempting to think the prompt is enough. It is not, and not because the model is malicious. Models get YAML wrong, retry in creative ways and misunderstand requests.

  • It happened to me while checking the commands for this post. The prompt spells out the tool server name, kagent-tool-server, and one run still produced an Agent pointing at kagent-tools. My curl approved it blindly, as scripts do. The controller refused it: Accepted=False, RemoteMCPServer "kagent-tools" not found. Nothing broke, but it is a good reminder of where the real checks live. Each layer catches what the previous one lets through:
  • The allowlist. If the model reaches for k8s_delete_resource, the tool simply is not there.
  • The approval. If it writes a manifest you did not expect, you see it before it exists.
  • RBAC. If you approve something you should not have, the API server still refuses anything that is not an Agent.

You can check that last one yourself:

SA=system:serviceaccount:kagent:kagent-tools

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder auth can-i create
agents.kagent.dev --as=$SA -n kagent   # yes

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder auth can-i create
deployments       --as=$SA -n kagent   # no

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder auth can-i get secrets              
--as=$SA -n kagent   # no
The part this lab leaves open

So building the agent took one YAML file and a couple of Helm installs. That was the easy part, and it is exactly why I do not think it is the interesting part anymore.

Look again at the box at the bottom of Figure 4. On this laptop nobody knows who asked for the agent, because everyone is the same user. Nobody knows what its model calls cost, or for which team. And nobody decided whether the agent should exist, beyond one click by whoever happened to be in the chat. Now imagine a company with a builder like this, a few frameworks, a hosted agent platform and a couple of assistants on developers’ machines. Each one answers those questions differently, if it answers them at all.

That is the argument for a governance layer that sits in front of the agents, wherever they come from, instead of inside each one. In the open source world one option is agentgateway, a Linux Foundation project. It proxies LLM, MCP and A2A traffic, with authentication (JWT, API keys), fine-grained authorization with CEL, and OpenTelemetry metrics, logs and traces for every call. Wiring it in front of this lab is a good next exercise, and probably my next post.

Clean up

Everything lives in the kind cluster, so one command removes it:

kind delete cluster --name kagent-builder
Where to go from here

The kagent docs cover more tool servers, other model providers and agents written in code, and the project lives at github.com/kagent-dev/kagent. If you build something on top of this, or you find a smaller local model that handles the builder well, I would really like to hear about it.

items.title: Phishing emails are baiting your AI assistant
items.summary: You ignored the suspicious email. You didn’t open the attachment, click the link, or reply to the sender. Then you asked your AI assistant to summarize your inbox. Could the message you wisely avoided find its way back onto your to-do list—only this time presented as an urgent recommendation from a tool you trust? That’s the risk behind phishing emails containing hidden instructions aimed at AI assistants. Instead of relying only on persuading you, attackers are also trying to influence the software that reads your messages. Recent research from Barracuda describes emails designed to target both audiences at once. For the human recipient, there was a password-protected attachment, with the password supplied in the email. For an AI assistant processing the message, there were hidden instructions intended to influence how it summarized or handled the content. By including a prompt injection , attackers give themselves another way to reach you. The malicious instructions could try to make the assistant describe the email as legitimate or urgent, encouraging you to revisit it. In another example, a hidden block instructed a summarizing AI to add a fake priority action: Change a vendor’s payment details. That could result in an employee sending money to an attacker’s account. The attacker isn’t simply asking the AI to repeat a fraudulent request. They’re trying to turn that request into the assistant’s recommendation. How prompt injection works Prompt injection means planting instructions in material an AI system is supposed to read, hoping it will follow those instructions instead of treating them as part of the material. When the instructions arrive through an outside source, such as an email or webpage, it’s often called indirect prompt injection. The malicious instructions don’t have to appear as ordinary, readable paragraphs. Barracuda identified concealment techniques including comments in the email’s underlying HTML code, text made invisible through styling, encoded content, and invisible “zero-width” characters. These can obscure instructions from a person viewing the message while leaving content available for an AI system to process. Whether that content actually reaches the model depends on how the particular tool extracts and prepares the email. That means this problem cannot be solved simply by asking people to look more carefully at their emails. Part of the defense must sit inside the tools handling those messages. Apollo Raines , developer of the AI code review service ShipItClean , explains: “The real flaw is that the model can’t tell the difference between text it’s supposed to read and instructions it’s supposed to follow. Stripping hidden content before it reaches the model is worth doing, and every vendor should do it. But it’s an arms race. Each new encoding trick is a new hole.” He adds: “People have learned to distrust the email. They haven’t learned to distrust their AI assistant. So, the defense has to live inside the tools. I’d go one step further: some of it has to live inside the model itself. Wrappers, filters, sandboxing and human sign-off on payments are all necessary.” Before taking action An assistant that summarizes messages could mislead you about which email deserves attention or what action it requires. An assistant with additional permissions could create a more serious problem. Depending on its capabilities and safeguards, malicious instructions might try to make it carry out unauthorized actions or disclose sensitive information . You don’t need to abandon AI tools that help with email. But you do need to consider what you trust them to do and what permissions you give them. The familiar phishing advice still applies. When an assistant reads your inbox on your behalf, check its recommendations before acting: Check the original message before acting on a recommendation involving money or sensitive information. If a summary tells you to pay an invoice, change account details, or share sensitive information, don’t treat the summary itself as verification. Always verify payment changes through a separate, established channel. Contact the person or organization using details you already trust, rather than relying on information supplied in the suspicious message. Keep your AI assistant’s permissions limited to what you need and, at work, what your organization allows. An assistant used to summarize emails should not need broad authority to carry out unrelated actions. Limiting access can reduce the consequences if it follows malicious instructions. Require human approval for high-impact actions like payments and changes to vendor payment details. Approval should include checking the underlying request, not simply accepting the assistant’s recommendation. From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today .

You ignored the suspicious email. You didn’t open the attachment, click the link, or reply to the sender.

Then you asked your AI assistant to summarize your inbox.

Could the message you wisely avoided find its way back onto your to-do list—only this time presented as an urgent recommendation from a tool you trust?

That’s the risk behind phishing emails containing hidden instructions aimed at AI assistants. Instead of relying only on persuading you, attackers are also trying to influence the software that reads your messages. Recent research from Barracuda describes emails designed to target both audiences at once.

For the human recipient, there was a password-protected attachment, with the password supplied in the email. For an AI assistant processing the message, there were hidden instructions intended to influence how it summarized or handled the content.

By including a prompt injection, attackers give themselves another way to reach you. The malicious instructions could try to make the assistant describe the email as legitimate or urgent, encouraging you to revisit it.

In another example, a hidden block instructed a summarizing AI to add a fake priority action: Change a vendor’s payment details. That could result in an employee sending money to an attacker’s account.

The attacker isn’t simply asking the AI to repeat a fraudulent request. They’re trying to turn that request into the assistant’s recommendation.

How prompt injection works

Prompt injection means planting instructions in material an AI system is supposed to read, hoping it will follow those instructions instead of treating them as part of the material. When the instructions arrive through an outside source, such as an email or webpage, it’s often called indirect prompt injection.

The malicious instructions don’t have to appear as ordinary, readable paragraphs. Barracuda identified concealment techniques including comments in the email’s underlying HTML code, text made invisible through styling, encoded content, and invisible “zero-width” characters. These can obscure instructions from a person viewing the message while leaving content available for an AI system to process. Whether that content actually reaches the model depends on how the particular tool extracts and prepares the email.

That means this problem cannot be solved simply by asking people to look more carefully at their emails. Part of the defense must sit inside the tools handling those messages.

Apollo Raines, developer of the AI code review service ShipItClean, explains:

“The real flaw is that the model can’t tell the difference between text it’s supposed to read and instructions it’s supposed to follow. Stripping hidden content before it reaches the model is worth doing, and every vendor should do it. But it’s an arms race. Each new encoding trick is a new hole.”

He adds:

“People have learned to distrust the email. They haven’t learned to distrust their AI assistant. So, the defense has to live inside the tools. I’d go one step further: some of it has to live inside the model itself. Wrappers, filters, sandboxing and human sign-off on payments are all necessary.”

Before taking action

An assistant that summarizes messages could mislead you about which email deserves attention or what action it requires.

An assistant with additional permissions could create a more serious problem. Depending on its capabilities and safeguards, malicious instructions might try to make it carry out unauthorized actions or disclose sensitive information.

You don’t need to abandon AI tools that help with email. But you do need to consider what you trust them to do and what permissions you give them.

The familiar phishing advice still applies. When an assistant reads your inbox on your behalf, check its recommendations before acting:

  • Check the original message before acting on a recommendation involving money or sensitive information. If a summary tells you to pay an invoice, change account details, or share sensitive information, don’t treat the summary itself as verification.
  • Always verify payment changes through a separate, established channel. Contact the person or organization using details you already trust, rather than relying on information supplied in the suspicious message.
  • Keep your AI assistant’s permissions limited to what you need and, at work, what your organization allows. An assistant used to summarize emails should not need broad authority to carry out unrelated actions. Limiting access can reduce the consequences if it follows malicious instructions.
  • Require human approval for high-impact actions like payments and changes to vendor payment details. Approval should include checking the underlying request, not simply accepting the assistant’s recommendation.

items.summary: NVIDIA patched high-severity flaw CVE-2026-47483 in DCGM Exporter that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to exhaust server resources, crash GPU monitoring , and disrupt AI workloads. DCGM Exporter is a common monitoring tool for GPU servers and Kubernetes clusters. It reads details such as GPU model, temperature, memory use, power draw, errors, and workload activity, then serves the data in a Prometheus-friendly format over HTTP. A unique UUID also lists each GPU. If this endpoint is public, an outsider can map valuable hardware, watch busy periods, and learn details about the software and workloads around it. The weakness sits in Go profiling routes under /debug/pprof. These routes were meant to help developers inspect CPU and memory use. However, vulnerable builds exposed them without login checks or safe request limits. By sending many profiling requests at once, an attacker could cause uncontrolled memory and CPU use until the exporter slowed, stopped responding, or crashed. NVIDIA DCGM Exporter Bug Exposes NVIDIA rated the issue 8.2 out of 10 and classified it as CWE-770 , which covers resource allocation without proper limits. A crash would remove the live view of GPU health, errors, temperature, and use. The same resource pressure could also slow nearby AI tasks when the exporter lacks strict container or host limits. The researchers tested the resource exhaustion only in a controlled environment and did not target the public systems they found. Shodan scans found 2,100 exposed DCGM Exporter hosts revealing 12,000+ GPU UUIDs over unauthenticated HTTP (source : lava.security ) Lava Security researcher Michael Katchinskiy found the flaw while studying public DCGM Exporter systems. Four internet scans between March and May 2026 identified about 2,100 hosts serving metrics without authentication. They exposed more than 12,000 unique GPU identifiers across about 300 organizations. Around one quarter of the DCGM hosts also exposed the risky profiling routes. The visible hardware included H100, H200, B200, Blackwell Ultra B300, RTX 4090, and RTX 5090 GPUs. The United States accounted for 5,274 exposed GPUs, or 44 percent of the observed total. Exposed AI infrastructure uses both NVIDIA H100/H200 accelerators and consumer RTX 4090/5090 GPUs (source : lava.security ) Researchers also found customer-run endpoints on networks linked to GPU cloud providers, including Voltage Park, Lambda, Northern Data, DigitalOcean, and others. The providers helped alert customers after receiving the findings. The case shows why AI monitoring ports should receive the same care as other management services. Cyber Security News has previously covered NVIDIA GPU driver flaws that enable code execution and published an AI data center security checklist covering GPU, firmware, and management-layer risks. NVIDIA’s security bulletin directs DCGM Exporter users to install version 4.8.2 or later. Operators should also keep –enable-pprof disabled unless profiling is needed. Exposed GPU exporters appeared on 2,000+ hosts across nearly 300 organizations (source : lava.security ) Exporter, Prometheus, and Node Exporter services should bind to a private or loopback interface and accept traffic only from approved monitoring systems through firewall rules, cloud security groups, or Kubernetes NetworkPolicies. Security teams should review internet-facing port 9400, block public access to /debug/pprof, and inspect logs for repeated or long-running profiling requests. Sudden memory growth, CPU spikes, Prometheus scrape failures, or gaps in GPU alerts may signal probing or exploitation. Teams should confirm that patched containers are deployed across every GPU node, not merely updated in a registry or configuration file. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. items.title: Admin Password “123456” Led to 8.8 Million Danish CPR Data Breach
items.summary: A weak administrator password is linked to a major Danish data breach that exposed information tied to about 8.8 million national identification numbers . At least three accounts at Pays, an IT company on the island of Funen, reportedly used “123456”, including an administrator account. The case shows how poor security at a company with trusted access can place a national database at risk. Pays had permission to search Denmark’s Central Person Register, known as CPR. An attacker allegedly used that access to collect personal records rather than breaking directly into the register’s underlying systems. Danish CPR Breach Unfolded According to Politiken’s investigation , the hacker shared stolen data with the newspaper and claimed the password “123456” helped unlock access to CPR numbers and addresses. Politiken reported 8,749,975 records, explaining why coverage describes the breach as either 8.7 million or roughly 8.8 million. The reported data covered about 5.5 million living people and 3.3 million deceased people. Those rounded figures should not be read as an exact total. The CPR register holds personal information about people living in Denmark or previously registered there. The Copenhagen Post reported that the attacker gained access through a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly built two programs to retrieve CPR information and save it outside the system. These details remain attributed to the hacker’s account, not a published forensic report. Access reportedly began on September 10 and lasted 21 days and 17 hours. That lengthy window raises questions about whether monitoring controls could detect repeated searches or unusual data collection before millions of records were exposed. Pays Confirms Misuse of Authorized Access Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 that its lawful access to search the CPR system had been abused. Managing director and owner Sophie Laursen acknowledged the attack in an email, according to The Copenhagen Post. Private companies and associations can receive CPR access when they have a legitimate need, such as checking customer or member addresses. This arrangement makes the security of each approved organization important, because valid credentials can provide a route into sensitive public records. The pattern resembles the Veradigm third-party data breach , where stolen vendor credentials allowed an attacker to download patient information through an approved interface. The systems differ, but both cases show why trusted access needs close limits and oversight. Cybersecurity News previously covered research into passwords used in RDP attacks , with “123456” leading the reported list. That research concerns remote desktop access, not Denmark’s CPR system, but highlights how predictable passwords remain useful to attackers. Organizations handling identity data should block common passwords, require unique credentials and enable multifactor authentication. Former employee accounts should be disabled promptly. Access should also be limited to necessary records, with alerts for unusual search volumes and bulk downloads. The breach also underlines the need to review partner access regularly, rather than treating approval as a permanent safeguard. The hacker told Politiken there were no plans to sell or publish the information. That claim does not remove the privacy risk created by unauthorized copies of personal records. The available reporting does not establish that exposed information has already been used for fraud, and it should not present such misuse as confirmed. Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min. items.title: KFC Named in Gentlemen Ransomware Group’s Latest Breach Claim
items.summary: The Gentlemen ransomware group has allegedly claimed to have breached KFC, with a listing observed on October 10, 2026. The supplied alert identifies the target as United States KFC and places it in the hospitality sector. The claim remains unverified, and the available material does not establish a confirmed compromise of KFC’s U.S. systems. A public ransomware tracker also records KFC as being named by The Gentlemen on October 10. That supports the existence of the listing, rather than proving the reported intrusion. The supplied image shows KFC branding, the kfc.com domain, and a business description, but it contains no visible stolen files or technical evidence. The alert does not specify the amount of allegedly exposed data or the types of records involved. It also provides no entry method, ransom demand, affected systems, or evidence of file encryption. The October 10 observation date should therefore not be treated as the date attackers first entered a network. No KFC-specific malware hashes, attacker addresses, or verified attack timeline are provided. The image mainly describes KFC’s restaurant network, franchise model, sales, and suppliers. These business details do not demonstrate access to internal systems. The material does not identify whether the alleged target is a corporate network, a franchise operator, or another business connected to the brand. That scope remains an important unanswered question. The alert includes an ESIX score of 5.23, but supplies no explanation of its scoring method. The number cannot establish breach severity or confirm data theft. The supplied material and the sources reviewed for this report include no company confirmation, leaving the allegation pending independent verification. How The Gentlemen Operates Sophos tracks the operation behind The Gentlemen as GOLD SHERWOOD. Its researchers describe a ransomware service in which affiliates carry out attacks using the group’s tools. The operation uses double extortion, stealing data before encrypting files and then using the threat of publication to pressure victims into paying. In an analysis of 15 separate intrusions , Sophos found a repeated pattern involving rapid gains in access rights, legitimate remote access tools, data theft, and efforts to disable security controls. Some cases reached ransomware deployment within 24 hours of the first identified activity after compromise. These findings concern earlier cases, not the KFC allegation. Cyber Security News previously covered The Gentlemen’s efforts to disable endpoint detection and response tools and backup services . Attackers used vulnerable drivers and other utilities to stop security processes. They also changed Windows Defender settings and disrupted recovery tools, reducing the chance that defenders could detect the activity or restore encrypted systems. KFC’s parent company, Yum! Brands, previously disclosed a separate ransomware incident in January 2023. Cyber Security News reported that the attack disrupted systems, involved stolen information , and temporarily closed fewer than 300 restaurants in one market for one day. That historical incident does not confirm or explain the current claim. For security teams, Sophos recommends protecting remote access with multifactor authentication, patching exposed systems, watching changes to administrator accounts, and keeping backups protected. Investigators reviewing this allegation would need evidence tied to the affected organization, such as validated file samples, access logs, or a company statement. items.title: from plesiochronous to synchronous
items.summary: Up until the 1960s, telephone calls were carried as analog signals. There was a great deal of frequency division multiplexing onto open wire , and sometimes coaxial cables , but in the post-war period buried multipair telephone cables began to dominate. While the network was surprisingly functional—long distance calls from coast to coast were still quite intelligible—there were fundamental limitations to analog carriers. The quality of the call would degrade with each step, a problem that was much more acute for the sensitive digital connections that were already the apparent future of the telephone system. These were digital signals modulated over the top of telephone lines: the telephone system itself still handled them as analog calls, just ones that required special care for quality. During the Second World War, it became apparent that many of the long distance network's challenges could be greatly simplified by using digital signaling as the basis of the entire long distance system. In 1943, Bell Labs contributed to the design of an early encrypted voice communications system called SIGSALY. Unlike the "voice scramblers" and other analog techniques of the early phase of the war, SIGSALY was recognizably similar to modern encryption. The voice data was quantized into numerical values, so that digital arithmetic could be used to encode it. In the quest to build a cryptosystem for voice, Bell Labs incidentally built the first applied system for PCM digital voice transmission. After the war, it was an obvious next step to refine this technology and apply it to regular service. This didn't necessarily mean direct digital service, at least not at first: most subscriber loops remain analog to the present day. For the first years of the digital network, even the exchanges themselves switched purely analog signals. Between offices, though, encoding the analog channels into digital ones solved problems from audio quality, to microwave path overloading, to flexibility in traffic routing. Digitization became a core part of AT&T's concept of a carrier, just like frequency division multiplexing had in the 1920s. That's the background to the 1962 introduction of T-carrier , the first digital carrier in the commercial telephone system. The Digital Hierarchy Back in the article on T-carrier (which you should read if you are at all interested in this topic!), I explained that T1, T2, T3, etc. are hierarchically larger-bandwidth connections that carry the DS1, DS2, DS3, etc. digital signals respectively. Let's quickly review this hierarchical concept and, just to keep things interesting, add the further confusion of the D1 channel bank. A D1 channel bank is the physical piece of equipment that digitizes 24 voice channels and multiplexes them into a DS1 signal, which will be carried over T1 carrier. Similarly, four DS1 signals can be combined into a DS2 signal and carried over T2. Seven DS2 signals can be combined into a single DS3 signal and carried over T3. And so on, at least as far as they were able to get with the technology of the time. The DS2 level maps generally to the D2 channel bank, but that relationship can be confusing as the subsequently developed channel banks added features as well as capacity. The D2 channel bank could multiplex 96 channels onto a DS2 signal, but it also increased the overall quality of the audio channel to meet the technical requirements for general mixed toll service (the D1 had originally only been approved for conventional voice channels, not other applications like data-grade leased lines). In order to make that improvement, the D2 had to reduce the amount of quantization noise introduced into the signal. The D1 channel bank had used PCM audio with seven bits per sample, and calculations showed that eight bits per sample would be required for a toll-grade connection 1 . In a way, that looked easy: DS1 already used 8-bit units. But the eighth bit, not used as part of the PCM sample, was reserved for signaling purposes. No bother: the D1 channel bank hadn't really used the full signaling bandwidth anyway, so it could comfortably be reduced to meet a compromise position. The D2 channel bank used 8 bits for most PCM samples, but every six frames the last bit of each sample was reserved for signaling use rather than audio. This created a slight increase in quantization noise, and a significant decrease in signaling rate, but the resulting numbers for both fell within acceptable margins. A perfect compromise, but one that feels technically inelegant: in a sense, the D2 channel bank used 7.833 bits per sample. Ouch. This must have given the Bell System's engineers similar discomfort, but the aesthetic offense was worth it for backwards-compatibility. By the time the D2 channel bank was fielded in 1970, there were a huge number of D1 channel banks and T1 connections in service. Backwards-compatibility to existing T1 lines was a firm requirement. The D2 multiplexed 96 channels, four times a D1, and could carry those channels over four T1 links—in fact, initially, this was only the option. T2 and subsequent carriers were not fielded until after the D2. This backwards compatibility provided an upgrade path, as well as a way to subdivide the 96-channel capacity. You might realize that it is also a completely alternate explanation of the "hierarchy." You might wonder why the multipliers at the levels of the hierarchy are so inconsistent—24, 4, 7, 6. Reading the thing about signaling bits in every six samples above might have stirred deep memories of a concept called "robbed-bit signaling," a general concept of stealing occasional bits for other purposes that was widely used with T1. These are all smells, indications that a system was not architected , but grown . The "digital hierarchy" of T1, T2, T3, etc. is not some elegantly-designed system, at least not nearly as much as T4-era Bell Laboratories Record articles like to make it sound. It's mostly a result of happenstance, as the history of the Dn channel banks shows: each new channel bank, the D3, the D4, was designed to carry many more channels than those before. They were also required to be backwards-compatible with the use of the older channel banks and carriers. This process of exponential improvement with backwards compatibility led to the digital hierarchy as a natural consequence, not as a designed outcome. Plesiochronicity This emergent concept of layers of successively larger muxes explains the digital hierarchy, but we now need to consider the problem of timing and synchronization. In any system based on digital sampling, you have to be aware at the point at which those samples are taken in order to combine multiple signals. Consider the scenario where several simultaneous phone calls are being combined into a single digital mux for transmission. When the phone calls reach a D1 (or D2, D3, etc) channel bank, it samples all of the inputs at an appropriate time to build its DS1 (or higher) output stream. Nothing about this case is particularly complicated, except that it does require that all of the calls involved in the digital stream are sampled under the control of the same clock. But what about cases where lines need to be digitized in different locations? Say you have two smaller offices in a city, that need to deliver inter-office traffic to a tandem in the next city over. An obvious approach would be to digitize the calls in each of their local offices, send them as digital signals to one of the offices (perhaps the city's main downtown exchange), and then combine all of those digital signals together to be sent to the tandem switch. Doing this with channel banks wasn't very desirable: you would actually need to convert the calls back to analog, and then back to digital, in order to relay them from the first digital leg to the second. The first digital telephone leads were like this: completely point-to-point, without the possibility of switching or routing in the digital realm. That wasn't so big of a limitation early on when all of the switches were analog and digital leads just made the lines between them denser, but it prevented the construction of the fully digital network that Bell Labs envisioned. What was clearly needed was some sort of mux that could take four DS1s, already in that form, and combine them into a DS2. Repeat this for the higher levels as well, and you have the basis of a system that can combine and separate traffic as needed to meet the level of demand between various offices. But what about the sample timing? If you have four DS1 streams from four different places, at least back in the 1970s, they are not going to be synchronized. The four D1 channel banks would each be operating on their own sample clocks, and because of the imperfection of the physical world some of these clocks would run slightly faster or slower than others. When our four DS1 streams arrived at our notional multiplexer, the four streams would be not only out of phase, they would actually run at slightly different speeds. We can imagine a lot of modern solutions to this problem, probably by buffering relatively large blocks of samples in memory and then transmitting out of that buffer. In the '70s, things weren't so simple: first, memory was expensive and slow compared to the bitrates involved, and second, the latency involved in such extensive buffering was not considered acceptable in a network that had previously been all-analog and thus had no more latency than that implied by the speed of light. The solution to this problem, the Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy or PDH, is not easy to understand from our contemporary perspective. Many textbooks on networking and communications make some nod to PDH, but it's often short and cursory, and leaves you with a nagging feeling that the whole thing doesn't make much sense. PDH is hard to relate to for two reasons: first, it was developed to solve a set of problems that (due to broader technical advancements) we no longer have. Second, even within those constraints, it is a solution that has been obsoleted by newer approaches. PDH is not something that anyone would design today, and in retrospect, it's probably best to think of it as a hack. PDH was an interim measure, if you will, that bridged a gap between the development of digital channel banks and the later development of a good approach to synchronizing a digital network. It would have been more convenient if those two systems had been designed at the same time, but in practice, they weren't: digital long distance lines were in common use a solid decade before AT&T had a reasonable architecture for a digital network. You can already see that they were thinking through these requirements in the late 1960s, leading to the concept of the PDH as a hierarchical network architecture, but most of the actual technology to provide that network was built later, in the '70s and '80s. For a while, there was just, you know, something that worked. A duct tape fix. Conceptual bailing wire. So what even was the PDH? It is helpful to start by defining the word "plesiochronous," which every textbook has to do since the term was invented by Bell Labs to describe their design. I will spare the roots, but plesiochronous means "almost synchronized" or "approximately synchronized." And that's what the PDH was: it was a synchronous digital system with some slop. There was a little wiggle room. A DS1 signal is 1.544 Mbps, so if you multiplex four of them, you might expect 6.176 Mbps. You would be wrong: a DS2 is actually 6.312 Mbps. The overhead here comes from the plesio part of plesiochronous. To understand how that works, we should look at the design of the multiplexer from the beginning. AT&T practice would call a multiplexer from the DS1 level to the DS2 level an M12, for, well, multiplexer from 1 to 2. In practice M13s seem to have been more common equipment, which were often implemented internally as seven M12s feeding one M23. In any case, the M12 takes in four different DS1 streams and then bit-interleaves them, such that every 4th bit of the output is the next bit from one of the inputs. This is simple to reason about and has the advantage that virtually no buffering ever happens. But what if one of the inputs is running slightly fast, and another slightly slow? The first thing to know is that the output stream is intentionally slightly faster than all of the inputs. A typical PDH system allowed a 50 PPM plus or minus variation in the rate of the inputs, which means that the output had to be at least 50 PPM fast relative to the sum of the inputs. That way, the multiplexer will never "fall behind" because an input is providing bits faster than the output can interleave them. The other thing to know is that the multiplexer must perform a function known as either stuffing or justification. It is said that the term justification was introduced within AT&T because it sounded more technical, while stuffing was more popular with the actual engineers. Certain parts of each outgoing frame are defined (by standard) as stuffable, and they're sometimes called gaps. These are sections where the multiplexer is allowed to either include real data, or to include some nonsense data called stuffing bits (or, if you want to sound more technical, justification bits ). By choosing to either include real data or stuffing in the gaps, the multiplexer can actually adjust the "real" output data rate up or down. That way, it converges onto the correct average (the sum of the inputs) despite the "timing noise" of the inputs varying slightly up and down in real speed. If that didn't make sense to you, here's a different way to think about the same thing: we can imagine the DS2 output frame as consisting of four "slots" into which the four DS1 input frames are inserted (this isn't quite intuitive because they are interleaved bit-by-bit, but the math works out the same). Under the PDH design, these slots are all slightly wider than the input frames, so that there is "free space" for the input frames to be shifted a bit in either direction or stretched out. That allows the multiplexer to "catch up" on a fast input or to "draw out" the frames from a slow input. Thinking about it in terms of a wide slot that you can place the input into as desired also gives more value to the term "justification:" you can shift bits around, or add extra space in between them, just like you would to justify text. The actual implementation of this idea is pretty complicated, because the demultiplexer on the other end needs to know which bits were stuffed so that they can be discarded. That's why PDH specified gaps at fixed positions: the control signaling included a set of flags that indicated whether the fixed gaps were used for data or stuffing. When the multiplexer decided whether or not to use a stuffable bit (based on whether or not the input was getting ahead of the output mux), it also had to store that decision for the end of the frame so that the flag could be set correctly. PDH wasn't an elegant solution, but it was a solution, and multiplexers were designed up to the DS4 level based on the PDH approach. We all owe PDH a huge thanks for providing the clunky stopgap that allowed the construction of a nationwide digital telephone network. That said, well, it had quite a few downsides. First, PDH was never all that well standardized. Researching PDH is tricky because there aren't a lot of documents that provide conclusive detail about the actual implementation in the US, mostly just summaries, conceptual sketches, and examples from Europe. As far as I can tell 2 , Western Electric never really offered a standalone PDH multiplexer. Larger integrated systems from Western Electric (like, say, a microwave carrier equipment bay) might include a PDH multiplexer, but it's not clear to me if WE even made them—the advertisements and pricing information I can find for PDH multiplexers are from other vendors like Farinon and NEC. In North American practice, it doesn't seem like PDH was ever robustly standardized, and there were implementation differences between equipment from different manufacturers. That's probably one of the reasons for the scarcity of information on PDH equipment: you wouldn't usually buy a single PDH multiplexer, but instead would specify a specific model as part of a larger system. That meant that the PDH network was far less flexible than AT&T had hoped. The problem was even bigger when you looked overseas: AT&T tended to field the best thing that Bell Labs and Western Electric could come up with, and then promulgate that as a standard later on. The European telcos tended not to adopt new American developments until they were mature, giving them the opportunity to make standards before any equipment was in place. Thus the European versions of US telephone carriers are often a bit better, and PDH is no exception. In fact, the US, Europe, and Japan used three different hierarchies for PDH signaling. The European standard put more channels into a stream (the "E1" at about 2 Mbps), and used a consistent multiplier of 4 for each level. European PDH practices even got a complete published standard from CCITT. The Japanese system used the same DS1 standard as the US but with different multipliers (4, 5, 3, 4 instead of 4, 7, 6). PDH could thus not be used for international calling without completely remuxing everything. Another shortcoming of PDH had to do with that remuxing. The decision to bit-interleave the input frames together, stuff some bits, and then put flags on the bit stuffing into the interleaved stream, meant that a PDH multiplexer effectively "scrambled" the input streams. If you had, say, a DS3 stream and wanted to extract a single voice channel from it, you had a lot of work in front of you. It simply wasn't feasible with the electronics of the era to analyze the stream to determine the interleaving and stuffing bits at each level. Instead, you would have to put the DS3 through demuxers all the way back down to the bottom of the hierarchy, pull out the channel you wanted, and then remux it all the way back up. Pulling a single channel out of a DS3 could require two 11.5 foot tall equipment bays, and even further quantization noise due to the nature of the robbed bit scheme. Two things happened that pushed PDH to its limit: first, fiber optics. AT&T was famously a late adopter of fiber, and 1970s documents on the digital hierarchy talked about conveying it over T-carrier, microwave, and coaxial. We have talked about coaxial before , but L-carrier was an analog system. Digital coaxial did emerge as the T3, T4, and T5 carriers, but these were relatively short range and mostly only saw use on shorter inter-office links. Things were changing, though: by the time DS3 equipment was appearing in telephone exchanges, competitors were already evaluating fiber optics. AT&T dipped their toe in the water in 1976, with an experimental DS3 fiber optic link in Atlanta. The next year, both AT&T and competitor GTE had DS3 fiber lines in service (in Chicago and the LA area, respectively). Outside manufacturers started offering T1-over-fiber equipment around 1980, and in 1983 AT&T had a multimode fiber system stretching from New York to Washington. Sparing the (fascinating) story of the business and competitive factors, the writing was on the wall: fiber was the future of long lines. AT&T engineers realized that the PDH design did not scale well to the enormous capacities that fiber could reach, and even worse, that complex fiber networks would require exactly the capability that PDH lacked: extracting single channels from the mux. Besides, despite the systems in use, there really wasn't any standard for conveying PDH signals over fiber, which only meant more compatibility issues. Something else was coming over the horizon in 1983: divestiture. The complete reorganization of AT&T in the mid-1980s, breaking the Baby Bells up into independent companies, made the interoperability problems with PDH much more severe. Bell operating companies (BOCs) would need to easily exchange traffic with both AT&T Long Lines and, eventually, with other BOCs and competitive phone companies and long distance carriers. That was very difficult when that traffic was mostly conveyed in loosely-standardized black-box muxes. Many aspects of US telephony were loosely standardized prior to the Bell System breakup because AT&T ran the entire network and didn't really need to cooperate with others. After 1984, the US became a lot more like Europe: for technology to be widely adopted, it would need to have a well-defined, published standard. That meant a standards body—the part of AT&T that had formerly published the practices used by all of the BOCs, after divestiture, became an independent company called Bellcore.
